  - Shareholders/SRI investors: climate adaptation, biodiversity, natural resources, decarbonization; sustainable finance/investments; standard ESG policies; inclusion and diversity; employee well-being; development and digitalization; ESG integration in strategy; gender pay gap; workers’ rights and governance.
  - People (employees): customer-perceived image; employment protection in restructuring; youth recruitment; recognition, pride, merit, autonomy, pay; talent development/retention; training and growth; well-being and work-life balance; job satisfaction; performance assessment transparency; awareness of D&I policies; customer satisfaction drivers; ESG initiatives/products. Survey reached over 72,000 people.
  - Trade unions: employment protection amid digitalization; community support; financial inclusion; non-financial reporting; environmental issues and biodiversity; renewables and sustainable mobility for employees; youth unemployment in Southern regions; gender pay gap.
  - Suppliers: environmental topics, biodiversity, circular economy; labor protection, health and safety, diversity & inclusion, well-being across the supply chain; supplier relationship management.
- Notes compliance with Legislative Decree 125/2024: employee representatives engaged in the assessment and involved in Board approval of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Summarizes the context analysis informing IRO mapping, drawing on updated 2024 external sources: ESG indices (DJSI, Morningstar ESG, Euronext ESG, CDP 2023); global standards/reports (WEF Global Risks, OECD Guidelines, BSR, WBCSD, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights); EU regulations and directives referenced by ESRS (CSDDD 2024/1760, SFDR, CRR Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law); and sector-specific materials (SASB Materiality Map, S&P and Fitch research, OECD guidance for institutional investors).

nodes.title: Context analysis
nodes.heading: 2.3.3 Context analysis
nodes.start_phrase: In order to map IROs, the Group analysed the context in which it defines and implements its business activities and relationships.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of stakeholder engagement and key sustainability topics raised across shareholders/investors, employees, trade unions, and suppliers.
- Shareholders/ESG investors’ priorities: climate adaptation, biodiversity, natural resources, decarbonisation; sustainable finance; standard sustainability policies; diversity and inclusion; employee well-being; digitalisation; ESG integration in strategy; gender pay gap; workers’ rights and corporate governance.
- Employees (Italy and abroad) engagement via interviews and a large-scale survey (>72,000 people) on: customer perception of the Group, employment safeguards during restructuring, youth recruitment, recognition and compensation, talent development/retention, training and growth opportunities, well-being and work-life balance, job satisfaction, transparency of performance assessments, awareness of Group policies (e.g., D&I), customer satisfaction drivers, and ESG initiatives/products.
- Trade unions’ focus: employment protection amid digitalisation, community support, financial inclusion, non-financial reporting, environmental issues and biodiversity, ecological transition (renewables and sustainable mobility), youth unemployment in Southern regions, and gender pay gap.
- Suppliers’ concerns: environmental topics, biodiversity and circular economy; job protection, health and safety, D&I and well-being across the supply chain; and supplier relationship management.
- Compliance and governance: engagement of employee representatives under Legislative Decree 125/2024 in the double materiality assessment and their subsequent involvement in Board approval of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Context analysis underpinning IRO mapping draws on 2024-updated external standards and benchmarks (e.g., DJSI, Morningstar ESG, Euronext ESG, CDP, WEF Global Risks, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, CSDDD/EU Directive 2024/1760, SFDR, CRR “Pillar 3”, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law), sector frameworks (SASB, S&P, Fitch, OECD guidance for institutional investors, MSCI ESG Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy/ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD, PRB, IFRS), internal documents (Business Plan 2022–2025, Code of Ethics, prior Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, governance communications), benchmarking peers, and stakeholder feedback.
- Double materiality scope covers own operations and the full upstream and downstream value chain.
- Identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) aligned to ESRS, considering how the Group’s operating model and strategic decisions create impacts and related financial effects.
- Illustrative IROs: ESG-weak exposures increasing credit/market risk via concentration; ESG programmes, donations and controls enhancing reputation and stakeholder trust; ESG criteria and strategies enabling product range expansion in line with sustainability goals.
- Materiality assessment methodology: formalised internally; combines internal analysis, interviews with operating structures, and stakeholder input; conducted simultaneously for impact and financial materiality.
- Impact materiality metrics and scoring: scale (severity), scope (breadth), irremediable character, and likelihood (for potential impacts), with scores assigned and averaged against pre-set thresholds.
- Tailored assessment for the value chain, identifying sectors most exposed to adverse impacts for each sustainability topic.
- Calculation rules: positive actual impacts = average of scale and scope; negative actual impacts = average of scale, scope, and irremediable character; potential impacts multiply likelihood by the relevant average (positive: scale+scope; negative: scale+scope+irremediable).

nodes.title: Identification of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.3.4 Identification of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The analyses conducted identified and assessed, for each ESRS, the Group's possible IROs, applied to own operations and the value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement detailing the Group’s approach to double materiality in line with ESRS.
- Sources used for the assessment:
  - External frameworks and expectations: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, MSCI ESG Industry Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy and ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD recommendations (especially Climate-Related Risks, Opportunities, and Financial Impacts), Principles for Responsible Banking, and IFRS for sustainability reporting.
  - Internal sources: 2022–2025 Business Plan, Code of Ethics, prior three years’ Consolidated Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, top management communications, Shareholders’ Meeting minutes, and company policies.
  - Sector benchmarking of Italian and international financial groups and stakeholder engagement feedback.
- Scope: Assessment covers own operations plus upstream and downstream value chain.
- IRO identification: For each ESRS topic, potential impacts, risks, and opportunities are identified across operations and the value chain; impact and financial materiality are assessed concurrently.
- Link between impacts and risks/opportunities:
  - Negative examples: Financing/investing in weak ESG sectors/countries may increase credit/market risks due to concentration in high-risk geographies or activities.
  - Positive examples: ESG initiatives, donations, programs, and controls can enhance brand and stakeholder trust; integrating ESG criteria into financing/investment can expand product offerings aligned with sustainability goals.
- Governance and methodology:
  - Materiality assessment aligned with ESRS metrics, validated via interviews with internal functions and stakeholder processes.
  - Methodology formalized in internal regulations.
- Impact assessment metrics and scoring:
  - Metrics: scale (severity), scope (reach), irremediable character (ability to remediate), and likelihood (for potential impacts, across time horizons).
  - Each impact receives a score; downstream analysis identifies counterparties/sectors most exposed to adverse impacts by sustainability issue.
- Materiality determination:
  - Materiality is defined by exceeding a threshold based on averaged metric scores.
  - Positive actual impacts: average of scale and scope.
  - Negative actual impacts: average of scale, scope, and irremediable character.
  - Potential positive impacts: likelihood multiplied by average of scale and scope.
  - Potential negative impacts: likelihood multiplied by average of scale, scope, and irremediable character.

nodes.title: Assessment of the materiality of IROs
nodes.heading: 2.3.5 Assessment of the materiality of IROs
nodes.start_phrase: The materiality of IROs was assessed by conducting an internal analysis based on metrics aligned with the ESRS requirements, discussed and consolidated through interviews with the Group's internal operating structures and, as described earlier, through a stakeholder management process.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: This section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement explains the Group’s double materiality assessment under CSRD/ESRS, covering how it identifies, evaluates, prioritizes, and governs sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across own operations and the full value chain (upstream and downstream).

- Reference frameworks and inputs: The assessment integrates external standards and expectations (OECD Guidelines, MSCI ESG Materiality Map, GRI Sector Standards, Bank of Italy/ECB supervisory expectations, TCFD, Principles for Responsible Banking, IFRS for sustainability reporting, EFRAG IG 1) with internal sources (2022–2025 Business Plan, Code of Ethics, prior Non-financial Statements, Financial Statements, top management communications, Shareholders’ Meeting minutes, policies), peer benchmarking, and stakeholder engagement.

- Scope and identification of IROs: IROs are mapped for each ESRS topic across own operations and value chain. Impacts derive from the business model and strategy; risks/opportunities arise from those impacts, dependencies, and sustainability issues. Examples include:
  - Credit/market risks from exposure to sectors/countries with weak ESG profiles.
  - Reputation and trust benefits from ESG initiatives, donations, programs, and controls.
  - Product and customer expansion through ESG-aligned financing/investment criteria.

- Impact materiality methodology: Impacts are scored using ESRS-aligned metrics—scale, scope, irremediable character, and likelihood (for potential impacts)—with thresholds based on average scores. Potential positive/negative impacts incorporate likelihood in the materiality calculation. For potential human rights–related negative impacts, impact severity outweighs likelihood as required by ESRS. Downstream analysis reflects portfolio exposure by sector/country. Time horizons (short: 1 year; medium: up to 5 years; long: >5 years) are considered.

- Financial materiality methodology: Assessed in parallel with impact materiality and linked where relevant. Quantitative assessments leverage existing risk data/processes (e.g., ICAAP, stress scenarios, projections, prudential risk frameworks), inherent risk (pre-mitigation) exposures by sector/country and financial asset class, and potential operating losses/penalties tied to sustainability issues. Opportunities are aligned with budget and Business Plan targets for ESG products. Financial risk/opportunity metrics include magnitude, likelihood, and time horizon.

- Qualitative assessment: Complements quantitative work using internal policies, strategies, and initiatives, notably the 2022–2025 Business Plan.

- Governance and decision-making: The IRO map is consolidated via internal structures, validated through stakeholder management processes, and discussed with the Steering Committee and the Risks and Sustainability Committee, which support the Board of Directors’ approval.

- Material topics outcome: All ESRS macro-topics are deemed material except Water and Marine Resources. Not all sub-topics and sub-sub-topics are material. The section highlights materiality outcomes and boundaries for:
  - E1 Climate Change (mitigation, adaptation, energy),
  - E2 Pollution (air, soil, microplastics),
  - E4 Biodiversity and Ecosystems (direct drivers of biodiversity loss),
  - E5 Circular Economy (resource inflows/use, resource outflows in products/services, waste),
  across own operations, upstream, and downstream, with both impact and financial materiality considered.

nodes.title: Consolidating and sharing the list of sustainability matters material for the Group
nodes.heading: 2.3.6 Consolidating and sharing the list of sustainability matters material for the Group
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has a structured decision -making process designed to consolidate and verify material impacts, risks and opportunities.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Intesa Sanpaolo’s approach to sustainability materiality and governance. It defines scenario time horizons for risk and planning (short: 1 year, medium: up to 5 years, long: over 5 years) and describes a structured process to identify, review, and consolidate impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) through a double materiality assessment aligned with CSRD/ESRS. All ESRS macro-topics are deemed material except Water and Marine Resources, though not every sub-topic/sub-sub-topic is material; materiality is mapped across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains for environmental (climate, energy, pollution, biodiversity, circular economy), social (own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and governance (business conduct, whistleblowing, lobbying, supplier practices, compliance/training) areas. The results were reviewed by internal functions, discussed with the Steering Committee and the Risks and Sustainability Committee, and support Board approval. The analysis confirms the resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model, with actions planned to mitigate ESG risks and capture opportunities over the long term. The governance section details the one-tier model with a Board of Directors and a Management Control Committee, roles of the Chair (non-executive) and the Managing Director/CEO, and four internal Board committees (Nomination, Remuneration, Risks and Sustainability, Related Parties). The Board has 19 directors (18 non-executive, 1 executive), appointed in April 2022 for three years, meeting suitability and independence requirements.

nodes.title: Governance structure
nodes.heading: 2.4 Governance structure
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company Intesa Sanpaolo has adopted the “one -tier” management and control model, whereby management and control duties are performed, respectively, by the Board of Directors and the Management Control Committee set up within it, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement outlines the Group’s analysis of impacts, risks and opportunities informing its materiality assessment, confirming the resilience of Intesa Sanpaolo’s strategy and business model. ESG-related negative impacts are being managed through current and planned actions to mitigate risks, capture opportunities and support long‑term sustainability.

- Governance model: Intesa Sanpaolo adopts a one-tier system with management by the Board of Directors and control by the Management Control Committee within the Board, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting. Detailed governance and remuneration information is available in dedicated reports on the Bank’s website.

- Board roles and responsibilities: 
  - The Board provides strategic guidance and supervision, deciding on significant corporate actions and transactions, with certain major decisions subject to shareholder approval.
  - The Chair is non-executive, oversees and organizes Board work, and does not perform management functions.
  - The Managing Director and CEO, also General Manager, oversees company management within powers aligned to the Board’s strategic guidelines.

- Control and advisory bodies:
  - Management Control Committee: five independent Directors, performing control functions and acting as the internal control and audit committee (Legislative Decree 39/2010).
  - Board committees: Nomination; Remuneration; Risks and Sustainability; Transactions with Related Parties.

- Board composition and suitability: As of 29 April 2022, the Board has 19 members (18 non-executive, 1 executive) appointed for a three-year term. Directors meet legal and bylaw suitability requirements, including independence of mind under banking rules.

- Business conduct materiality focus (G1): The Statement frames impacts, risks and financial/materiality outcomes across the value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream) for subtopics including:
  - Protection of whistleblowers
  - Political engagement and lobbying activities
  - Management of supplier relationships, including payment practices
  - Prevention and detection (e.g., training) and incident management

nodes.title: Role and composition of the administration, management and control bodies and of sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 2.4.1 Role and composition of the administration, management and control bodies and of sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company Intesa Sanpaolo has adopted the “one -tier” management and control model, whereby management and control duties are performed, respectively, by the Board of Directors and the Management Control Committee set up within it, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting.
nodes.summary:
- The chapter introduces the impacts, risks and opportunities identified through analysis that informed the materiality assessment, confirming the resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model. It notes that potential negative ESG impacts are being managed through existing and planned actions aimed at risk mitigation, opportunity capture and long‑term sustainability.
- Governance structure: Intesa Sanpaolo adopts a one‑tier model in which the Board of Directors (management) and the Management Control Committee within it (control), both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting, perform oversight and control functions.
- Board of Directors: responsible for strategic guidance and major corporate decisions (ordinary and extraordinary), with certain significant matters submitted to the Shareholders’ Meeting. The Chair is non‑executive and oversees Board work without managerial functions. The Managing Director and CEO, also the General Manager, supervises management in line with Board directives.
- Management Control Committee: composed of five independent directors; performs control functions and acts as the internal control and audit committee pursuant to Legislative Decree 39/2010.
- Board committees: Nomination Committee; Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee; Committee for Transactions with Related Parties.
- Board composition: as of 29 April 2022, 19 directors elected for a three‑year term; 18 non‑executive and 1 executive (the MD/CEO). Directors meet suitability requirements, including independence of mind; further details on governance, diversity and remuneration are available in the Bank’s published reports.
- Governance materiality focus (G1 Business conduct): coverage of subtopics such as corporate culture, protection of whistleblowers, political engagement and lobbying, management of supplier relationships and payment practices, and prevention/detection including training and incidents. The content references assessment of positive/negative impacts and financial and impact materiality across own operations, upstream and downstream value chains.

nodes.title: Board of Directors: role and main characteristics
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.1 Board of Directors: role and main characteristics
nodes.start_phrase: The Board of Directors is responsible for exercising the Company’s guidance and strategic supervision duties and for resolving on all the most important corporate actions,
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines how identified impacts, risks and opportunities informed the materiality assessment, confirming the Group’s strategic and business-model resilience and the management of ESG risks through current and planned actions to mitigate risks, seize opportunities and support long-term sustainability.

It details the sustainability and corporate governance framework: Intesa Sanpaolo adopts a one-tier model with management by the Board of Directors and control by the Management Control Committee within the Board, both appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting. The Board provides strategic guidance and approves major corporate actions; the Chair is non-executive and oversees Board activities; the Managing Director/CEO, also General Manager, oversees management in line with Board guidelines. The Management Control Committee, composed of five independent directors, performs control functions and acts as the internal control and audit committee under Legislative Decree 39/2010.

Four internal Board committees support oversight: Nomination; Remuneration; Risks and Sustainability; and Transactions with Related Parties. As of the 29 April 2022 Shareholders’ Meeting, the Board comprises 19 members (18 non-executive, 1 executive), all meeting suitability and independence-of-mind requirements; detailed governance and remuneration information is available in dedicated reports on the Bank’s website.

The text also introduces the “Business conduct” material topic (G1), listing sub-topics such as protection of whistleblowers, political engagement and lobbying, management of supplier relationships and payment practices, and prevention/detection including training and incident management, with references to positive/negative impacts and materiality across own operations, upstream and downstream value chains.

nodes.title: Composition of the Board of Directors
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.2 Composition of the Board of Directors
nodes.start_phrase: The Ordinary Shareholders' Meeting of 29 April 2022 set the number of members of the Board of Directors at 19, appointing directors for the three -year term of office on the basis of the lists submitted by shareholders.
nodes.summary:
- Confirms the Group’s ESG materiality assessment, outlining key impacts, risks and opportunities; states the strategy and business model are resilient, with actions in place to mitigate ESG risks and capture opportunities.
- Describes the governance structure: a one-tier model with a Board of Directors and a Management Control Committee appointed by the Shareholders’ Meeting; Chair is non-executive; the Managing Director/CEO is also General Manager and manages within the Board’s strategic guidelines.
- Lists Board committees and their roles/composition: Nomination, Remuneration, Risks and Sustainability, and Transactions with Related Parties; all have five non-executive members, majority independent, and are chaired by independent Directors; the Related Parties Committee is entirely independent.
- Details Board composition and independence: 19 Directors (18 non-executive, 1 executive); all meet suitability and independence of mind; 14 independent (74%); minority shareholders hold 5 seats (26%) and are represented across committees; no employee representatives; no recent similar roles in public administration among Directors.
- Highlights diversity and competence policies: commitment to diversity in experience, age, gender, and international orientation; legal gender quota (≥40%) met with 8 women (42%); strong female presence on committees (e.g., 80% on Related Parties Committee) and chairing of Risks & Sustainability and Nomination Committees; Board assesses its composition as adequate.
- Outlines Group-wide approach to appointing senior officers of subsidiaries, ensuring diverse, fit-for-purpose profiles aligned with each subsidiary’s activities and risks, informed by annual self-assessments.
- Notes professional qualifications: at least four Directors must be registered statutory auditors; currently 9 Directors (47%), including all Management Control Committee members, meet this.
- Presents the Board’s Skills Directory (2022–2024) and prevalence of key competencies among Directors: financial/ non-financial reporting literacy (95%), strategy (95%), governance (95%), financial markets (100%), banking products (89%), regulation (84%), internal controls (74%), risk management (79%), and information/digital technology (16%).
- Introduces Governance Topic G1: Business conduct, with sub-topics including whistleblower protection, political engagement and lobbying, supplier relationship and payment practices, and prevention/detection with training and incident management; considers impact and financial materiality across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains.

nodes.title: Competences and diversity
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.3 Competences and diversity
nodes.start_phrase: According to Intesa Sanpaolo's Articles of Association, the Board shall adopt the necessary measures to ensure that each Director, and the Board as a whole, have a continually adequate level of diversification,
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and independence: The Board of Directors meets and exceeds independence requirements (14 independent directors, 74%). All committees consist of five non-executive members; most have a majority of independents, and the Related Parties Committee is entirely independent. All committees are chaired by independent directors.
- Minority representation: Minority shareholders hold 5 board seats (26%) and are present in all committees; they chair the Management Control Committee and the Related Parties Committee. No employee representatives sit on the Board. No director held comparable public administration roles in the two years prior to appointment.
- Diversity and composition: The Board pursues diversified composition in experience, age, gender, and international outlook. Shareholders were guided in 2022 to ensure broad gender and age diversity and comprehensive skills. Legal gender quota (at least two-fifths) is met: 8 women (42%) on the Board; strong female presence in committees and female chairs for the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Nomination Committee. The Board deems its composition and committee balance adequate.
- Group-wide appointments: Senior officers of subsidiaries are appointed following uniform Group policies emphasizing diversity (age, gender, seniority, geography, international orientation) and alignment to each entity’s business and risk profile, informed by subsidiaries’ annual self-assessments.
- Professional qualifications: At least four directors must be registered statutory auditors with relevant experience; currently 9 directors (47%), including all members of the Management Control Committee, meet this criterion.
- Skills and expertise: A 2022–2024 “Skills Directory” defines the optimal competencies. High levels of very good/distinctive expertise are reported in financial statement analysis and strategic planning (95%), financial markets (100%), banking products (89%), regulations (84%), internal controls (74%), risk management (79%), banking business and sector strategies (95%), and socio-economic/market knowledge of operating geographies (74%). Only 16% report very strong IT/digital expertise. ESG knowledge is strong: 84% report very good/distinctive expertise and integration into strategy.
- External engagements: Several directors serve on boards of universities, foundations, and non-profits across culture, health, environment, poverty, circular economy, and nutrition. The chair of the Risks and Sustainability Committee also chairs the same committee in another listed company.
- Ongoing assessment and renewal: Following the 2022 renewal, the Board confirmed the adequacy and balance of its composition. Guidelines for the optimal qualitative-quantitative composition ahead of the April 2025 renewal are available on the Group website.
- Induction and training: Comprehensive onboarding and ongoing training are overseen by the Nomination Committee, tailored by initial and annual self-assessments, with options for individual requests. In 2024, 11 induction sessions covered ESG topics, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA. The Board rated the program very positively.
- Information access and oversight: Directors have a regularly updated electronic repository of governance documents, regulatory references, supervisory correspondence, and accounting positions. Corporate control functions provide periodic reports on activities, findings, and remediation proposals, including anti-corruption and AML matters.
- Next section header: Introduction to the allocation of ESG responsibilities across Intesa Sanpaolo’s bodies and structures (“Sustainability governance”).

nodes.title: Board induction
nodes.heading: 2.4.1.4 Board induction
nodes.start_phrase: The skills and expertise were subsequently strengthened and supplemented on the basis of training programmes as well as of intensive induction activities for both the new directors (onboarding) and the entire Board.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Board composition, expertise, and governance in Intesa Sanpaolo’s sustainability context.
- Directors’ competencies: 95% with strong banking and risk-management knowledge; 74% with knowledge of socio-economic/market dynamics; 84% declaring very good/distinctive ESG expertise and integration into strategy.
- Directors’ external roles include boards of major universities and non-profits (art, culture, health, environment, poverty, circular economy, nutrition); one director chairs the Risks and Sustainability Committee and holds the same role in another listed company.
- Post-2022 renewal assessment confirms diverse, well-balanced Board and Committees; guidelines for the optimal qualitative-quantitative Board composition ahead of April 2025 renewal are available on the Group website.
- Board induction and training: structured onboarding and ongoing programs led by the Chair with Nomination Committee support; content covers business areas, Group dynamics, risk management, regulatory/self-regulatory frameworks, and strategic topics; individualized training available.
- Annual Board self-assessment evaluates and refines induction quality and effectiveness.
- In 2024, 11 induction sessions addressed ESG, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA; feedback was extremely positive on scope, depth, and relevance.
- Board members have access to a regularly updated digital repository of governance documents, regulatory references, supervisory correspondence, and accounting positions.
- Corporate control functions provide periodic reports on checks, results, weaknesses, and remediation actions, including anti-corruption and AML coverage.
- Lead-in to sustainability governance section outlining ESG responsibilities of corporate bodies and structures per Articles of Association and internal regulations.

nodes.title: Sustainability governance
nodes.heading: 2.4.2 Sustainability governance
nodes.start_phrase: The main ESG responsibilities of Intesa Sanpaolo Bodies and Structures are specified below in line with the Articles of Association, the Bodies’ regulations and the Group’s internal regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Board composition and expertise
  - Directors possess strong banking, risk, and market knowledge; high self-declared ESG expertise (84% with very good/distinctive sustainability competence).
  - Many directors hold roles in universities, foundations, and non-profits; one director also chairs a Risks & Sustainability Committee in another listed company.
  - 2022 renewal confirmed diversified and adequate composition; guidelines for optimal qualitative-quantitative board composition ahead of April 2025 renewal are available.

- Induction and training
  - Ongoing onboarding and training plans defined after appointment and via annual self-assessment; directors can request tailored training.
  - In 2024, 11 induction sessions covered ESG topics, risk data aggregation/reporting, Basel IV changes, new EBA AML Guidelines, and Digital Finance/MiCA; feedback was highly positive.
  - Directors access updated governance and regulatory documents via a dedicated platform; control functions provide periodic reports, including on anti-corruption and AML.

- ESG governance roles and responsibilities
  - Board of Directors (supported by the Risks & Sustainability Committee) sets ESG strategies/policies, integrates ESG risks into the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF), approves materiality analysis and the Consolidated Sustainability Statement (CSS), and updates the Code of Ethics and DE&I policy. In 2024, 21 meetings (16 with ESG matters).
  - Risks & Sustainability Committee supports all ESG oversight, approves ESG-sensitive sector lists, oversees materiality for CSS, benchmarks against best practices/indices; 47 meetings in 2024 (23 with ESG), monitored CSS preparation, ESG KPIs for Budget 2024, NZBA sector targets, and climate risk processes.
  - Management Control Committee supervises Code of Ethics compliance; examines CSS under Legislative Decree 125/2024 before Board review; fulfills Control and Audit Committee duties (Legislative Decree 30/2019).
  - Managing Director and CEO governs sustainability performance, proposes ESG decisions, ensures risk process consistency, and jointly certifies financial and sustainability information.

- Internal governance structures for ESG
  - Steering Committee (Business Plan & ESG session) co-defines ESG strategy/policies, identifies material topics, pre-reviews CSS, and aligns tech development with ethical principles (AI/ML); met 26 times in 2024; reports quarterly to the Board.
  - Group Control Coordination and Non-Financial Risks Committee (Operational & Reputational Risk session), chaired by CRO, examines ESG risk profiles; reports quarterly to the Board.
  - CFO area prepares the CSS, tracks evolving regulation, and sets methodology.
  - Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) area (established April 2024) drives ESG strategy, supports reporting and culture, fosters community development and innovation (startups, circular economy, ecosystems), and promotes heritage assets. Includes the Chief Social Impact Officer (CSIO) for social impact and direct environmental footprint mitigation.
  - ESG Control Room (strengthened in 2024) advises on ESG strategy, policies, KPIs/targets, voluntary commitments, reporting, integration into investments/credit, regulatory monitoring, and regulator requests. It reports to the Steering Committee and operates through:
    - ESG Coordination Panel (shares/monitors ESG goals across areas/divisions),
    - Sustainable Investments & Insurance Panel (oversees Wealth Management ESG initiatives),
    - Social Impact Panel (from 2025).
    - Sustainability Managers in each area/division monitor ESG topics, including subsidiaries.
  - CRO area develops the ESG risk framework, proposes RAF tolerances/limits/indicators for ESG and reputational risk, leads climate risk management, and issues the “Tableau de Bord of Risks” including ESG/reputational risk monitoring.

- ESG impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) in strategy and risk management
  - In 2024, the Board approved new sector targets supporting climate transition, new tools for community support, and key internal policies (RAF, reputational risk governance, conduct principles, DE&I).
  - Regular Board and Committee discussions on material IROs: reputational risk governance, climate/environmental risks, NZBA-aligned indirect GHG reduction targets, culture and social/environmental responsibility, DE&I, worker health and safety, community support and local development.
  - Ongoing KPI monitoring of ESG performance and Business Plan targets, reviewed by the Risks & Sustainability Committee.

- Incentive systems linked to sustainability
  - The CEO, as the sole executive director, is the only beneficiary of the annual Incentive System and the Long-Term Performance Share Plan; both integrate ESG metrics.
  - Annual Incentive System: scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs across Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; includes a cross-Group ESG KPI; weighted, deterministic payout with gateways, malus, and clawback; partly cash and partly shares with 5-year deferral.
  - Long-Term Incentive Plan: share-based, tied to Business Plan targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR) with de-multipliers for Composite ESG KPI and CET1 capital target; gateways, deferral (60% over five years), retention, malus, and clawback apply.
  - A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to about 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: Incentive systems linked to sustainability factors
nodes.heading: 2.4.3 Incentive systems linked to sustainability factors
nodes.start_phrase: The Managing Director and CEO is the only executive member of the Board of Directors and, therefore, is the only beneficiary of an annual Incentive System and a long -term Incentive Plan for the role of General Manager.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and oversight of ESG commitments:
  - Setting targets for reducing indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with private initiatives (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance).
  - Promoting corporate culture and social/environmental responsibility, diversity, equity and inclusion, worker health and safety, and community support/local development.
  - Monitoring Group ESG performance and main sustainability KPIs, with results and target progress assessed by the Risks and Sustainability Committee in Q1.

- Incentive systems linked to sustainability:
  - The Managing Director and CEO, as the sole executive director, is the only Board member with an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan, both embedding sustainability metrics.

- Annual Incentive System:
  - Performance Scorecard combining financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions support Plan objectives.
  - A transversal ESG KPI assigned in 2024; each KPI carries a 10%–30% weight; annual accrual; deterministic calculation based on results.
  - Payout partly in cash and partly in shares; five-year deferral with ex-post malus; claw-back possible for five years post-payment.
  - Subject to gateway conditions, absence of compliance breaches, and corrective mechanisms.

- Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP):
  - Granted to the CEO and ~3,100 managers; share awards tied to Business Plan targets: PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, and relative TSR.
  - De-multipliers: Composite ESG KPI (10%–20% reduction if 2022–2025 ESG targets missed) and Capital target (CET1 above RAF; 10% reduction per breach year, up to 40%).
  - 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; 60%–55% delivered in shares subject to retention; malus and claw-back apply; gateway and compliance checks required.

- Centrality of ESG in CEO pay:
  - ESG KPI included in the annual plan since 2021 (evolving from a prior Diversity & Inclusion KPI) and an ESG composite KPI acts as a de-multiplier in the PSP.
  - A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to about 3,000 managers (weight 10% or 15%).
  - Additional details referenced in the Group’s remuneration policy and compensation report.

nodes.title: Structure of the annual incentive system
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.1 Structure of the annual incentive system
nodes.start_phrase: The annual Incentive System49 is formalised through a Performance Scorecard with both financial and non -financial KPIs.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on governance and targets for ESG performance across the Group, including setting goals to progressively reduce indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with commitments such as the Net Zero Banking Alliance, promoting corporate culture and social/environmental responsibility, advancing diversity, equity and inclusion, ensuring worker health and safety, and supporting communities and local development.
- ESG performance oversight through monitoring of key sustainability KPIs and Business Plan targets, with results presented to the Risks and Sustainability Committee in the first quarter.
- Incentive systems linked to sustainability: the CEO, as the only executive director, is the sole beneficiary of an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan; both integrate sustainability metrics.
- Annual Incentive System: performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped into Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions enable plan delivery. A cross-Group ESG KPI is assigned (2024), KPI weights range 10–30%, accrual is annual, and payouts are determined formulaically. Payments are split between cash and Intesa Sanpaolo shares, with a five-year deferral, malus on deferred tranches, and a five-year post-payment clawback; subject to gateway conditions and compliance checks.
- Long-Term Incentive Plan (Performance Share Plan): extended to about 3,100 managers including the CEO; share awards depend on Business Plan targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR). Two de-multipliers apply: a Composite ESG KPI (reduces vesting by 10–20% if 2022–2025 ESG targets are missed) and a Capital target tied to CET1 above RAF (10% reduction per breach year, up to 40%). Plan includes gateway/compliance checks, 60% deferral over five years, significant share delivery with retention, and malus/clawback provisions.
- Centrality of ESG in CEO pay: an annual ESG KPI (evolved from a prior Diversity & Inclusion KPI, in place since 2021) and an ESG composite de-multiplier in the LTI. A cross-Group ESG KPI is also assigned to roughly 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: Structure of the Long-Term Incentive Plan
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.2 Structure of the Long-Term Incentive Plan
nodes.start_phrase: The CEO is also a beneficiary of the Long -Term Incentive Plan (PSP), which is also awarded to the remaining Management (around 3,100 beneficiaries).
nodes.summary:
- Outlines sustainability priorities: reducing indirect greenhouse gas emissions in line with private initiatives (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance), fostering a responsible corporate culture, advancing diversity, equity and inclusion, ensuring worker health and safety, and supporting communities and local areas.
- Describes ESG governance and oversight: ongoing control of Group ESG performance, monitoring key sustainability KPIs and Business Plan targets, and submission of results to the Risks and Sustainability Committee for assessment in Q1.
- Details incentive systems tied to sustainability for the Managing Director and CEO (the Board’s only executive), comprising an annual Incentive System and a Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP), both embedding ESG criteria.
- Annual Incentive System: a performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability; qualitative strategic actions; a cross-Group ESG KPI; KPI weights of 10–30%; annual accrual; deterministic payout calculation subject to gateway conditions, compliance checks, and corrective mechanisms; payment in cash and shares with five-year deferral, malus and post-payment claw-back provisions.
- Long-Term Incentive Plan (PSP): for the CEO and ~3,100 managers; share-based awards contingent on Business Plan-aligned targets (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR); two de-multipliers—Composite ESG KPI (Environmental, Social, Governance) reducing vesting by 10–20% if Plan ESG targets are missed, and a CET1 capital target reducing vesting by 10% per year of breach (up to 40%); 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; majority delivered in shares with retention; gateway, malus, and claw-back apply.
- Emphasizes the centrality of ESG in CEO variable pay: a dedicated ESG KPI in the annual plan and an ESG composite de-multiplier in the PSP; a cross-Group ESG KPI also assigned to about 3,000 managers (10–15% weight).

nodes.title: The ESG Component in CEO Incentive Plans (Annual and Long-Term)
nodes.heading: 2.4.3.3 The ESG Component in CEO Incentive Plans (Annual and Long-Term)
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to the variable remuneration of the Managing Director and CEO, the ESG component is of central importance and is included both in the annual Incentive Plan through the provision of a specific KPI, and in the long -term Performance Share Plan in which an ESG composite KPI is envisaged that acts as a de -multiplier of any bonus earned.
nodes.summary:
- ESG governance priorities and targets: progressive reduction of indirect greenhouse gas emissions aligned with commitments (e.g., Net Zero Banking Alliance), promotion of a responsible corporate culture, diversity-equity-inclusion, worker health and safety, and community support. Ongoing monitoring of Group ESG KPIs and Business Plan targets, with results submitted to the Risks and Sustainability Committee in Q1.
- Incentive systems tied to sustainability: the CEO (sole executive director) is beneficiary of an annual incentive system and a long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP), both embedding sustainability metrics, subject to gateway conditions, compliance checks, malus and clawback.
- Annual incentive system: performance scorecard with financial and non-financial KPIs grouped under Growth, Profitability, Productivity, and Cost of Risk/Sustainability. Includes a transversal Group ESG KPI; KPI weights 10–30%; annual accrual; deterministic payout calculation; payment split between cash and shares with a five-year deferral, malus on deferred portions, and five-year post-payment clawback.
- Long-term PSP: extended to ~3,100 managers; awards shares based on Business Plan metrics (PON/RWA, Cost/Income, NPL ratio, relative TSR). Two de-multipliers reduce vesting for underperformance: (i) Composite ESG KPI (Environmental, Social, Governance sub-KPIs versus 2022–2025 Plan targets) and (ii) CET1 capital target relative to RAF. 60% of any bonus deferred over five years; significant portion in shares with retention.
- ESG components in incentives: 
  - Annual CEO ESG KPI (15% weight) with drivers covering: inclusion in sustainability indices; inclusive workplace and gender equity (hires and candidate pools for first managerial appointments); Group ESG initiatives (green/circular economy support, financed emissions targets in priority sectors, exposure reduction in ESG risk sectors, ESG Credit Framework completion); growth of Sustainable Investments (ESG share of AuM); youth orientation and employability.
  - PSP ESG composite KPI: Environmental—new loans for green/circular economy and Corporate/SME transition (40%); Social—successful re/up-skilling with reallocation to new roles (40%); Governance—women in new senior appointments at -1/-2 levels below CEO (20%).
- LECOIP 3.0 for Professionals in Italy: long-term plan based on certificates linked to Intesa Sanpaolo shares; includes the same ESG composite KPI; guarantees a minimum 4% return if KPI achieved; if not, the foregone amount is invested by the Bank in ESG projects aligned with those objectives.
- Governance and approvals: Shareholders’ Meeting approves annual and long-term plans on Board proposal supported by the Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee reviews alignment with current and prospective risks.
- Sustainability reporting controls: three lines of defense model—Level I line controls; Level II risk and compliance (Chief Compliance Officer and Chief Risk Officer areas); Level III Internal Audit assessing overall control and IT systems. A structured, risk-based control framework ensures the Consolidated Sustainability Statement’s compliance and quality across:
  - Planning: regulatory analysis, scope of consolidation definition, complete/accurate double materiality analysis.
  - Data collection/preparation: verification of data sources; formal systems and procedures to ensure completeness, accuracy, consistency, and comprehensiveness with contributor/validator checks.
  - Aggregation/finalization: validation outcomes review, metric checks, and harmonization of policies/actions/targets to meet regulatory and quality requirements.

nodes.title: Risk management and internal controls of sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 2.4.4 Risk management and internal controls of sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group adopts an internal control system based on three levels, in line with the legal and regulatory provisions in force.
nodes.summary:
- Executive remuneration and incentives linked to ESG:
  - CEO’s ESG KPI (15% weight) assessed on: presence in sustainability indices; initiatives for an inclusive workplace with divisional gender equity targets (in hiring and candidate pools for first-time managerial appointments); Group ESG initiatives (support for green/circular economy, targets to cut financed emissions in additional sectors, reduction of exposures in ESG risk sectors, completion of the ESG Credit Framework); growth of sustainable investments (ESG share of AuM); youth orientation and employability programs.
  - Long-term Performance Share Plan (PSP): composite ESG KPI used as a de-multiplier with sub-KPIs and weights:
    - Environmental (40%): new loans to green/circular economy and ecological transition, prioritizing Corporate/SME transition.
    - Social (40%): number of people completing re-/up-skilling with reallocation for re-skilling.
    - Governance (20%): share of women in new senior appointments at -1 and -2 levels below the CEO.
  - LECOIP 3.0 Plan (for Professionals in Italy): 45,629 participants (~63% of those entitled); certificates linked to Intesa Sanpaolo shares; same ESG composite KPI guarantees a 4% minimum return if achieved; if not achieved, the foregone amount is invested by the Bank in ESG projects aligned to the KPI’s objectives.
  - Governance of incentive systems: Annual Incentive System and PSP approved by the Shareholders’ Meeting upon Board proposal supported by the Remuneration Committee; Risks and Sustainability Committee reviews consistency with current and prospective risks.

- Risk management and internal controls for sustainability reporting:
  - Three lines of defense model:
    - Level I: line controls embedded in processes/IT and performed by operating/business structures.
    - Level II: risk and compliance controls separate from production, including Chief Compliance Officer (regulatory compliance) and Chief Risk Officer (risk management), with corresponding units in Group companies.
    - Level III: internal audit assessing completeness, adequacy, effectiveness, and reliability of the internal control and IT systems.
  - Structured, risk-based control framework for the Consolidated Sustainability Statement:
    - Planning: interpret applicable regulation, define scope of consolidation, verify completeness/accuracy of double materiality analysis.
    - Data collection/preparation: verify data sources; use formal systems/procedures to ensure completeness, accuracy, consistency, and comprehensiveness; contributor/validator checks.
    - Aggregation/finalization: verify validation outcomes, check metrics, harmonize policy/action/target information to meet regulatory and quality standards.
  - Manager responsible for preparing financial reports oversees compliance of the Statement with CSRD-adopted reporting standards; results reported to governance bodies.
  - Reporting: annual report to the Board on sustainability statement risk within the “Report on the internal control system for the financial reporting process”; periodic reports by corporate control functions.

- Environmental information (ESRS E1 – Climate change):
  - Double materiality approach:
    - Impact materiality (inside-out): effects on people and environment over short/medium/long term.
    - Financial materiality (outside-in): risks and opportunities affecting development, financial position/performance/cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over varying time horizons.
  - Identification of climate-related impacts, risks, opportunities aligned with Group frameworks (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines, 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan, climate risk analyses), covering sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy; includes physical and transition risks.
  - Impact materiality methodology: interviews with internal units and external stakeholders; qualitative and quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
    - Own operations: positive material impacts on adaptation driven by internal policies and strategies targeting climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
    - Upstream supply chain: no material impacts identified given the Group’s service-based model; assessed via supplier ESG questionnaires.
    - Downstream value chain: both positive material impacts (through financing/investment criteria supporting clients’ mitigation/adaptation and energy reduction) and negative material impacts (due to portfolio exposures to high-emitting, high-risk sectors); references to commitments (UN Global Compact, NZBA) and internal policies (e.g., transition plans).
  - Financial materiality: dual quantitative/qualitative assessment across scopes.
  - Physical climate risk assessment: structured process distinguishing acute (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) and chronic (e.g., sea level rise) risks; further details continue beyond the excerpt.

structure.title: Environmental information
structure.heading: 3 Environmental information
structure.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
structure.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from the Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement under ESRS E1 – Climate change within Environmental information.
- Focus: Double materiality assessment covering impacts, risks, and opportunities related to climate change across three ESRS E1 sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy (all forms of production and consumption).
- Approach:
  - Double perspective:
    - Impact materiality (inside-out): effects on people and environment over short/medium/long term.
    - Financial materiality (outside-in): climate-related risks and opportunities affecting development, financial position, performance, cash flows, and access/cost of capital over various time horizons.
  - Reference framework and governance: Group policies and guidelines (Rules for Environmental and Energy Policy; Group Guidelines on ESG Risk Governance), 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan, materiality analysis of climate risks, and existing controls.
  - Inclusion of both transition and physical climate risks as required by ESRS E1.
- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Criteria: scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood.
  - Evidence gathering: interviews with internal units and external stakeholders/experts.
  - Value chain scopes:
    - Own operations: evaluated against internal policies and initiatives for climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
    - Upstream: supplier ESG questionnaires and response analysis.
    - Downstream: portfolio analysis of exposures to high-GHG sectors and sectors exposed to physical/transition risks; review of external commitments (e.g., UN Global Compact, Net-Zero Banking Alliance) and internal financing/investment policies favoring counterparties with credible climate actions/transition plans.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts identified for climate adaptation due to adopted policies/strategies.
  - Upstream value chain: no material impacts identified given the Group’s primarily financial-services profile.
  - Downstream value chain: both material positive impacts (across mitigation, adaptation, energy) and material negative impacts due to exposures to high-risk/high-emission counterparties.
- Financial materiality:
  - Assessed using a combined quantitative and qualitative approach across own operations, upstream, and downstream scopes.
- Physical climate risk assessment:
  - Structured process initiated with identification of material climate hazards.
  - Differentiation between acute risks (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) and chronic risks (e.g., sea-level rise).

nodes.title: ESRS E1 – Climate change
nodes.heading: 3.1 ESRS E1 – Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
- The section presents the Group’s ESRS E1 (Climate change) materiality assessment within its Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- It applies a double materiality lens: impact materiality (inside-out effects on people and environment) and financial materiality (outside-in risks and opportunities affecting performance, cash flows, and capital access over different time horizons).
- Identification and mapping of climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities are grounded in internal frameworks and governance (Environmental and Energy Policy Rules, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines), the 2022–2025 Business Plan, the Business Environment Scan, and climate risk materiality analyses, alongside established controls.
- Analysis is structured across ESRS E1 sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy (covering all energy production and consumption types), and distinguishes between physical and transition risks.
- Impact materiality methodology combines interviews with internal functions and external stakeholders with qualitative and quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood).
- Scope-specific impact findings:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts identified, particularly for climate adaptation, due to internal policies and efficiency/neutrality strategies.
  - Upstream value chain: no material impacts found, reflecting the Group’s primarily financial-services profile and supplier assessment via ESG questionnaires.
  - Downstream value chain: material positive impacts from financing and investment criteria supporting counterparties’ transition/adaptation and energy/emission reduction; material negative impacts also identified due to exposures to high-emitting sectors and those vulnerable to climate risks.
- Financial materiality is assessed through a combined quantitative and qualitative approach across the same scopes.
- For physical climate risks, the Group uses a structured identification and assessment process that differentiates acute hazards (e.g., heat waves, storms, floods, wildfires) from chronic hazards (e.g., sea-level rise), with further steps implied beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.1.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Impacts, risks and opportunities within the scope of ESRS E1 – Climate Change were identified taking into consideration the specific features of the Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framework: The Group’s ESRS E1 – Climate change disclosure is built on a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) across three sub-topics: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy. It draws on internal policies and governance (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines, 2022–2025 Business Plan, Business Environment Scan), and assesses both transition and physical risks.

- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Own operations: qualitative assessment via internal policies and initiatives tied to climate neutrality and energy efficiency.
  - Upstream value chain: ESG questionnaires and feedback analysis from suppliers.
  - Downstream value chain: portfolio analysis of exposures to high GHG-emitting sectors; review of external commitments (UNGC, NZBA) and internal financing/investment policies prioritizing counterparties with credible climate actions.
  - Outcomes: 
    - Own operations: material positive impacts on adaptation.
    - Upstream: no material impacts identified given the Group’s services profile.
    - Downstream: material positive impacts across all sub-topics from supportive criteria/strategies; material negative impacts due to exposure to high-risk sectors.

- Methodology for financial materiality:
  - Physical risk process: identify acute and chronic hazards (using IPCC SSP5-8.5 and regional projections), apply geospatial tools and climate models, assess exposure/sensitivity for own sites, analyse suppliers/counterparties’ vulnerabilities, and integrate into risk management.
  - Scenario use: NGFS climate projections; sovereign bond analysis via scenario-driven interest rate projections and yield curve shocks.
  - Risk focus by scope:
    - Own operations: operational and reputational risks from extreme weather-related disruptions.
    - Upstream: reputational risk if suppliers have weak resilience/BCP/DR plans.
    - Downstream: credit, market, liquidity, strategic, and reputational risks.
  - Material outcomes:
    - Physical risk: downstream credit and reputational risks are material in the medium to long term.
    - Transition risk: 
      - Own operations: operational and reputational risks if actions fall short of targets.
      - Upstream: operational/reputational risks where suppliers have weak GHG controls.
      - Downstream: credit, market, liquidity, and reputational risks; material (credit, market, reputational) in the medium to long term. Upstream reputational risk is also material.

- Energy sub-topic:
  - Upstream: reputational risk if suppliers lag on energy efficiency; material.
  - Downstream: credit and reputational risks from counterparties’ energy management inefficiencies affecting asset values; material.

- Opportunities assessment:
  - Adaptation: downstream opportunities identified but not financially material.
  - Mitigation (transition-related):
    - Own operations: material opportunities from emissions-reduction initiatives (Own Emissions Plan).
    - Downstream: material opportunities from expanding sustainable/Taxonomy-aligned products and financing for mitigation.
  - Energy (own operations): brand/positioning gains from energy efficiency targets not financially material beyond broader mitigation opportunities.

- Time horizons: all analyses consider short, medium, and long term, aligned with internal RAF, business plan projections, and risk simulations.

- Resilience assessment via Business Environment Scan (BES):
  - Integrates external trends into strategy: macroeconomic variables under three climate scenarios (Hot House World, Orderly Transition, Disorderly Transition), competitive landscape, regulatory and technology trends, social/demographic trends, and quantitative transition/physical risk impacts on exposures.
  - Produces an integrated view of how climate- and environment-related risks/opportunities may affect the business model over short, medium, and long terms.

nodes.title: Resilience Assessment
nodes.heading: 3.1.2 Resilience Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: Using an in -depth analysis of external factors such as global sustainability trends, changes in public policy and evolving stakeholder expectations, banks can accurately identify risks and opportunities that influence their operations and long -term strategy.
nodes.summary:
- Financial materiality of opportunities:
  - Climate adaptation opportunities identified only in the downstream value chain were deemed immaterial.
  - Climate mitigation–related opportunities are material across own operations and the downstream value chain, supported by existing initiatives (e.g., Group Own Emissions Plan), alignment with the EU Taxonomy, and commercial objectives.
  - Energy-sector opportunities tied to brand/positioning via energy-efficiency targets in own operations (outside broader mitigation initiatives) were assessed as not financially material.

- Resilience assessment via Business Environment Scan (BES):
  - Purpose: integrate climate and environmental considerations into strategic planning, informed by global trends, policy changes, and stakeholder expectations.
  - Scope: 14 business areas across retail, SMEs, large corporates (manufacturing, trade, construction, real estate, oil & gas, power generation, automotive), international banking, private banking, asset management, insurance, and Corporate Centre (including Treasury/ALM).
  - Variables analyzed: macroeconomic, competitive landscape, regulatory trends, technology trends, social/demographic trends, transition risk, and physical risk.
  - Scenarios/time horizons: NGFS-aligned scenarios (Hot House World, Orderly, Disorderly) with short term to 2027, medium term to 2030, long term to 2050; macro projections from Oxford Economics and NGFS.
  - Results:
    - Six areas show all variables at medium/high and at least one high impact: Residential Real Estate (Italy), SMEs (Italy), Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Automotive, and International Banks Division.
    - Expected impact timing: 30% short term, 60% medium term, 10% long term.
    - Dimension insights: macroeconomic impacts mainly medium term (energy prices affect Oil & Gas and Power Generation short and long term); competitive impacts short–medium term; regulatory impacts high for 13/14 areas in short–medium term (both risks and opportunities); technology impacts mainly medium term; social/demographic impacts more limited and area-dependent.

- Quantified portfolio risk findings:
  - Transition risk: limited short-term exposure rising over time; increasing exposure for SMEs and large corporates, notably in Power Generation and Oil & Gas; residential real estate faces medium/long-term regulatory impacts from emissions reductions.
  - Physical risk: long-term flood risk significant for residential properties; SMEs face moderate exposure (drought and wildfires); large corporates see significant long-term exposure to drought, wildfires, and floods.

- Follow-up actions informed by BES:
  - Ongoing monitoring of ESG regulation and participation in climate initiatives.
  - Integration of climate/ESG risks into credit processes and creditworthiness assessments; ESG sector mapping to NACE/ATECO.
  - NZBA-aligned sector targets to reduce financed emissions with monitored transition plans.
  - Implementation/monitoring of the Own Emissions Plan; business continuity and physical risk mitigation for facilities; energy-efficiency measures.

- Integration into incentive systems:
  - ESG/climate metrics embedded in variable remuneration for the CEO and workforce via the Annual Incentive System and Long-Term Performance Share Plan (PSP).
  - 2024 CEO Annual Incentive includes a 15% ESG KPI; PSP includes a composite ESG KPI acting as a 10–20% de-multiplier on vested shares.
  - 2024 outcome: ESG KPI contributed 16% of the CEO’s annual bonus.
  - Annual ESG KPI drivers: support for green/circular economy (ESG commitments progress, sectoral financed-emissions targets, reduced exposures in ESG risk sectors, completion of ESG Credit Framework) and growth in ESG investments as a share of AuM.
  - PSP environmental component emphasizes new credit to green/circular transition, especially for SMEs (40% weight).

nodes.title: Integration of sustainability performance into incentive systems
nodes.heading: 3.1.3 Integration of sustainability performance into incentive systems
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group is aware that it also has a significant social and environmental impact in the settings in which it conducts its business, choosing to act not only in the pursuit of profit, but also with the aim of creating long -term value for the Group, our people, customers, the community and the environment.
nodes.summary:
- Climate risk assessment: Transition risks for the Group’s portfolios are limited short term but rise over longer horizons, with SMEs and large corporates—especially in Power Generation and Oil & Gas—most exposed; residential real estate faces medium/long-term regulation-driven impacts. Physical risks intensify long term: floods for residential properties; drought and wildfires as main drivers for SMEs; drought, wildfire and flood risks material for large companies across sectors.
- Follow-up actions: Ongoing monitoring of ESG regulation; participation in climate initiatives; integration of climate/ESG risks into credit processes and creditworthiness; ESG sector mapping to NACE/ATECO; sector targets under NZBA to cut financed emissions and implement a sector transition plan; execution of the Own Emissions Plan; business continuity and physical site protection; energy efficiency measures.
- Strategic intent: Manage climate and environmental risks while pursuing sustainable growth by recognizing impacts, executing defined actions, and monitoring the operating context.
- ESG-linked remuneration: Climate and broader ESG performance embedded in variable pay for the CEO and workforce via the Annual Incentive System and the Performance Share Plan (PSP).
- CEO incentives: 2024 Annual Incentive includes a 15% ESG KPI; outcome led to 16% of bonus vesting. PSP uses a composite ESG KPI as a de-multiplier, reducing vested shares by 10–20% based on achievement; failure to meet the KPI cuts vesting accordingly.
- KPI design: Annual ESG KPI emphasizes support for green/circular economy via commitments, setting additional financed-emission reduction targets, reducing exposure in ESG-risk sectors, completing the ESG Credit Framework, and increasing ESG investments as a share of AuM. PSP environmental component focuses on new credit for green/circular transition, prioritizing corporate/SME transition (weight 40%).
- Operational climate strategy and governance: Code of Ethics promotes efficient resource use and climate, nature, and biodiversity protection, and backs green/circular economy. Environmental and Energy Policy aligns with Italian regulations (Leg. Decree 152/06 and 231/01), targets climate action, ESG risk management, impact prevention, resource efficiency, and responsible sourcing aligned with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
- Roles, systems, and controls: Environmental Manager leads the Environment & Energy structure; operational oversight by Real Estate Management and Group Technology. Certified management systems (ISO 14001, ISO 50001) with periodic audits, checks on waste and energy versus building characteristics, and regulatory compliance reviews.
- Sustainable procurement: Green Banking Procurement Rules guide purchasing (energy, office materials, renovations, events) to optimize resources, cut CO2, and advance efficiency and circularity; overseen by the Environment & Energy head.
- Policy scope and transparency: Policies apply across all Group companies and are communicated internally (Intranet) and externally (website).
- Own Emissions Plan (SBTi 1.5°C-aligned): Target a 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 versus 2019 (−51,427 tCO2e from a 96,192 tCO2e baseline), reach carbon neutrality concurrently via high-quality offsets, and procure 100% renewable electricity. Coverage spans the full Group; the 2019 baseline is retained despite minor boundary changes (<1% additional impact).
- Decarbonization pathway methodology: Bottom-up process engaging multiple internal stakeholders to identify key levers, complemented by an integrated approach (top-down element implied beyond the excerpt).
- Additional note: No direct investments in carbon capture and storage; the Group holds EU ETS emission rights from proprietary trading activities.

nodes.title: Strategies to counter climate change in own operations
nodes.heading: 3.1.4 Strategies to counter climate change in own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has developed and adopted a series of policies to monitor and address issues related to climate change and energy efficiency.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s operational strategies to mitigate and adapt to climate change, grounded in a Code of Ethics that promotes resource efficiency, combats climate change, protects biodiversity, and supports a green, circular economy.
- An Environmental and Energy Policy translates these values into actionable objectives: compliance with environmental laws (Legislative Decrees 152/06 and 231/01), climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, efficient resource use, and ethical/sustainable supplier selection; it aligns with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
- Governance and accountability are assigned to the Environmental Manager heading the Environment and Energy structure, with operational monitoring delegated to functions such as Real Estate Management and Group Technology.
- Dedicated environmental and energy functions oversee regulatory compliance, conduct periodic checks, inspections, and audits across sites, and monitor energy use against expected consumption considering building characteristics.
- The Group maintains ISO 14001 (environment) and ISO 50001 (energy) certified management systems, audited periodically by an international third party.
- Green Banking Procurement Rules guide sustainable purchasing (energy, office materials, renovations, events) with goals to optimize resources, cut CO2 emissions, drive efficiency, and foster circularity; responsibility rests with the head of the Environment and Energy structure.
- Policies are communicated to all relevant stakeholders via the corporate intranet and the public website and apply across the Parent Company and all subsidiaries.
- The Own Emissions Plan (launched in 2022 under the 2022–2025 Business Plan) follows SBTi 1.5°C criteria, targeting a 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 (–51.427 kt CO2e from a 2019 baseline of 96.192 kt CO2e) and carbon neutrality by 2030 via offsetting residual emissions with carbon credits; the Group aims for 100% purchased electricity from renewable sources.
- Targets are based on 2019 data, anticipated green certificate availability and PPAs through 2030; the scope covers the entire Group and remains unchanged, with new subsidiaries adding <1% CO2e impact and not altering the baseline.
- The emissions reduction pathway uses an integrated approach beginning with a bottom-up process engaging internal stakeholders (Real Estate, HR/People, Workers Benefits, branches, foreign companies) to identify key decarbonization levers; the text notes no direct investment in carbon capture/storage and mentions holding EU ETS emission rights from trading activities.

nodes.title: Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change
nodes.heading: 3.1.4.1 Policies to mitigate and adapt to climate change
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has developed and adopted a series of policies to monitor and address issues related to climate change and energy efficiency.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Strategies to counter climate change in Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s own operations, within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.

- Policy framework:
  - Code of Ethics promoting efficient, conscious resource use; combating climate change; protecting nature/biodiversity; supporting a sustainable, green, circular economy.
  - Environmental and Energy Policy aligned with Italian Environmental Code (Legislative Decree 152/06) and Model 231/01; objectives include climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, efficient resource use, and responsible supplier selection; alignment with initiatives like the UN Global Compact.
  - Governance: Environmental Manager (head of Environment and Energy structure) accountable for implementation; operational monitoring delegated to specialized units such as Real Estate Management and Group Technology.

- Controls and management systems:
  - Environmental and energy functions conduct regulatory compliance audits, periodic checks, inspections, and site audits focused on waste and energy performance versus expected levels considering building characteristics.
  - ISO-certified management systems: ISO 14001 (environment) and ISO 50001 (energy), third-party certified and periodically audited.

- Sustainable procurement:
  - Green Banking Procurement Rules covering energy, office materials, sustainable renovations, and event organization; goals include resource optimization, sustainable purchasing, CO2 reduction, efficiency, and circularity.
  - Responsibility resides with the head of the Environment and Energy structure.

- Transparency and scope:
  - Policies accessible to internal stakeholders via the intranet and to external stakeholders via the official website.
  - Applicability across the Parent Company and all subsidiaries.

- Own Emissions Plan (per 2022–2025 Business Plan; SBTi 1.5°C-aligned):
  - Target: 53% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 vs. 2019 baseline (96,192 tCO2eq), equivalent to a reduction of 51,427 tCO2eq.
  - Carbon neutrality target by 2030 through offsetting residual emissions with carbon credits; aim for 100% purchased electricity from renewable sources (via green certificates and options such as PPAs).
  - Emissions calculation covers the entire Group; 2019 baseline retained despite subsequent inclusion of additional subsidiaries (collectively <1% of total CO2eq).
  - Note: As of 31 Dec 2024, the Group does not directly invest in GHG capture and storage; it holds EU ETS emission rights from proprietary trading.

- Decarbonization pathway definition:
  - Integrated approach combining methods, including a bottom-up process engaging multiple internal stakeholders (e.g., Real Estate Management, People Management & Development, Workers Benefits, branches, and foreign companies) to identify key levers.

nodes.title: Own Emissions Plan
nodes.heading: 3.1.4.2 Own Emissions Plan
nodes.start_phrase: In accordance with the "2022 -2025 Business Plan", in 2022 the Intesa Sanpaolo Group implemented a plan to reduce its own emissions, called "Own Emissions Plan", following the Science Based Target Initiative (SBTi) protocol that calls for keeping the global temperature increase below 1.5°C compared to pre -industrial levels, as envisaged by the Paris Agreement.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategies to mitigate and adapt to climate change within its own operations, governance structures, management systems, procurement rules, and progress toward emission-reduction targets.

- Policies and governance:
  - Code of Ethics promoting efficient resource use, climate action, biodiversity protection, and support for a green/circular economy.
  - Environmental and Energy Policy aligned with Italian legislation (Legislative Decrees 152/06 and 231/01), targeting climate change mitigation, ESG risk management, prevention of environmental impacts, resource efficiency, and responsible supplier selection; aligned with UN Global Compact principles.
