- ESG integration: a proprietary ESG scoring model incorporates pollution-related factors (e.g., environmental certifications, waste and pollution data from external providers) and feeds into the credit framework and strategies.
- Stakeholder engagement: the Group promotes a pollution-reduction and nature-protection mindset through partnerships, training, research, working groups, and campaigns; it is a signatory to the Finance Leadership Statement on Plastic Pollution.
- ESRS E3 – Water and Marine Resources: the Group conducted a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/portfolios), considering internal policies, supplier ESG questionnaires, exposure to high-impact industries, and relevant partnerships (e.g., One Ocean Foundation; blue economy initiatives).
- Risk findings: no material water-related risks for own operations; potential upstream reputational risks from less advanced suppliers; downstream credit and market risks (and related reputational risks) considered but not material.
- Outcome: ESRS E3 topics (water and marine resources) are not material at Group level for either impact or financial materiality. Water-focused lending and efficiency initiatives exist but are currently marginal and not material for disclosure purposes.

nodes.title: ESRS E3 – Water and marine resources
nodes.heading: 3.3 ESRS E3 – Water and marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS E3 – Water and Marine Resources section of a consolidated sustainability statement, detailing the Group’s double materiality assessment (impact and financial).
- Methodology: Used inside-out (impact) and outside-in (financial) lenses; combined qualitative and quantitative analyses; involved environmental experts and internal interviews.
- Contextual inputs: Considered internal policies (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines), risk governance, partnerships (e.g., One Ocean Foundation), and academic collaborations (blue economy study centre).
- Impact materiality scope:
  - Own operations: Reviewed policies, strategies, and initiatives on responsible water use.
  - Upstream value chain: ESG questionnaires to suppliers and analysis of responses.
  - Downstream value chain: Assessed indirect impacts via portfolio exposures to high water-impact sectors; considered investment/lending criteria.
- Financial materiality scope:
  - Risks: None identified for own operations; potential reputational risk from suppliers (upstream); credit and market risks (and related reputational risk) in downstream portfolios.
  - Opportunities: Assessed in the downstream value chain by examining targets and KPIs in budgets and business plans.
- Outcome: ESRS E3 topics deemed not material at Group level for both impact and financial materiality.
- Rationale: Own operations show no material impact on water consumption/management; upstream and downstream exposures and supplier concentration related to water/marine impacts are not significant.
- Note on business activities: The Group offers some lending aimed at improving water-use efficiency, but volumes are currently marginal and not material for disclosure.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.3.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement covering ESRS E3 (Water and Marine Resources) and ESRS E4 (Biodiversity and Ecosystems), focusing on the Group’s double materiality assessment process and outcomes.
- Methodology
  - Applies double materiality: impact materiality (inside-out) and financial materiality (outside-in).
  - Assesses across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (portfolios/exposures), using qualitative and quantitative analyses, interviews with internal experts, external stakeholders, ESG supplier questionnaires, and portfolio screening against high-impact sectors.
  - Considers internal governance frameworks, policies, and partnerships (e.g., One Ocean Foundation, university collaborations, “Think Forestry” initiative).
- ESRS E3 – Water and Marine Resources
  - Impact materiality: Evaluated policies and initiatives on water use; supplier ESG feedback; downstream portfolio exposure to water-intensive/high-impact industries.
  - Financial materiality: 
    - Own operations: no risks identified.
    - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weak water practices.
    - Downstream: potential credit and market risks, with associated reputational risk.
  - Opportunities: Considered mainly downstream (targets/KPIs for water-related finance), but current water-efficiency lending is marginal.
  - Conclusion: Water and marine resources are not material at Group level for either impact or financial materiality due to limited operational impact and non-significant supplier/portfolio concentration.
- ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and Ecosystems
  - Impact materiality: 
    - Own operations and suppliers assessed via policies/strategies and ESG questionnaires.
    - Downstream portfolio exposures to sectors affecting biodiversity (e.g., climate change, resource overuse, pollution) identified as creating negative indirect material impacts; no material impacts found on affected communities regarding commodity production/procurement given business model.
  - Financial materiality:
    - Own operations: no direct risks (offices not in protected/high-biodiversity areas).
    - Upstream: potential reputational risk from less mature suppliers.
    - Downstream: material credit risk and related reputational risk due to exposure to sectors dependent on ecosystem services or negatively impacting biodiversity; market risk also considered.
  - Opportunities: 
    - Own operations: initiatives supporting biodiversity may enhance reputation.
    - Downstream: potential to expand products aligned with biodiversity objectives; review of budget/business plan targets and lending indicators supporting biodiversity.
- Overall
  - Clear delineation of perimeters (own operations, upstream, downstream), risk types (credit, market, reputational), and use of structured governance and partnerships.
  - Differentiated conclusions: ESRS E3 deemed non-material; ESRS E4 identifies material downstream impacts and financial risks, with associated opportunities for product development and reputation enhancement.

nodes.title: ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.heading: 3.4 ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and ecosystems section detailing the Group’s double materiality assessment (impact and financial) for biodiversity-related impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Methodology: Mapping based on the Group’s business context, risk governance, and initiatives (e.g., Think Forestry); qualitative and quantitative analyses using criteria of scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood; stakeholder interviews; supplier ESG questionnaires; portfolio-based downstream analysis of exposures to high-impact sectors.
- Perimeters assessed: own operations, upstream value chain, and downstream value chain.
- Impact materiality findings: Negative, indirect, material impacts identified in the downstream value chain due to portfolio exposures to sectors contributing to biodiversity loss (e.g., climate change, intensive resource use, pollution); no material impacts on affected communities from commodity production/procurement given the Group’s business nature.
- Financial materiality—risks: 
  - Own operations: no direct biodiversity-related risk (offices not in protected/high-biodiverse areas).
  - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weak environmental practices.
  - Downstream: potential credit and market risks from biodiversity threats, with associated reputational risk.
- Financial materiality—outcomes: Material credit risk in exposures to sectors dependent on ecosystem services or with high negative biodiversity impacts; related reputational risk deemed material.
- Opportunities: 
  - Own operations: biodiversity-supporting initiatives that can enhance reputation.
  - Downstream: expansion of products aligned with biodiversity goals; consideration of targets, KPIs, and lending indicators that improve biodiversity outcomes.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.4.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framework: The excerpt covers ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and ecosystems within a consolidated sustainability statement, applying a double materiality lens (impact materiality and financial materiality).

- Identification approach: Impacts, risks, and opportunities were mapped considering the Group’s business model, governance measures, and biodiversity initiatives (e.g., reforestation/natural capital projects), plus an assessment of biodiversity-related risks.

- Impact materiality methodology: 
  - Used interviews with internal units and external environmental experts and qualitative/quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
  - Own operations: assessed via internal policies and strategies.
  - Upstream: ESG questionnaires to suppliers and analysis of responses.
  - Downstream: portfolio-based analysis of exposures to high-biodiversity-impact sectors, including counterparties’ strategies/criteria.

- Impact materiality findings:
  - Negative indirect material impacts identified in the downstream value chain due to exposures to sectors driving climate change, intensive resource use, and pollution that contribute to biodiversity loss.
  - No actual or potential negative material impacts on affected communities tied to commodity production/procurement, given the Group’s business nature.

- Financial materiality methodology and findings:
  - Own operations: no direct biodiversity-loss risks identified (offices not in protected/high-biodiverse areas).
  - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weaker environmental management.
  - Downstream: potential credit and market risks from biodiversity threats, also leading to reputational risk.
  - Material risks identified: credit risk in exposures to sectors dependent on ecosystem services or with negative biodiversity impacts; associated reputational risk is also material.
  - Opportunities assessed (own operations and downstream offerings aligned to biodiversity objectives), but none deemed financially material.

- Resilience assessment (2024):
  - CRO-led pilot assessed biodiversity impacts and ecosystem-service dependencies for a sample of corporate borrowers, prioritizing TNFD “priority sectors” and largest exposures in IMI C&IB and Banca dei Territori portfolios.
  - With no finalized NGFS nature scenarios, focused on actual impacts/dependencies using 2023 sector estimates and ecosystem maps; introduced 2030–2050 forward-looking ecosystem scenarios via the Mean Species Abundance (MSA) metric.
  - Data sources: exclusively public information; no direct counterparty engagement.
  - Metrics and approach: set risk levels and measured exposure (gross carrying value); evaluated transaction (impact “pressures” via seven indicators) and physical risks (three dependency indicators), aligned to TNFD and the LEAP process.
    - Locate: mapped company sites and local ecosystems.
    - Evaluate: combined sector-level materiality (top-down) with local resource state (bottom-up).
    - Assess: quantified portfolio vulnerability by combining sector and location scores with exposure; adjusted for upstream via input-output matrices; normalized scores for comparability.
    - Prepare: laid groundwork to scale assessment to the full parent-company loan portfolio and inform strategy.
  - Results: only a small portion of the analyzed loan portfolio shows medium/high sectoral and local environmental risk exposure.
  - Next steps: defined follow-up actions to adapt strategy to biodiversity-related changes.

nodes.title: Resilience Assessment
nodes.heading: 3.4.2 Resilience Assessment
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the governance area of the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) carried out a risk assessment of the natural capital of Intesa Sanpaolo Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Segment of Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement focused on biodiversity- and nature-related risk assessment, portfolio resilience, and policies.
- Materiality outcome: The financial materiality assessment did not identify material opportunities linked to managing or reducing biodiversity loss in customer counterparties or own operations.
- 2024 resilience assessment: Led by the CRO, piloted a nature-related risk analysis of the corporate loan portfolio, examining biodiversity impacts and dependencies on ecosystem services.
  - Portfolio sample: Core-business loan book; companies selected by TNFD “priority sectors” and largest exposures in IMI C&IB and Banca dei Territori.
  - Methodology: Aligned to TNFD LEAP; integrated top-down sector materiality with bottom-up local area vulnerability; used public, sectoral estimates and ecosystem maps (as of end-2023); considered 2030–2050 scenarios via Mean Species Abundance (MSA); no NGFS nature-specific macro-scenarios available.
  - Data and scoring: Located head offices and facilities; assessed seven impact (“pressure”) indicators and three dependency (ecosystem service degradation) indicators; normalized sector and location scores; considered upstream value chain via input–output matrices; exposure measured by gross carrying value; results expressed in qualitative tiers (very low to very high).
  - Findings: Only a small share of the top 1,000 priority-sector counterparties showed medium/high combined sector and local area environmental risk.
  - Follow-up actions: Broaden assessment coverage and forward-looking metrics; adopt biodiversity rules; monitor evolving regulation; participate in climate/nature initiatives; embed ESG risk in lending and credit assessments; conduct ESG sector mapping.
- Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level:
  - Governance and standards: Biodiversity considerations embedded in the Group Code of Ethics and a specific policy for own operations.
  - New “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared 2024, adopted Jan 2025): Apply Group-wide to lending, wealth management & protection, direct impacts, and transition initiatives.
    - Exclusions and heightened scrutiny: Declines financing for certain projects/counterparties based on location (e.g., non-ratifying countries, protected areas), sectors with high biodiversity impact (e.g., intensive farming, deforestation, indiscriminate marine resource use), and projects deemed controversial for nature impacts/dependencies.
    - Risk processes: ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing for high-exposure sectors/regions; references international frameworks (CBD, Cartagena, Rotterdam) and Equator Principles.
    - Transition support: Prioritizes EU Taxonomy-aligned, environmentally sustainable lending, including biodiversity and ecosystem conservation/restoration.
    - Governance and transparency: Rules sit within ESG risk management and risk appetite; overseen by CSO and CRO; publicly available and regularly updated.
- Asset management integration:
  - Fideuram ISPB Asset Management SGR, Fideuram AM (Ireland), and Eurizon consider Principal Adverse Impacts (PAI) and report on them.
  - Eurizon’s Commitment Policy includes the “Eurizon Naturewatch” framework, aligned with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, screening issuers for proximity to sensitive ecosystems and operational impacts, to prioritize engagement with high-exposure investees.

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.4.3 Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: Intesa Sanpaolo Group acknowledges the risks arising from biodiversity loss and pollution, the benefits that can come from preserving and restoring nature, and the key role that financial institutions can play in this regard.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on integrating ESG, especially biodiversity and nature, into risk management and business decisions to mitigate environmental risks and capture opportunities.
- Development of enhanced ESG assessment frameworks: broader counterparty coverage, forward-looking metrics, ESG integration in lending and creditworthiness, ESG sector mapping, and proactive regulatory monitoring and participation in climate initiatives.
- Establishment of Group-wide policies on biodiversity and ecosystems, anchored in the Group Code of Ethics, with specific limitation/exclusion criteria, refined risk assessments, and promotion of sustainable lending that supports biodiversity, ecosystem services, and local communities.
- Introduction of “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared in 2024, adopted Jan 2025) covering lending, wealth management and protection, direct impacts, and initiatives for ecological transition.
- Lending exclusions and heightened due diligence for new projects/counterparties based on geography (e.g., non-ratifying countries, protected areas), sectoral impacts (e.g., intensive farming, deforestation, marine resource exploitation), and controversial project classifications.
- Use of an ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process for high-ESG-risk sectors/geographies; alignment with international frameworks (CBD, Cartagena Protocol, Rotterdam Convention) to promote sustainable practices, biosafety, chemical risk controls, and value-chain traceability; application of the Equator Principles.
- Support for clients transitioning to sustainable models, prioritizing EU Taxonomy-aligned and environmentally sustainable financing tied to biodiversity conservation and restoration objectives.
- Governance and transparency: rules integrated into the Group’s ESG risk appetite and strategy; public overview available; ongoing updates managed by CSO and CRO governance areas to reflect evolving regulations and best practices.
- Asset management integration: Fideuram and Eurizon entities consider Principal Adverse Impacts (PAI) and disclose results.
- Eurizon’s “Commitment Policy” and Naturewatch framework (inspired by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework) to screen issuers for biodiversity risks (site proximity to sensitive ecosystems and operational impacts), assess exposure and potential value loss, and prioritize engagement with high-exposure investees.

nodes.title: Policies related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.heading: 3.4.3.1 Policies related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.start_phrase: Intesa Sanpaolo Group acknowledges the risks arising from biodiversity loss and pollution, the benefits that can come from preserving and restoring nature, and the key role that financial institutions can play in this regard.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ESG risk governance and portfolio-level management, emphasizing mitigation of environmental risks and integration of ESG (including biodiversity) into lending, creditworthiness assessments, and sector mapping.
- Introduction and scope of new Group “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature” (prepared in 2024, adopted January 2025): apply Group-wide to lending, wealth management & protection, direct impacts, and transition initiatives; include exclusion, heightened assessment, and monitoring criteria for new projects/counterparties.
- Exclusions and risk criteria target high-impact sectors (e.g., intensive farming, deforestation, indiscriminate marine resource use), projects in countries not ratifying key biodiversity conventions, and activities in protected areas; controversial project types are identified for stricter treatment.
- Alignment with international frameworks: CBD, Cartagena Protocol, Rotterdam Convention, and Equator Principles; emphasis on biosafety, hazardous chemicals control, product traceability, and sustainable value chains.
- Governance and transparency: the rules are part of the Group’s ESG risk framework and risk appetite; public overview available; ongoing updates managed by CSO and CRO governance areas.
- Support for ecological transition financing: EU Taxonomy–aligned lending; S-Loan Progetti Green; SACE Green–guaranteed loans; Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework including biodiversity, land, and living natural resources projects.
- ESG scoring enhancement: incorporation of biodiversity and natural resources indicators (certifications, restoration/cleanup actions, impacts on biodiversity and water) into credit frameworks and strategies.
- Asset management approaches:
  - Consideration of Principal Adverse Impacts (PAI) and public reporting by Fideuram ISPB AM SGR, Fideuram AM (Ireland), and Eurizon Capital SGR.
  - Eurizon’s “Naturewatch” screening aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework to identify issuers with high biodiversity risk and prioritize engagement.
  - Commitment policies at Fideuram entities naming biodiversity loss mitigation as a cross-sector “macro-theme,” alongside GHG reduction, human rights/controversial weapons, and governance.
- Targets and methodology status: priority is integrating environmental (including biodiversity and ecosystems) risks into risk management and decision-making; acknowledges current data/methodological gaps and lack of specific quantitative targets pending standardization and improved data.
- Partnerships and initiatives: participation in climate change working groups; Nature Action 100 membership (Eurizon, Fideuram entities); applied research with Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center on behavioral drivers of climate/biodiversity action and urban biodiversity measurement using sensor-equipped robots.

nodes.title: Targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.heading: 3.4.3.2 Targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.start_phrase: In relation to environmental risks, including biodiversity and ecosystems, the aim of the Group is to incorporate measures into the risk management framework and related decision -making processes to ensure their governance.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s consolidated sustainability approach to biodiversity and ecosystems. It highlights group-wide commitment and sustainability policies—across Eurizon, Fideuram entities, and others—that set four cross-sector macro-themes: GHG reduction, biodiversity loss mitigation, human rights and anti–non-conventional weapons, and good governance. The Group aims to embed biodiversity-related risks into its risk management and decision-making, noting current materiality assessments rely on evolving methodologies and data, and that no specific quantitative biodiversity targets have yet been set. Governance is supported by newly adopted Rules on Biodiversity and Nature. Actions include financing tools for ecological transition (S-Loan Progetti Green, SACE Green guarantees) and a Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework that funds projects in living natural resources, land, and biodiversity. The Group’s corporate ESG scoring incorporates biodiversity and natural resource factors from external data providers and feeds into credit strategies. In 2023, key asset management units joined Nature Action 100 to advance investor best practices on biodiversity and deforestation. The Group also pursues partnerships, training, and applied research—such as neuroscientific studies on environmental behavior and robotic sensing to measure urban biodiversity—via the Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center.

nodes.title: Actions related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.heading: 3.4.3.3 Actions related to biodiversity and ecosystems
nodes.start_phrase: While the public information of a quantitative and verifiable nature required for the measurement of this risk and for targeted action to be taken is lacking, the Group has nevertheless started up a number of initiatives and actions to support undertakings in their ecological transition.
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s asset management companies have commitment and sustainability policies that prioritize four cross-sector “macro-themes”: reducing GHG emissions, mitigating biodiversity loss, respecting human rights/avoiding non-conventional weapons, and ensuring good corporate governance.
- For biodiversity and ecosystems, the Group is integrating environmental risk considerations into its risk management and decision-making, acknowledging current methodological/data limitations and a medium/long-term horizon; governance is guided by newly adopted “Rules on Biodiversity and Nature,” but no quantitative targets are set yet.
- Actions supporting biodiversity include financing tools (S-Loan Progetti Green, SACE Green guarantees) that can fund biodiversity projects, and a Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework that finances management of natural resources, land, and biodiversity.
- The Group’s ESG scoring for corporate clients incorporates biodiversity and natural resource factors (e.g., environmental certifications, restoration/cleanup initiatives, and impacts on biodiversity and water), and is embedded in credit frameworks and strategies.
- In 2023, Eurizon Capital SGR and Fideuram AM entities joined Nature Action 100 to combat biodiversity loss and deforestation.
- Partnerships, training, and applied research are used to advance awareness and solutions, including neuroscientific studies on environmental behavior and projects to measure urban biodiversity using sensor-equipped robots.
- Under ESRS E5 (Resource use and circular economy), the Group conducted a double materiality assessment (impact and financial), mapping impacts/risks/opportunities based on internal policies, recycling actions, partnerships (e.g., Ellen MacArthur Foundation, Circular Economy Lab), and sector exposures.
- Impact materiality findings: positive impacts in the downstream value chain via lending/investment strategies and products that support circularity; negative indirect impacts due to exposures to sectors with higher waste impacts.
- Financial materiality findings on risks: no material risks in own operations; potential reputational risks in the upstream supply chain from less mature suppliers; in the downstream value chain, potential credit and market risks (and reputational risks) linked to circular economy/resource-use challenges; significant credit and reputational risks identified around waste management in customers’ production processes.
- Financial opportunities are concentrated downstream, notably in financing clients to improve circularity and production efficiency, supported by dedicated lending facilities tied to specific business initiatives and monitored through budget/plan metrics.

nodes.title: ESRS E5 – Resource use and circular economy
nodes.heading: 3.5 ESRS E5 – Resource use and circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Part of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement under ESRS E5 (Resource use and circular economy), describing the Group’s double materiality assessment.
- Frameworks and enablers considered: Internal policies (Environmental and Energy Policy, ESG Risk Governance Guidelines), operational controls (recycling systems, use of recycled/recyclable/biodegradable materials), and partnerships (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, Cariplo Factory/Circular Economy Lab).
- Methodology: Dual perspective assessment—impact materiality (inside-out) and financial materiality (outside-in); qualitative and quantitative analyses using criteria of scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood; inputs from internal interviews, external environmental experts, supplier ESG questionnaires, and portfolio exposure reviews aligned with investment/lending strategies.
- Scoping across the value chain:
  - Own operations: assessed via internal policies and strategies.
  - Upstream: evaluated via supplier ESG questionnaires and responses.
  - Downstream: focused on indirect portfolio impacts, especially high-impact sectors and investment/lending criteria.
- Impact materiality results:
  - Positive: Downstream benefits from lending/investment strategies and products promoting circularity.
  - Negative: Indirect impacts from exposures to sectors with significant waste generation.
- Financial materiality—risks:
  - Own operations: no material risks identified.
  - Upstream: potential reputational risk from suppliers with weak environmental management.
  - Downstream: potential credit and market risks, with associated reputational risk, linked to circular economy/resource use challenges.
  - Overall: significant credit and reputational risks identified specifically around waste management in the downstream value chain.
- Financial materiality—opportunities:
  - Primarily downstream commercial opportunities to finance clients’ circular economy improvements and production efficiency.
  - Consideration of Budget/Business Plan targets and KPIs.
  - Material opportunities confirmed via dedicated lending facilities for defined circular economy projects.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.5.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS E5 – Resource use and circular economy within Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Double materiality approach: assessment of impact materiality (inside-out) and financial materiality (outside-in), covering own operations, upstream suppliers, and downstream portfolios.
- Impact materiality findings: positive impacts via lending/investment strategies and products that support circular economy; negative indirect impacts tied to portfolio exposures in high-waste sectors.
- Financial risk assessment: no material risks in own operations; potential reputational risk in the supply chain if suppliers lack environmental policies; in downstream portfolios, potential credit, market, and reputational risks from circular economy and resource-use challenges; significant credit and reputational risks identified related to waste management in production processes (downstream only).
- Financial opportunity assessment: material commercial opportunities in financing clients to enhance circularity and production efficiency; dedicated lending facilities identified as key levers.
- Policy framework: Group-wide circular economy policies aimed at resource efficiency, waste reduction, and value creation across product life cycles; alignment with climate mitigation, biodiversity restoration, and pollution reduction; addresses internal resource management and financing for circular business models.
- Governance: Chief Sustainability Officer Governance Area oversees policies; Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center (ISPIC) acts as competence center for circular economy.
- Integration and transparency: alignment processes for EU Taxonomy (including the circular economy objective); internal sustainable lending framework category “Ecological efficiency and circular economy” built with Ellen MacArthur Foundation (not yet fully aligned with EU Taxonomy for this objective); Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework aligned with ICMA principles and best-efforts Taxonomy alignment; internal ESG Scoring includes circular indicators; Green Procurement Rules promote circular purchasing.
- Lending process: circular economy and green criteria embedded; ISPIC evaluates circularity and funding eligibility for corporate initiatives.
- Eligibility criteria for circular financing: extending product life and use cycles (design, modularity, reverse logistics, repair, reconditioning, product-as-a-service/sharing); sourcing secondary/renewable/recycled materials and renewable energy for self-consumption; significant resource-efficiency gains (industrial symbiosis, waste-to-input models, closed-loop/ecodesign/systemic design, nature-based/CCU solutions for decarbonization); fully reusable/recyclable/compostable products within effective post-use collection and reuse systems.

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.heading: 3.5.2 Policies, targets and actions at portfolio level
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group's strategic approach, the circular economy policies adopted set out the principles, rules and processes for pursuing the Group's objectives in the transition towards a circular economy model, focused on resource efficiency, waste reduction and especially the creation of value throughout the entire product life cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s portfolio-level policies on resource use and the circular economy within its Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Strategic aim: drive an inclusive circular economy to boost resource efficiency, reduce waste, create value across product lifecycles, and support climate mitigation, biodiversity restoration, and pollution reduction, while managing resource price volatility risks.
- Scope: applies across all Group activities, covering internal resource management (e.g., procurement) and financing for circular business models.
- Governance: Chief Sustainability Officer Governance Area oversees sustainability policies; Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center (ISPIC) acts as the competence center for circular economy; collaboration with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (EMF).
- Integration into ethics and transparency: Code of Ethics embeds circular principles; public disclosure of key circular policies and rules via company channels.
- Frameworks and tools:
  - EU Taxonomy: internal processes for identifying/reporting aligned exposures, including the objective “Transition to a Circular Economy.”
  - Sustainable lending framework: “Ecological efficiency and circular economy” category based on five circular economy criteria defined with EMF; currently not fully aligned with EU Taxonomy.
  - Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework: allocates proceeds to green categories including circular economy; aligned with ICMA principles and with EU Taxonomy on a best-effort basis.
  - ESG Scoring: incorporates circular economy factors for corporate counterparties.
  - Green Procurement Rules: promote circular purchasing for items such as stationery, toner, gadgets, and gifts.
- Lending process: circular economy principles embedded via circular and green criteria; ISPIC conducts technical assessments of circularity and funding eligibility for corporate initiatives.
- Eligibility examples for the circular framework: extending product life/use cycles; use of secondary or sustainably sourced renewable inputs and recycled materials (including self-consumed renewable energy); significant resource-efficiency gains via industrial symbiosis, closed-loop models, eco/systemic design, and nature-based/technological CO2 capture and utilization; products designed to be fully reusable, recyclable, or compostable with effective post-use systems.
- Footnotes note ISPIC’s role in innovation and reference the Group’s Green, Social & Sustainability Bond Framework.

nodes.title: Policies on resource use and circular economy
nodes.heading: 3.5.2.1 Policies on resource use and circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group's strategic approach, the circular economy policies adopted set out the principles, rules and processes for pursuing the Group's objectives in the transition towards a circular economy model, focused on resource efficiency, waste reduction and especially the creation of value throughout the entire product life cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s portfolio-level policies, objectives, and actions on resource use and the circular economy within its Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Policy framework: Group-wide circular economy policies aimed at resource efficiency, waste reduction, lifecycle value creation, climate mitigation, biodiversity restoration, and pollution reduction; applies to internal operations (e.g., procurement) and financing activities.
- Governance: Oversight by the Chief Sustainability Officer Governance Area; Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center (ISPIC) acts as the competence center for circular economy; principles embedded in the Group’s Code of Ethics.
- Transparency and frameworks: 
  - Internal rules for identifying/reporting EU Taxonomy exposures, including the “Transition to a Circular Economy.”
  - Internal sustainable lending framework with the “Ecological efficiency and circular economy” category based on criteria co-developed with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (EMF); not fully aligned with EU Taxonomy CE criteria.
  - Green, Social & Sustainability Bond Framework aligned with ICMA principles and best-effort EU Taxonomy, dedicating proceeds to defined green categories including circular economy.
  - ESG Scoring includes circular economy aspects.
  - Green Procurement Rules promote circular procurement (stationery, toner, gadgets, gifts).
- Lending integration: Use of EMF-defined circular criteria and green criteria in credit processes; ISPIC performs technical assessments of circularity and funding eligibility.
- Circular framework eligibility criteria: 
  - Extending product life/use cycles (design for modularity, repair, reverse logistics, product-as-a-service/sharing).
  - Use of secondary/sustainably sourced renewable and recycled materials (incl. renewable energy for self-consumption).
  - Significant resource efficiency improvements and industrial symbiosis, cycle closure, eco/systemic design, and CO2 capture/use.
  - Fully reusable/recyclable/compostable products with effective post-use systems.
  - Enabling technologies and regenerative practices (IoT, AI, cloud, predictive maintenance, regenerative agriculture, hydroponics/aeroponics/precision farming).
- Green framework eligibility criteria: Non-self-consumption renewables; energy efficiency (storage, smart grids, efficient building equipment); zero-emission mobility and enabling infrastructure; high-performance green buildings (EPC A, LEED/BREEAM); sustainable land, natural resources, and biodiversity management.
- EU Taxonomy alignment note: Internal CE framework does not fully overlap with Taxonomy CE criteria; related loans are not counted as Taxonomy-aligned for Green Asset Ratio.
- Objectives: Strong strategic commitment to circular economy with EMF partnership since 2015 and ISPIC support; no specific quantitative targets set.
- Key actions and financing: 
  - €8bn dedicated credit facility (2022–2025 Plan) for projects meeting internal green/circular criteria, expanded from the 2018–2021 Plan.
  - Ongoing financing across Divisions with potential incentives for Italian and international clients adopting circular solutions (e.g., material substitution with recycled/organic inputs, biomethane/compost from urban organic waste with CO2 recovery, renewable plant revamping, industrial waste recovery).
  - 2024 synthetic securitisation (~€2.5bn portfolio) targeting loans to high-ESG/circular companies, releasing capital to fund additional circular/sustainable lending.
  - 2019 €750m Green Bond focused on circular economy to back related lending.
- Wealth management and advocacy: Eurizon Capital SGR positions as a circular transition leader, promotes CE strategies with clients in Italy and abroad, and updates digital training materials (2024).

nodes.title: Objectives for resource use and circular economy
nodes.heading: 3.5.2.2 Objectives for resource use and circular economy

nodes.summary:

nodes.title: FINANCE
nodes.heading: 3.5.2.3.1 FINANCE
nodes.start_phrase: With a view to concretely supporting undertakings in the circular economy transition process, the Group offers customers of the Banca dei Territori, IMI Corporate & Investment Banking and International Banks Divisions (IBD) the opportunity to access financing dedicated to the circular economy and which may include specific incentives.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of section: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s circular economy strategy within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, including its internal green framework and related financing, innovation, advocacy, and operational initiatives.
- Circular-enabling technologies highlighted: IoT for tracking/reverse logistics/predictive maintenance; Big Data/AI/Cloud to dematerialise services and build secondary material markets; regenerative agriculture and controlled-environment farming (hydroponics/aeroponics/precision) to improve soil health, biodiversity, local production, and cultivation in unfavourable areas.
- Internal green framework eligibility criteria:
  - Renewable energy (production, transmission, infrastructure; solar, wind, bioenergy/biomass, hydro).
  - Energy efficiency (renewable energy storage, smart grids, efficient building equipment).
  - Sustainable mobility (zero-CO2 passenger/light commercial vehicles and supporting infrastructure; zero-emission urban/suburban transport).
  - Green buildings (EPC Class A; high-level LEED/BREEAM; new/existing/renovated).
  - Sustainable management of natural resources, land use, and biodiversity (sustainable agriculture; conservation/restoration of habitats and ecosystems).
- Taxonomy note: Internal framework does not fully overlap with EU Taxonomy for the Circular Economy; loans under this framework are not considered aligned for the Green Asset Ratio.
- Strategic commitment: Ongoing partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (since 2015) and central role of Intesa Sanpaolo Innovation Center (ISPIC); no precise quantitative targets, but circular economy embedded in sustainability strategy.
- Major financing action: €8 billion credit facility for undertakings aligned with internal green/circular criteria under the 2022–2025 Business Plan, renewed and increased from the 2018–2021 plan.
- Financial support examples: Projects replacing critical/fossil materials with recycled/organic inputs; urban organic waste to biomethane/compost and CO2 recovery; revamping renewable plants to extend life/increase capacity; industrial waste recovery for new product lines.
- Capital optimisation: 2024 completion of a second ESG/Circular Economy synthetic securitisation (~€2.5bn portfolio) to free resources for additional circular/sustainable lending, with capacity to add loans over time.
- Sustainable bonds: 2019 issuance of a €750m Green Bond focused on the circular economy to back dedicated lending.
- Wealth management: Eurizon Capital SGR’s leadership in circular transition through investor education, events (Italy and abroad), and updated digital training in 2024, including collaboration with the Group’s Private Banking and the Italian Chamber of Commerce in Zurich.
- Innovation platform: Circular Economy Lab (Intesa Sanpaolo, ISPIC, Fondazione Cariplo, Cariplo Factory) provides non-financial services to accelerate circular models; 2024 outputs included 18 academic/specialised lectures, 18 dissemination events (6 within BdT ESG Workshops), and 7 innovation consulting projects for corporate clients.
- Advocacy and partnerships (international): Collaboration with UNEP FI; Circular Economy Lab cited as a case study in UNEP FI guidance; Group’s green bond referenced; active role in UNEP FI task force linking circularity with climate, nature, pollution, and inclusive economies; July 18, 2024 publication of non-binding banking guidelines (“Circular Economy as an Enabler for Responsible Banking” and “Circular Solutions to Achieve Climate Targets,” with sector insights for construction and textiles). New collaboration with IFC (World Bank Group) to spread circular finance practices, including a webinar hosted by ISPIC.
- Advocacy and partnerships (national): Participation in the Italian Alliance for the Circular Economy (as promoter), partnership with Freight Leaders Council (including contribution to its annual Topical Notebook), and renewed sponsorship of The European House Ambrosetti’s Water Value Community (2024/25 focus on circularity across the extended water supply chain).
- Internal operations: Ongoing pilots for circular ICT asset management; in 2024, sale of 600 decommissioned notebooks for reconditioning/reuse, reducing warehousing costs and saving ~101 kg CO2, supporting the Group’s Own Emissions Plan.
- Overall approach: A multi-pronged strategy—finance, innovation, advocacy, and internal practices—to accelerate the circular economy, supported by internal frameworks and international collaboration, even as full EU Taxonomy alignment for GAR purposes is not yet achieved.

nodes.title: INNOVATION
nodes.heading: 3.5.2.3.2 INNOVATION

- EU Taxonomy reporting framework: Overview of Regulation (EU) 2020/852, including six environmental objectives, minimum safeguards, and delegated acts defining eligible/aligned activities and screening criteria, plus disclosure rules under Delegated Regulations (EU) 2021/2178 and 2022/1214.

nodes.title: Reporting pursuant to the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852)
nodes.heading: 3.6 Reporting pursuant to the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852)
nodes.start_phrase: Introduced within the framework of the EU Action Plan on Financing Sustainable Growth, Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (the “Taxonomy Regulation”) establishes that activities can be defined as “environmentally sustainable” if they contribute to at least one of the following environmental objectives, without significantly harming the other objectives, and are carried out in compliance with minimum safeguards94:
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s 2024 reporting under the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 explains the framework for classifying environmentally sustainable activities across six environmental objectives, the need to meet minimum safeguards, and the role of delegated acts and technical screening criteria. It references the applicable disclosure rules (Commission Delegated Regulations 2021/2178 and 2022/1214) and the European Commission’s 2024 guidance applied on a best-efforts basis.

- KPIs disclosed for 2024: Green Asset Ratio (GAR, stock and flow), KPI for financial guarantees, KPI for assets under management (AuM), KPI for asset managers, insurance Investment and Underwriting KPIs, disclosures on fossil gas and nuclear energy activities, a Group Weighted Average KPI, KPIs of subsidiaries exempted from sustainability reporting, and the share of exposures to Taxonomy-eligible and non-eligible activities for the four additional environmental objectives and new activities under the first two objectives. Templates are provided in Annex I.

- GAR stock (main KPI): 
  - Environmentally sustainable assets: €20,516m; Turnover-based 3.63%; CapEx-based 4.36%.
  - Coverage over total assets: 73.80%.
  - Exclusions: 44.02% of covered assets excluded from the numerator; 26.20% of total assets excluded from the denominator (per Article 8 rules).
  - Composition of Turnover-based GAR stock: 2.41% from Taxonomy-aligned residential mortgage lending; 1.22% from aligned exposures to counterparties subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - Change vs 2023: ~37% increase, mainly from residential mortgages; inclusion of aligned exposures to financial counterparties in the numerator for the first time.

- GAR flow (additional KPI): €5,859m; Turnover-based 8.11%; CapEx-based 11.32%; coverage 9.43%; same exclusion percentages as stock.

- Other KPIs:
  - Financial guarantees: €161m; Turnover-based 2.72%; CapEx-based 4.65% (broadly in line with 2023).
  - Assets under management: €4,417m; Turnover-based 1.97%; CapEx-based 3.20%.
  - Trading book KPI and Fee & Commission KPI will apply starting from 2025 (publication in 2026).

- Methodological notes: Amounts are in € million; numerator exclusions include derivatives, exposures to non-NFRD/CSRD entities, on-demand interbank loans, cash/equivalents, other asset classes, and trading book; denominator exclusions include exposures to central governments, supranationals, central banks, and trading book. For buildings, DNSH for climate change adaptation (physical risk) was assessed.

- Subsidiary disclosures: Per FAQ No. 8, GAR KPIs are reported for exempted subsidiaries (e.g., PBZ, Intesa Sanpaolo Bank Slovenia, Fideuram-Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking, CIB Bank).

nodes.title: TEMPLATE 0: SUMMARY OF KPIs TO BE DISCLOSED BY CREDIT INSTITUTIONS UNDER ARTICLE 8 TAXONOMY REGULATION
nodes.heading: 3.6.1 TEMPLATE 0: SUMMARY OF KPIs TO BE DISCLOSED BY CREDIT INSTITUTIONS UNDER ARTICLE 8 TAXONOMY REGULATION
nodes.start_phrase: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Turnover -based GAR stock of 3.63% consists of the following exposures:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Disclosure of EU Taxonomy KPIs for Intesa Sanpaolo Group under Article 8, including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and additional metrics, with methodology, composition, year-on-year changes, and strategic integration.

- Key results (amounts in €m):
  - GAR (stock): environmentally sustainable assets 20,516; Turnover-based 3.63%; CapEx-based 4.36%; coverage 73.80% of total assets; exclusions from numerator 44.02%; exclusions from denominator 26.20%.
  - GAR (flow): 5,859; Turnover-based 8.11%; CapEx-based 11.32%; coverage 9.43%; same exclusion rates as stock.
  - Financial guarantees: 161; Turnover-based 2.72%; CapEx-based 4.65%.
  - Assets under management (AUM): 4,417; Turnover-based 1.97%; CapEx-based 3.20%.
  - Trading book and Fees & commissions KPIs to apply from 2025 (publication in 2026).

- GAR composition and change vs prior year:
  - Turnover-based GAR stock (3.63%) consists of:
    - 2.41% from taxonomy-aligned residential mortgage lending (climate change mitigation per EU 2021/2139, with DNSH checks for climate adaptation/physical risk).
    - 1.22% from taxonomy-aligned exposures to financial and non-financial counterparties subject to NFRD/CSRD.
  - ~37% increase vs 2023, mainly due to taxonomy-aligned mortgages; inclusion of aligned exposures to financial counterparties in the numerator for the first time.

- AUM KPI scope and caveats:
  - Includes consolidated investments managed by Eurizon, Fideuram AM entities, and VUB (including assets delegated to third parties), excluding assets managed under delegation for third-party financial undertakings.
  - KPI is dampened by significant holdings in derivatives and in issuers not subject to NFRD/CSRD, which are excluded from the numerator.

- Methodology highlights:
  - For counterparties with unknown use of proceeds:
    - Non-financials weighted by taxonomy-eligible turnover/CapEx for all objectives and taxonomy-aligned figures for climate mitigation/adaptation, based on published targets (actual data) sourced via a specialist provider.
    - Financials weighted by taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned turnover/CapEx for the first two objectives, based on published targets (actual data).
  - For known use of proceeds: include only financed assets that are taxonomy-aligned for climate mitigation/adaptation.
  - Group Turnover-based and CapEx-based KPIs (revenue-weighted across business segments, dominated by banking, followed by insurance) are 3.14% and 4.00%, up +0.84pp and +0.90pp year-on-year.

- Strategic integration:
  - Alignment with the 2022–2025 Business Plan to strengthen ESG leadership, with net-zero by 2050 targets across lending, investments, asset management, and insurance (participation in NZBA, NZAMI—under review, NZAOA, and related initiatives).
  - Ongoing “EU Taxonomy Green Enhancement” program since 2022 to meet regulatory requirements, assess loan alignment, steer new lending, develop taxonomy-linked products, and refine pricing incentives.

nodes.title: Taxonomy in the business and financial strategy and in product design
nodes.heading: 3.6.2 Taxonomy in the business and financial strategy and in product design
nodes.start_phrase: Through the 2022 -2025 Business Plan, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group aims to continue to generate increasing and sustainable value, further strengthening its leading position in ESG issues with a world -class position in terms of social impact and a strong focus on climate.
nodes.summary:
- EU Taxonomy KPIs and methodology
  - Scope and perimeter for the asset management KPI cover consolidated investments of Eurizon, Fideuram AM, and VUB entities, include delegated-out assets to third parties, and exclude assets managed under delegation for third-party financial institutions.
  - Adjustments/exclusions: large derivative exposures and investments in non-EU and EU companies not subject to NFRD/CSRD excluded from the numerator.
  - Weighting rules for exposures when “use of proceeds” is unknown:
    - Non-financial counterparties weighted by their published Taxonomy-eligible and (for objectives 1–2) Taxonomy-aligned Turnover and CapEx.
    - Financial counterparties weighted by published Taxonomy-eligible and aligned Turnover and CapEx for objectives 1–2.
    - When “use of proceeds” is known, only taxonomy-aligned assets for climate mitigation/adaptation are counted.
  - Data sourced from counterparties’ non-financial statements via a specialist infoprovider; references to EC FAQs for methodological guidance.
  - Group results: Turnover-based KPI 3.14% and CapEx-based KPI 4.00%, up +0.84 pp and +0.90 pp year over year, driven by higher KPIs in business segments (banking predominant, then insurance).

- Integration of Taxonomy in strategy and products
  - 2022–2025 Business Plan targets ESG leadership with strong climate focus; Group commitment to net-zero by 2050 across lending, investment, asset management, and insurance, with interim targets for priority lending sectors.
  - Recognition of the EU Taxonomy’s role in financing the transition (−55% emissions by 2030; neutrality by 2050) and market transparency/comparability.
  - “EU Taxonomy Green Enhancement” project: ensure regulatory alignment, assess loan book alignment, proactively steer new lending, identify new business opportunities, design new products, and refine pricing incentives.
  - Note on UN-linked net-zero initiatives joined; NZAMI undergoing a 2025 review with tracking temporarily suspended.

- ESRS S1 – Own Workforce: double materiality assessment
  - Scope covers all own workers (employees on permanent/temporary/apprenticeship contracts and contractors on temp/project contracts).
  - Impact materiality: assessed via stakeholder interviews (including unions and safety reps) and qualitative/quantitative analysis per legal criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood). Drivers include policies on working conditions, equal opportunities, inclusion, privacy, OHS, recruitment, and talent development.
  - Findings: positive material impacts in own operations due to strong governance/policies on secure employment, working time, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association/works councils, information/consultation/participation, collective bargaining, work-life balance, health and safety; equal treatment and opportunities (gender equality, equal pay, training/skills, disability inclusion, anti-violence/harassment, diversity); and worker privacy.
  - Financial materiality: opportunities from good workforce policies (reputation, stakeholder trust, talent attraction); risks include operational, compliance, and resulting reputational risks from policy gaps.
  - Emerging context and risk management: need to upgrade HSE risk assessment to “4.0” given compliance, continuity, reputational, and emerging risks linked to hybrid work (Next Way of Working) and climate change; attention to digital technologies’ impacts on work and OHS; ongoing in-depth assessments by groups of similar workers; definition of “emerging risks” tied to digital transformation.

structure.title: Social information
structure.heading: 4 Social information
structure.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
structure.summary:
- Focus: ESRS S1 – Own Workforce within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, detailing the Group’s double materiality assessment for its own employees and contractors.
- Double materiality approach:
  - Impact materiality (inside-out): evaluates actual/potential positive and negative impacts across own operations and value chain.
  - Financial materiality (outside-in): evaluates sustainability-related risks and opportunities affecting financial performance, position, cash flows, access to finance, and cost of capital over multiple time horizons.
- Scope of workforce: all own workers, including permanent, temporary, apprentices, and contractors (temping and project-based).
- Impact materiality methodology: interviews with internal units and external stakeholders (trade unions, worker safety reps); qualitative and quantitative analysis using regulatory criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood); assessment anchored in governance measures (recruitment, talent development, health and safety, diversity and inclusion, privacy).
- Impact findings: predominantly positive material impacts due to internal policies ensuring:
  - Working conditions: secure employment, working time, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association, works councils, information/consultation/participation rights, collective bargaining, work-life balance, occupational health and safety.
  - Equal treatment and opportunities: gender equality and equal pay, training and skills development, inclusion of persons with disabilities, prevention of violence and harassment, diversity.
  - Worker privacy.
- Financial materiality methodology: dual qualitative/quantitative assessment linking impacts and dependencies to financial risks and opportunities.
- Opportunities: strengthened brand reputation, stakeholder trust, and talent attraction arising from policies on adequate working conditions, equality, flexible/hybrid work, and work-life balance.
- Risks: operational, compliance, and reputational risks stemming from deficiencies in policies protecting worker rights.
- Risk management enhancement: need to upgrade the HSE risk assessment model to “4.0” due to increasing complexity, compliance demands, business continuity and reputational concerns, and emerging risks tied to climate change and the “Next Way of Working”; emphasis on understanding digital technologies’ impacts on work and OHS; implementation of in-depth assessments for groups of similar workers.
- Next Way of Working: a program fostering inclusive behaviors and hybrid working (office/home) enabled by new technologies, with voluntary, flexible organization of time and activities.

nodes.title: ESRS S1 – Own Workforce
nodes.heading: 4.1 ESRS S1 – Own Workforce
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from the Consolidated Sustainability Statement (Social information, ESRS S1 – Own Workforce) describing the Group’s double materiality assessment.
- Approach: Explains impact materiality (inside‑out impacts across own operations and value chain) and financial materiality (outside‑in risks/opportunities affecting performance, cash flows, and capital).
- Scope: All own workers, including employees (permanent, temporary, apprentices) and contractors (temporary or project-based).
- Methodology: Mapping against the Group’s business plan, policies, and governance; interviews with internal units, trade unions, and safety reps; qualitative and quantitative analysis using legal criteria (scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood) within own operations.
- Impact findings: Positive material impacts due to policies and strategies protecting the workforce across:
  - Working conditions: secure employment, working time, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association, works councils, information/consultation/participation rights, collective bargaining, work‑life balance, health and safety.
  - Equal treatment/opportunities: gender equality and equal pay, training and skills development, inclusion of persons with disabilities, anti‑violence/harassment measures, diversity.
  - Privacy protection.
- Financial materiality: 
  - Opportunities: stronger brand reputation, stakeholder trust, and talent attraction arising from good working conditions and inclusion policies (e.g., flexible work, work‑life balance).
  - Risks: operational, compliance, and reputational risks from inadequate worker‑rights policies.
- Risk management and HSE: Commitment to upgrade the HSE risk assessment model to “4.0” given rising complexity, compliance and continuity challenges, reputational exposure, climate change, and “emerging” risks from new ways of working and digital transformation; emphasizes awareness of digital technology impacts on work and OHS; conducts in‑depth assessments on groups of similar workers.
- Next Way of Working: Hybrid, flexible, tech‑enabled work model promoting inclusive behaviors; “emerging risks” defined as new or transformed risks linked to digital transformation.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.1.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ESRS S1 – Own Workforce, detailing the Group’s double materiality assessment approach and outcomes.
- Definitions and scope:
  - Impact materiality (inside-out) and financial materiality (outside-in) applied to all own workers (employees and contractors), though headcount data exclude non-employee contractors.
  - Mapping aligned with the 2022–2025 Business Plan, segment policies, and governance measures on working conditions, equality, inclusion, privacy, and HSE.
- Impact materiality:
  - Assessed via interviews with internal units and external stakeholders (e.g., unions, safety reps) and criteria of scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood.
  - Identified positive material impacts in own operations across working conditions (secure employment, working time, wages, social dialogue, freedom of association, works councils, worker participation, collective bargaining, work-life balance, health and safety), equal treatment and opportunities (gender equality, equal pay, training and skills, disability inclusion, anti-violence/harassment, diversity), and privacy.
- Financial materiality:
  - Quantitative and qualitative assessment of risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies.
  - Risks considered: operational, compliance, and related reputational risks from deficiencies in worker-rights policies; overall deemed not financially material for ESRS S1.
  - Opportunities deemed financially material: talent attraction (secure employment, work hours, work-life balance, training/skills, diversity); improved brand reputation (secure employment, work hours, adequate wages); enhanced stakeholder trust (social dialogue, freedom of association/works councils, information/consultation/participation rights, collective bargaining, work-life balance, health and safety, gender equality/equal pay, anti-violence/harassment, diversity).
- Emerging risk management and HSE:
  - Commitment to upgrade HSE risk assessment to “4.0” standards, reflecting complexity, compliance, business continuity, reputation, hybrid work (Next Way of Working), and climate change.
  - Emphasis on understanding digitalization’s impact on work and OHS; targeted assessments for groups potentially exposed to work-related stress (e.g., new branch models, extended hours, digital branches).
- Workforce profile (as of 31 Dec 2024, within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement scope):
  - Total employees: 93,539.
  - Gender: 50,725 women; 42,814 men.
  - Contract types: 90,917 permanent; 2,622 temporary; no non-guaranteed hours.
  - Turnover: 5,511 exits; turnover rate 5.89% (all termination reasons).
  - Geographic significance: Italy accounts for 71,174 employees (76% of total); only country meeting significance threshold.
- Human rights commitment:
  - Strong stance on respecting human rights, prohibiting forced and child labor, and protecting physical and moral integrity.
  - Management grounded in respect for personality and professionalism, fostering a culture of dignity, loyalty, and mutual trust.

nodes.title: Characteristics of Group employees and breakdown
nodes.heading: 4.1.2 Characteristics of Group employees and breakdown

nodes.title: The Group’s commitment to human rights
nodes.heading: 4.1.3 The Group’s commitment to human rights
nodes.start_phrase: Intesa Sanpaolo Group strives to promote respect for human rights and foster a corporate culture based on respect for the person and individual dignity by safeguarding the rights of all employees, combating any direct or indirect form of forced or child labour and protecting the physical and moral integrity of all Group people, through management based on respect for the personality and professionalism of each individual, within a framework of loyalty and mutual trust.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: The excerpt is from Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement and focuses on the “own workforce” topic, including a financial materiality assessment performed with internal units and stakeholders.
- Risk assessment: Potential exposure to work-related stress linked to new operating models (e.g., new-concept branches, longer hours, digital branches) was considered. The financial materiality assessment concluded that identified risks were not material in relation to the relevant standard.
- Opportunities assessment: Material opportunities were identified in:
  - Talent attraction: secure employment, work hours, work-life balance, training and skills development, diversity.
  - Brand reputation: secure employment, work hours, adequate wages.
  - Stakeholder trust: social dialogue; freedom of association and works councils; worker information, consultation and participation rights; collective bargaining; work-life balance; health and safety; gender equality and equal pay; measures against violence and harassment; diversity.
- Workforce snapshot (as of 31 Dec 2024; excludes project-based/agency contractors):
  - Total employees: 93,539 (Female 50,725; Male 42,814).
  - Contract types: Permanent 90,917; Temporary 2,622; no non‑guaranteed hours.
  - Exits and turnover: 5,511 departures; turnover rate 5.89% (all termination reasons).
  - Geography: Italy is the only significant country (71,174 employees; 76% of total).
  - Note: Headcount differs from consolidated financial statements’ KPI due to scope.
- Human rights governance and commitments:
  - Code of Ethics aligned with UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises; updated regularly and adopted across Group entities; accessible and distributed to all personnel; Group is a UN Global Compact signatory.
  - Core principles: listening and dialogue; transparency; equity and inclusion; respect for people; health and safety; appreciation and motivation; cohesion; fair and sustainable remuneration.
  - Principles on Human Rights (Board-approved) implement UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights; protect freedom of association and trade union/works council rights; oppose child and forced labor.
  - Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Principles to promote inclusion across the Group.
  - Annual Modern Slavery Statement covering actions to prevent modern slavery in operations and the value chain.
- Monitoring and metrics framework:
  - Incidents of discrimination: counts criminal/labor cases and internally verified non-compliance linked to discrimination/harassment.
  - Employee complaints: counts reports via internal channels (Code of Ethics inbox, whistleblowing, sexual harassment channel) on social and worker-rights issues.
  - OECD National Contact Points complaints: counts cases filed with NCPs on related matters.

nodes.title: Metrics on human rights in the own workforce
nodes.heading: 4.1.4 Metrics on human rights in the own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents a series of metrics for monitoring incidents and complaints concerning social matters and human rights in relation to Group employees.
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s overarching commitment to human rights, grounded in its Code of Ethics and Principles on Human Rights, and reinforced by adherence to the UN Global Compact and alignment with key international standards (UDHR, ICCPR, ILO Core Principles, OECD Guidelines).
- The Code of Ethics’ role in embedding social and environmental considerations into governance and decision-making; regular updates for transparency; universal adoption across Group entities; broad dissemination, including accessible formats for visually impaired users; distribution to all directors, employees, and contractors.
- Core ethical principles guiding conduct and policies: listening and dialogue; transparency; equity and inclusion; respect for individuals; health and safety protection; appreciation and motivation; cohesion; and fair, sustainable remuneration.
- The Principles on Human Rights operationalize commitments under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, including protection of freedom of association, and prohibition of child and forced labor; publicly available to employees and stakeholders.

nodes.title: Job protection and labour relations
nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Job protection and labour relations
nodes.start_phrase: Workers’ rights in the Group are protected by the general principles of the Code of Ethics, the Principles on Human Rights, the Principles on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion and by the collective bargaining system, which operates fully on two distinct and complementary levels, the national level and the Group level.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt summarizes the Group’s 2024 human rights incident reporting and its job protection and labor relations framework. It presents KPIs on incidents and responses: 9 discrimination incidents (including 6 verified sexual harassment cases that led to disciplinary measures and 3 litigation cases), 39 worker complaints submitted through internal channels (mainly on work–life balance, potential sexual harassment, and improper or discriminatory conduct), no complaints to OECD National Contact Points, material fines/penalties/compensation totaling €43,742 for social and human rights violations, and no severe human rights incidents connected to the own workforce or related fines. It adds context that approximately €43k pertains to an appeal ruling from a 2018 lawsuit, under further appeal to the Court of Cassation, and already provisioned.

It then outlines policies protecting workers’ rights grounded in the Code of Ethics, Principles on Human Rights, and Principles on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, implemented through a two-tier collective bargaining system (national and Group). The Group supports freedom of association and emphasizes compliance with CBAs and statutory rules to enhance workplace relations. Enterprise-level bargaining is handled by the Group Trade Union Delegation on performance bonuses, supplementary pensions, healthcare, job positions, and career development. Ongoing union engagement occurs via bilateral bodies: the Welfare, Safety and Sustainable Development Committee (focused on wellbeing, productivity, pensions, welfare, family services, education, and work–life balance, with expert input as needed) and the Consultation Committee (addressing Group-wide initiatives, interpreting agreements, and receiving updates on business plan progress).

nodes.title: Job protection and labour relations policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.1 Job protection and labour relations policies
nodes.start_phrase: Workers’ rights in the Group are protected by the general principles of the Code of Ethics, the Principles on Human Rights, the Principles on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion and by the collective bargaining system, which operates fully on two distinct and complementary levels, the national level and the Group level.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Consolidated Sustainability Statement section covering human rights incidents/violations, job protection and labour relations, remuneration policies, and collective bargaining/social dialogue.
- Human rights indicators defined: total fines/penalties/compensation from incidents; count of severe human rights incidents; count of severe incidents breaching UN Guiding Principles, ILO Declaration, or OECD Guidelines; total fines/compensation for severe incidents.
- 2024 human rights metrics (Table 18): 9 discrimination incidents; 39 complaints filed through worker channels; no complaints to OECD National Contact Points; €43,742 in material fines/penalties/compensation; no severe human rights issues connected to own workforce and therefore no related fines.
- Context on incidents: 6 confirmed sexual harassment cases (disciplinary measures applied) and 3 litigation cases over alleged discrimination; worker complaints primarily about work-life balance, potential sexual harassment, and improper/discriminatory conduct; the ~€43k relates to an appeal ruling from a 2018 lawsuit, expensed via provisions and under further appeal.
- Job protection and labour relations: Rights anchored in the Code of Ethics, Human Rights Principles, and Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Principles; dual-level collective bargaining (national and Group); commitment to freedom of association and valuing diversity; compliance with CBAs and laws to enhance workplace relations.
- Collective bargaining structures: Group Trade Union Delegation negotiates on performance bonuses/short-term plans, supplementary pensions, healthcare, job roles, and career paths; bilateral bodies include the Welfare, Safety and Sustainable Development Committee and the Consultation Committee; regular local-level meetings; new bilateral body (Oct 23, 2024) to monitor impacts of technological innovation/digitalization on branches.
- Governance: Labour policy development managed by a dedicated unit under the Chief People & Culture Officer; operational responsibility with the Head of Relations with Workers’ Representatives and Welfare.
- Remuneration policies: Application of the Italian National Collective Bargaining Agreement (renegotiated Nov 23, 2023); enterprise-level bargaining for pay structures, grades, career paths, and benefits (e.g., meal vouchers); outside Italy, adherence to local CBAs or labour law with broadly standard conditions (enhanced terms for top management).
- Broad-based short-term plan (PVR): In place since 2015; 2024 agreement (May 9, 2024) includes distributive-participative and incentive components; Base Bonus (€1,150–€2,950, with an extra quota for incomes up to €39,000) and Excellence Bonus (linked to outstanding performance; a quota reserved for network staff selling insurance); inclusive of employees on long absences, with protections for parental leave; option to convert PVR into welfare services for tax advantages.
- Pay increases: Average €435/month increase from the Nov 23, 2023 agreement, phased as €250 from Jul 1, 2023; €100 from Sep 1, 2024; €50 from Jun 1, 2025; €35 from Mar 1, 2026.
- Pay equity and governance: Guidelines for pay revisions emphasize consistency, market benchmarks, performance, and gender equality; commitment to equal pay for equal work and to being an employer of choice; cross-references to Equal Pay, DEI sections, and the Remuneration Policy report.
- Collective bargaining and unionization coverage (Dec 31, 2024): 89% of Group employees covered by national CBAs (100% in Italy); where no CB coverage exists, relations follow local labour law; 76% of the Italian workforce is unionized.

nodes.title: Remuneration policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.2 Remuneration policies
nodes.start_phrase: At the national level, Intesa Sanpaolo is a member of the Italian Banking Association and applies the National Collective Bargaining Agreement for the credit sector.
nodes.summary:
- Social dialogue and union engagement: quarterly local meetings; a new bilateral body (Oct 23, 2024 agreement) monitors impacts of technological innovation and digitalisation on bank branches and reports into Group negotiations.
- Governance of labor and remuneration: policies developed by the Governance Area of the Chief People & Culture Officer; operational lead is the Head of Relations with Workers’ Representatives and Welfare.
- Remuneration framework: adherence to Italy’s National Collective Bargaining Agreement (ABI); active role in the Nov 23, 2023 renegotiation; enterprise-level bargaining defines pay structures, grades, career paths, and benefits (e.g., meal vouchers). Outside Italy, compliance with local CBAs or labor law, aiming for standard conditions (enhanced terms for top management).
- Broad-based incentive (PVR) scheme: established in 2015; 2024 PVR agreed on May 9, 2024 for all employees except Risk Takers and Middle Management; combines:
  - Base Bonus: fixed for all plus extra for incomes up to €39,000; range €1,150–€2,950.
  - Excellence Bonus: tied to outstanding individual performance and team goals, with a quota reserved for the insurance sales network.
  Inclusive participation for employees on long absences (notably parental leave). Option to convert PVR into welfare services with tax advantages.
- Sector pay increases: average +€435/month from the Nov 23, 2023 agreement, phased as +€250 (from Jul 1, 2023), +€100 (from Sep 1, 2024), +€50 (from Jun 1, 2025), +€35 (from Mar 1, 2026).
- Pay review and equity guidelines: ensure consistency with market benchmarks and performance; prioritize gender equality and equal pay for equal work; merit- and skills-based decisions to attract and retain talent; cross-references to Equal Pay Policies, Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, and the Group’s Remuneration Policy Report.
