nodes.title: Policies relating to workers in the supply chain
nodes.heading: 4.2.2.2 Policies relating to workers in the supply chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Group defined internal procurement guidelines that apply to all companies, with the aim of defining the roles and responsibilities of the Corporate Bodies and structures of the Bank and the Group companies in the procurement management process, as well as the principles and macro -processes to be observed during all management phases for the purchases of goods and services, in compliance with:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How Intesa Sanpaolo Group (ISP) manages sustainability matters related to workers in its supply chain.
- Commitments and standards: Grounded in the Group’s Code of Ethics and Human Rights Principles, aligned with UN UDHR, ILO core conventions, UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines, and UN Global Compact membership. Core principles include non-discrimination, health and safety, and banning child and forced labor.
- Governance and policies: Group-wide procurement guidelines define roles, responsibilities, and processes, ensuring ESG, health and safety, and ethical compliance across all purchases. Approved by the Board of Directors; implemented by the Chief Cost Management Officer Governance Area. Applicable to both centralized and autonomous procurement models.
- Supplier selection and monitoring: Entry to the Suppliers List requires due diligence covering financial/reputational solidity and social responsibility. An ESG questionnaire is mandatory for all new suppliers. Ongoing monitoring integrates internal and external data to update each supplier’s score and qualification status.
- Contractual requirements and dissemination: Through the Supplier Portal, suppliers must acknowledge the Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Anti-Corruption Guidelines, DE&I disclosure, Organizational Model, and General Supply Terms. Contracts mandate compliance with labor, immigration, wage, social security, insurance, and safety rules for both suppliers and subcontractors; violations can trigger termination. Suppliers must cascade these principles through their supply chains.
- Future standard: A Procurement Code of Conduct will be adopted from 2025, to be shared with all registered suppliers and accepted by all suppliers impacting “green” and “social” categories by 2028.
- Worker involvement and safeguards: Engagement is indirect via appointed Operational Representatives. Contracts allow spot checks on wage and contribution payments; Italian suppliers’ social security compliance is continuously monitored. Suppliers must appoint a health and safety representative and ensure coordination, risk communication, and compliance with digital accessibility requirements.
- Remediation and exclusion: Negative events affecting supplier risk/qualification can prompt remedial actions up to contract termination and blacklisting, barring future engagements.
- Grievance mechanisms: Suppliers and their workers can use established reporting channels (Code of Ethics inbox, whistleblowing) that ensure confidentiality and non-retaliation. No serious human rights incidents were identified via these channels.
- Objectives and tools: Ongoing ESG mapping strengthens supplier assessment and selection to prevent exposure to labor-rights risks. Since 2023, the Qualification Portal 2.0 automates due diligence and monitoring, enhancing evaluation of business ethics, human and workers’ rights, and environmental performance based on questionnaires and certifications.

nodes.title: Involvement and remediation processes
nodes.heading: 4.2.2.3 Involvement and remediation processes
nodes.start_phrase: Given the type of goods and services purchased by the Intesa Sanpaolo Group, direct contact with individual workers is sporadic.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on supplier governance and human rights: outlines mandatory policies for all suppliers in the Group Supplier Register (Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Anti-Corruption Guidelines, DEI principles, Organisational Model, and General Supply Terms and Conditions).
- Contractual compliance requirements: adherence to labor and immigration laws; fair pay and benefits; social security, insurance, and workplace safety obligations; clauses re-submitted at each engagement; violations can lead to contract termination.
- Cascade responsibility: suppliers must disseminate these principles across their entire supply chain, including subcontractors and workers.
- Ongoing supplier qualification and monitoring: internal and external data feed qualification indicators; changes update overall scores and status; negative events trigger remedial actions up to contract termination; severe cases lead to blacklisting and ineligibility.
- Procurement Code of Conduct: to be adopted in 2025 and disclosed to all registered suppliers; commitment to ensure acceptance by all suppliers impacting “green” and “social” categories by 2028.
- Worker involvement mechanisms: direct contact with individual workers is rare; engagement occurs through appointed Operational Representatives per contract.
- Enforcement and checks: contractual clauses enable spot checks on wage, tax, and contribution payments; in Italy, continuous monitoring of compliance with social security and welfare contributions.
- Health, safety, and accessibility: requirement for a supplier health and safety representative; coordination with the Group on workplace risks; mandatory compliance with digital accessibility standards for websites and mobile apps.
- Grievance and whistleblowing: multiple confidential, non-retaliatory channels (e.g., Code of Ethics inbox, whistleblowing system) available to suppliers and their workers; no serious human rights incidents identified; references to ESRS G1 sections for details.
- Objectives and actions: continued ESG mapping of the supply base to enhance selection criteria and prevent exposure to higher labor-rights risks.
- Qualification Portal 2.0 (from 2023): digitizes due diligence and ongoing monitoring; emphasizes critical controls; evaluates suppliers on ethics, human rights, workers’ rights, and environment via questionnaires and certifications.

nodes.title: Objectives and actions relating to the workers in the supply chain
nodes.heading: 4.2.2.4 Objectives and actions relating to the workers in the supply chain
nodes.start_phrase: During the year, the mapping of social, environmental and governance sustainability continued with the aim of strengthening the assessment and selection criteria of the best suppliers.
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s supplier governance framework requires all registered suppliers to acknowledge and comply with key policies (Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Anti-Corruption Guidelines, DEI Principles, Organisational Model, General Supply Terms and Conditions), ensuring adherence to labor, immigration, fair pay, social security, insurance, workplace safety, and digital accessibility obligations, and cascading these to subcontractors; violations can trigger contract termination.
- A Procurement Code of Conduct will be adopted from 2025 and disclosed to all suppliers, with full acceptance targeted for all “green” and “social” category suppliers by 2028.
- Supplier involvement occurs via designated Operational Representatives; contractual clauses enable spot checks on wage, tax, and contribution payments, continuous monitoring of social security compliance documents (Italy), appointment of supplier health and safety representatives, and enforcement of accessibility requirements for digital services.
- Ongoing monitoring of supplier qualification indicators detects negative events that can lower scores, limit eligibility, or lead to blacklisting; remediation actions are defined by severity. Confidential, non-retaliatory reporting channels (Code of Ethics inbox and whistleblowing) are available to suppliers and their workers; no serious human rights incidents were identified.
- The Group advances ESG-driven supplier selection through continued social, environmental, and governance mapping, the Qualification Portal 2.0 for due diligence and monitoring, ESG questionnaires and certifications, and an ESG score that influences tender participation, with exclusion for non-compliance in high-impact categories.
- 2024 outcomes: over 2,400 criticality reports analyzed (about 13% of qualified suppliers), ~240 high-risk and ~50 medium-risk cases leading to score reductions; more than 30 suppliers blacklisted; ~23,800 compliance checks on supplier documents; irregular profiles incur a 30% score reduction; ESG certification validity checks initiated; ESG mapping coverage reached 86% of qualified and engaged suppliers.
- Procurement practices include competitive tenders for labor-intensive services to ensure fair rates and process traceability, with possible reference to sector CBAs. Supply-related risks feed the Risk Appetite Framework (e.g., high credit risk, dependency >60%), monitored quarterly by the Risks and Sustainability Committee, with early warnings on exposure to socially sensitive sectors.
- From late 2024, for suppliers who are also Group customers with a counterparty ESG score, that score is used in qualification to enhance selection decisions.
- Planned 2025 actions: supplier webinars focused on supply-chain employees; roll-out and cascading of the Procurement Code of Conduct; completion of ESG mapping to flag deviations; definition of mitigation and support measures for the most socially critical categories.
- For portfolio companies, the Group integrates ESG risk considerations into credit processes, applying exclusion criteria (e.g., activities in active conflict zones, evidence of human rights violations, forced or child labor) and aligning with international frameworks and initiatives (UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Principles for Responsible Banking and Investment, Principles for Sustainable Insurance, Equator Principles).

nodes.title: Management of sustainability matters related to workers of portfolio companies
nodes.heading: 4.2.3 Management of sustainability matters related to workers of portfolio companies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group takes into account the ESG risks associated with the activities of corporate customers and pays particular attention to the in -depth analysis of sustainability matters connected to the credit granting process.
nodes.summary:
- The Group assigns ESG scores to suppliers to evaluate sustainability performance and guide risk-based supplier selection; non-compliant suppliers in high-impact categories may be excluded from tenders.
- In 2024, over 2,400 criticality reports were analyzed (~13% of qualified suppliers); ~240 high-risk and ~50 medium-risk cases led to score reductions, and 30+ suppliers were blacklisted, including non-responders.
- About 23,800 compliance checks were conducted on Supplier Portal documents (e.g., tax/social security compliance). Irregular profiles receive a 30% score reduction and may face limits on new contracts; ESG certifications are specifically verified.
- ESG mapping coverage reached 86% of qualified and engaged suppliers by end-2024, with targeted actions to complete ESG questionnaires and a goal of full measurement by 2025.
- The Chief Cost Management Officer Governance Area runs competitive tenders via the Supplier Portal for labor-intensive contracts to ensure fair reference prices, equal participation, and process traceability; service specs may align with sector CBAs.
- Supply-chain risk oversight feeds the Risk Appetite Framework: monitors suppliers with high credit/default risk and those with >60% Group procurement share; results reported quarterly to the Risks and Sustainability Committee. An early-warning threshold addresses exposure to socially sensitive sectors, aligned with the Group’s sectoral ESG strategy and credit disincentives.
- From late 2024, when suppliers are also Group customers with a counterparty ESG score, that score replaces the qualification ESG assessment to inform selection.
- Planned 2025 actions: supplier webinars on supply chain workforce matters; adoption and cascading of a Procurement Code of Conduct; completion of ESG mapping and identification of outliers; mitigation and support for socially critical categories.
- For portfolio companies’ workers, the Group integrates ESG risks into credit processes and applies exclusion criteria: no financing for entities in active armed conflict areas or with evidence of human rights violations, forced or child labor.
- ESG risk guidelines draw on international best practices and supervisory developments; the Group aligns with and/or adheres to UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, UN Principles for Responsible Banking, UN Principles for Responsible Investment, UNEP FI Principles for Sustainable Insurance, and the Equator Principles.

nodes.title: Policies and processes related to workers of portfolio companies
nodes.heading: 4.2.3.1 Policies and processes related to workers of portfolio companies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group takes into account the ESG risks associated with the activities of corporate customers and pays particular attention to the in -depth analysis of sustainability matters connected to the credit granting process.
nodes.summary:
- Supplier ESG assessment and risk-based procurement:
  - Suppliers receive ESG scores influencing selection; noncompliant suppliers in high-impact categories may be excluded.
  - 2024 reviews: >2,400 criticality reports (≈13% of qualified suppliers); ≈240 high-risk and ≈50 medium-risk cases led to score reductions; >30 suppliers blacklisted (including non-respondents).
  - ≈23,800 compliance checks of portal documents (e.g., tax/social security); irregular profiles face a 30% score penalty during non-compliance; checks on ESG certification validity initiated.
  - ESG mapping reached 86% coverage of qualified and engaged suppliers by end-2024.

- Sustainable procurement governance:
  - Competitive tenders via Supplier Portal for labor-intensive contracts to ensure fair, traceable pricing; specifications may reference sectoral CBAs.
  - Risk Appetite Framework inputs and monitoring for supply risks (e.g., suppliers with high credit risk/default risk; procurement share >60%); quarterly reporting to the Risks and Sustainability Committee.
  - Early warning thresholds for exposure to sectors with significant social issues, aligned with sectoral ESG credit disincentives.

- Integration of customer ESG scoring in supply chain:
  - For suppliers who are also Group customers with a counterparty ESG score, that score replaces the qualification sustainability assessment in selection processes (cross-referenced to ESRS E1).

- Planned 2025 supply chain actions:
  - Supplier webinars on workforce-related topics.
  - Adoption and dissemination of a Procurement Code of Conduct (to suppliers and their workers).
  - Completion of ESG mapping, identification of deviations/criticalities.
  - Mitigation and support actions for socially critical categories.

- Management of sustainability matters for workers of portfolio companies:
  - Credit policies include exclusion criteria (no financing of activities/projects in active armed conflict areas or with evidence of human rights violations, forced or child labour).
  - Alignment with international frameworks: UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, UN PRB, UN PRI, UNEP FI PSI, Equator Principles.
  - CRO Governance Area sets ESG risk guidelines and maintains systems for reputational/ESG risk management (see ESRS E1).
  - Recognition of social risks in financing; promotion of thematic/impact investments to mitigate social issues and economic inequalities.
  - ESG counterparty score for corporate customers covers labour and social practices; ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process in place.
  - Practical limitations to directly engaging workers of portfolio companies or providing dedicated reporting channels; remediation occurs via dialogue with counterparties and risk monitoring.
  - Activities to support/monitor social ESG issues proceed without quantified targets due to limited data; by Dec 2024, ≈249,000 corporate customers covered by ESG scoring.

nodes.title: Objectives and actions related to the workers of portfolio companies
nodes.heading: 4.2.3.2 Objectives and actions related to the workers of portfolio companies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group conducts activities and initiatives to support and monitor ESG issues, particularly social ones, which may include (with direct or indirect impacts) also the employees of its portfolio companies, paying particular attention to sustainability matters related to sectors that are sensitive to ESG and/or reputational risks.
nodes.summary:
- The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) Governance Area defines and maintains Group Guidelines for ESG risk governance, implements related rules, and manages the internal system for assessing reputational and ESG risks, with cross-references to the ESRS E1 – Climate Change chapter.
- The Group acknowledges elevated social risks in certain sectors/countries within its investment and lending portfolios and promotes thematic and impact investments to mitigate social issues like inequality.
- An ESG score for corporate customers—covering about 249,000 clients as of December 2024—assesses social dimensions (labor practices, health and safety, diversity and inclusion, human capital development); an ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process evaluates related risks.
- Due to the Group’s role as a financial institution, it is currently difficult to directly engage workers of portfolio companies or provide them with dedicated reporting channels as envisaged by ESRS; remediation is pursued indirectly through dialogue with counterparties and CRO-led risk measurement/monitoring.
- The Group undertakes initiatives to support and monitor ESG—especially social—issues affecting employees of portfolio companies, with a focus on sectors sensitive to ESG/reputational risks; however, quantitative objectives, effectiveness monitoring, and resource quantification are constrained by limited data availability.
- ESRS S3 – Affected communities:
  - Double materiality approach applied:
    - Impact materiality: assessed through internal/external interviews and qualitative/quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood) across own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains.
    - Financial materiality: dual quantitative/qualitative assessment of risks and opportunities across the same scopes.
  - Impact findings:
    - Own operations: significant positive impacts via community support (e.g., adequate housing/food, educational inclusion, youth employment, cultural heritage, social inclusion, crowdfunding).
    - Upstream supply chain: no material impacts identified given the Group’s service-focused operations.
    - Downstream portfolio: significant negative impacts related to community safety and indigenous peoples’ rights in high-impact sectors.
  - Financial materiality findings:
    - Own operations and upstream: no material risks identified.
    - Downstream: material credit risk (and related market risk) tied to exposures affecting community safety and indigenous rights; associated reputational risk is material.
  - Opportunities: within own operations, the Business Plan includes initiatives and KPIs that support communities and local territories.

nodes.title: ESRS S3 – Affected communities
nodes.heading: 4.3 ESRS S3 – Affected communities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Topic: ESRS S3 – Affected communities within a Consolidated Sustainability Statement, focusing on a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) aligned with ESRS2.
- Scope of analysis: Own operations, upstream value chain (suppliers), and downstream value chain (clients/portfolio exposures). Communities considered include the local social fabric where the Group operates and people affected by its main activities.
- Methodology: Mapping of initiatives and safeguards; interviews with internal units and external stakeholders; qualitative and quantitative assessment of impacts using scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood; analysis of supplier categories and portfolio exposures to high-impact sectors.
- Impact materiality findings:
  - Own operations: Significant positive impacts from community support and territorial enhancement (e.g., adequate housing/food, educational inclusion, youth employability, cultural rights, social inclusion/cohesion, crowdfunding, cultural heritage promotion).
  - Upstream value chain: No material impacts identified given the Group’s financial-services focus.
  - Downstream value chain: Significant negative impacts identified via portfolio exposures, particularly related to community safety and indigenous peoples’ rights.
- Financial materiality findings (risks):
  - Own operations: No material risks identified.
  - Upstream value chain: No material risks identified.
  - Downstream value chain: Credit and market risks associated with counterparties impacting indigenous peoples’ rights and community safety; resulting reputational risk. Credit risk and related reputational risk deemed material.
- Financial materiality findings (opportunities):
  - Own operations: Presence of initiatives and KPIs in the Business Plan supporting communities and local territories confirmed.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.3.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS S3 – Affected communities. The Group performs a double materiality assessment (impact materiality: inside-out impacts; financial materiality: outside-in risks/opportunities) tailored to its business model and footprint.
- Methodology: Mapping of impacts, risks, and opportunities through analysis of community-support initiatives and safeguards across own operations and value chain; interviews with internal units and external stakeholders; qualitative/quantitative assessment using scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood.
- Scope of assessment:
  - Own operations
  - Upstream value chain (suppliers)
  - Downstream value chain (portfolio exposures to client sectors/industries)
- Impact materiality results:
  - Own operations: Significant positive impacts via initiatives on adequate housing and food, and territorial impacts (educational inclusion, youth employability, cultural rights, social inclusion/cohesion, crowdfunding, promotion of cultural heritage).
  - Upstream value chain: No material impacts identified given the Group’s primarily financial-services nature.
  - Downstream value chain: Significant negative impacts tied to portfolio exposures to sectors that may harm community safety and the rights of indigenous peoples.
- Financial materiality results:
  - Risks:
    - Own operations: No material risks identified.
    - Upstream value chain: No material risks identified.
    - Downstream value chain: Material credit risk (from exposures linked to community safety and indigenous rights), associated reputational risk; market risk also considered.
  - Opportunities (own operations): Material opportunities to enhance brand reputation and stakeholder trust through initiatives in adequate housing and food, territorial/community support (youth, minors and vulnerable people, female entrepreneurship, social inclusion, facilitated access to healthcare). These are embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan with specific initiatives and KPIs.
- Strategic commitment and policies:
  - Strong emphasis on supporting community social needs, reducing inequalities, and promoting social, educational, and cultural inclusion, with extensive community investment and partnerships with the non-profit sector.
  - Human rights commitments anchored in the Code of Ethics and aligned with the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines, ILO conventions; the Group is a UN Global Compact member.
  - Code of Ethics guides relations with local communities on material topics (Adequate Housing, Adequate Food, Impacts on the territory) and frames actions across three macro-areas: support to the non-profit sector and social enterprises; support to communities via donations/sponsorships/partnerships and heritage enhancement; promotion of local economies and SMEs with high social/environmental value.
  - Application across the Group, including co-planning and partnerships with NPOs; linkage to broader business conduct policies (ESRS G1).
- Governance and instruments for social impact:
  - “Charity Allowance” funded from distributable profits for charitable, social, and cultural contributions, managed by the Bank’s Presidency.
  - Board of Directors authority to make donations via an annual plan (including emergency responses), ensuring coordination, ESG alignment, criteria setting, and strategic supervision, supported by the Risks and Sustainability Committee.

nodes.title: Communities affected by own operations
nodes.heading: 4.3.2 Communities affected by own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Group places great importance on projects that promote growth and social, educational, cultural and civic inclusion in the communities where it operates, thereby contributing to the development of more innovative and inclusive societies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and materiality: A financial materiality analysis highlights opportunities to enhance brand reputation and stakeholder trust by addressing adequate housing, adequate food, and territorial impacts through initiatives for youth, vulnerable groups, social inclusion, employability (including female entrepreneurship), and facilitated healthcare access.
- Strategic integration: The 2022–2025 Business Plan embeds objectives to support communities, reduce inequalities, and promote social, educational, and cultural inclusion. The Group invests to uphold essential rights—food, housing, healthcare/medicines, and education (including financial education).
- Approach and partnerships: Local initiatives aim both to generate positive community impact and capture material opportunities, positioning the Group as a leader in social impact through collaborations with non-profit entities.
- Policy framework and human rights: Commitment to community rights is formalized in the Code of Ethics, aligned with the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, and ILO principles. The Group is a UN Global Compact participant.
- Code of Ethics application areas:
  - Support to the non-profit sector and social enterprises via partnerships, networks, and replicable models for inclusion and community services.
  - Support to communities’ material and cultural needs through donations, sponsorships, and partnerships that enhance historical, artistic, cultural, and natural heritage.
  - Promotion of local economies in Italy and abroad, including support for SMEs and initiatives with high social and environmental value.
- Scope and processes: Principles apply across all community-related interventions, including disadvantaged groups and youth, and govern relations with NPOs through co-planning and partnerships; linked to ESRS G1 – Business Conduct.
- Implementation: The Group undertakes multiple tools, initiatives, and programs to support territories and communities.
- Funding and governance: The Articles of Association permit allocating distributable profits to a “Charity Allowance” managed by the Bank’s Presidency. The Board of Directors can make donations under an annual plan, including for emergencies and local needs; it coordinates disbursements, approves regulations with ESG considerations, defines criteria and lines of intervention, and exercises strategic oversight with support from the Risks and Sustainability Committee.

nodes.title: Policies and processes relating to the communities affected by own operations
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.1 Policies and processes relating to the communities affected by own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Group places great importance on projects that promote growth and social, educational, cultural and civic inclusion in the communities where it operates, thereby contributing to the development of more innovative and inclusive societies.
nodes.summary:
- The Group identifies material opportunities tied to improving brand reputation and stakeholder trust through actions on adequate housing, adequate food, and positive local territorial impacts, including support for youth, vulnerable people, social mobility, employability (especially for youth and women), social inclusion, and facilitated access to healthcare.
- Community support is embedded in corporate strategy and the 2022–2025 Business Plan, with objectives to address social needs, reduce inequalities, and promote social, educational, and cultural inclusion via substantial community investments and collaborations with the non-profit sector.
- The Group’s commitment to community rights is formalized in its Code of Ethics, aligned with the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines, and ILO conventions; the Group is a UN Global Compact participant.
- The Code of Ethics links to material topics—Adequate Housing, Adequate Food, and Territorial Impacts—and guides actions across three macro-areas: supporting the non-profit sector and social enterprises; meeting communities’ material and cultural needs through donations, sponsorships, and partnerships while enhancing artistic, cultural, and natural heritage; and promoting local economies, especially SMEs, in Italy and abroad with high social and environmental value initiatives.
- Principles apply to projects benefiting local communities, disadvantaged groups, and youth, and to partnerships with social enterprises and NPOs through co-planning; alignment with ESRS G1 (Business Conduct) is referenced.
- The Group supports communities through multiple tools, initiatives, and programs designed to create positive social impact.
- Governance and funding mechanisms include: an “Allowance for charitable, social and cultural contributions” funded from distributable profits and overseen by the Bank’s Presidency; Board of Directors’ authority to coordinate donations via an annual plan, including emergency responses; and strategic oversight—supported by the Risks and Sustainability Committee—defining criteria and lines of intervention in alignment with ESG priorities.

nodes.title: The Group's commitment to community rights

nodes.title: Social impact on the community
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.2 Social impact on the community
nodes.start_phrase: In implementing the general principles and values described above, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group plays an active role in supporting the local territories and communities in which it operates, through multiple tools, initiatives and programmes.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: The Consolidated Sustainability Statement details how the Group addresses communities affected by its own operations, linking social initiatives to financial materiality and corporate strategy.
- Materiality outcomes: Opportunities identified include enhanced brand reputation (adequate housing) and greater stakeholder trust (adequate food, territorial impacts). Example initiatives target youth and vulnerable people, combating educational poverty, fostering social mobility, youth employability, female entrepreneurship, social inclusion, and easing access to healthcare.
- Strategic integration: The 2022–2025 Business Plan sets objectives to support communities, reduce inequalities, and promote social, educational, and cultural inclusion. The Group invests to uphold essential rights—food, housing, healthcare and medicines, and education (including financial)—pursuing both social impact and positioning among leaders in social performance through partnerships with non-profits.
- Policy and human rights framework: Commitment to community rights is formalized in the Code of Ethics, aligned with the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines, and ILO conventions; the Group is a UN Global Compact member.
- Code of Ethics application: It guides relations with local communities across material topics—Adequate Housing, Adequate Food, and Territorial Impacts—structuring action in three macro-areas:
  - Supporting the non-profit sector via partnerships, networks of social enterprises, and scalable models for inclusion.
  - Addressing material and cultural needs through donations, sponsorships, and partnerships that also enhance historical, artistic, cultural, and natural heritage.
  - Promoting local economies in Italy and abroad, supporting SMEs, and initiatives with high social and environmental value.
- Scope and processes: Principles apply Group-wide to interventions for local communities, disadvantaged people, and youth, and to cooperation with social enterprises and NPOs via co-planning and partnerships; further governance details are referenced in ESRS G1 – Business Conduct.
- Community impact instruments and governance: The Articles of Association enable allocation of distributable profits to a “Charity Allowance” managed by the Bank’s Presidency. The Board of Directors, supported by the Risks and Sustainability Committee, defines criteria and lines of intervention, coordinates and regulates donations, and approves plans for worthy initiatives and emergencies, ensuring ESG alignment and strategic oversight.

nodes.title: Charity Allowance
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.2.1 Charity Allowance
nodes.start_phrase: The Charity Allowance aims to contribute to the achievement of the social objectives of the Intesa Sanpaolo Business Plan, providing support to the most vulnerable people also with a view to contributing to the achievement of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set by the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s approach to communities affected by its own operations within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Materiality and opportunities: Financial materiality analysis highlights brand and trust opportunities tied to adequate housing, adequate food, and local territorial impact through initiatives for youth, vulnerable groups, social mobility, employability, female entrepreneurship, inclusion, and facilitated access to healthcare.
- Strategic integration: Community support embedded in the 2022–2025 Business Plan with objectives to address social needs, combat inequalities, and promote social, educational, and cultural inclusion; investment policy targets essential rights (food, housing, healthcare, medicines, education/financial education).
- Governance and policy framework:
  - Code of Ethics aligned with UN UDHR, UNGPs, OECD Guidelines, ILO principles; UN Global Compact participant.
  - Code guides community relations across three macro-areas: support for the non-profit sector; donations/sponsorships consistent with values and heritage enhancement; promotion of local economies (Italy and abroad), support for SMEs, and high social/environmental value initiatives.
  - Application across social enterprises and NPOs; linkage to ESRS G1 – Business Conduct.
- Organizational setup for social impact:
  - Strengthened ESG governance; establishment (Apr 2024) of the Chief Social Impact Officer Governance Area under the Chief Sustainability Officer.
  - “Intesa Sanpaolo for Social Impact” oversees strategy, governance, and implementation, stakeholder relations, impact finance governance, social housing coordination, institutional relations, and leadership in social responsibility.
  - Social Action Plan developed from social context analysis and stakeholder dialogue; four Social Routes: (1) combat material/financial/educational poverty and promote employment access; (2) support access to health, care, and treatment; (3) promote social integration, local development, asset/space re-use, and social housing; (4) co-develop scalable projects with public institutions and social players.
  - Beneficiaries include youth/minors, women, people in poverty, seniors, vulnerable groups, communities, immigrants, refugees. An Observatory monitors social trends and needs; multi-channel communication of initiatives.
- Charity Allowance (charitable fund):
  - Authorized by the Articles of Association; supports Business Plan social objectives and UN SDGs.
  - Governed by a Regulation (2016) and biennial Guidelines separating charity from business interests; eligibility limited to compliant NPOs; exclusions include private citizens, political parties, unions, and most public entities except specific cases.
  - Project selection prioritizes clear social impact, proven capability, and efficient resource use.
  - Two donation streams: local (≤€5k) via Banca dei Territori; central (>€5k) via the Chair’s Technical Secretariat.
  - Governance: BoD sets criteria, oversees use; Chair selects €5k–€300k (after consultation with the MD); BoD approves >€300k; annual plan approved by BoD and Shareholders’ Meeting; transparency via public reporting on website.
  - Geographic focus: mostly Italy, prioritizing high-need areas (suburbs, inner areas, degraded contexts), with international projects in countries where the Group operates; coordination with International Banks Division foundations.
- Cultural commitment:
  - Internal rules for protection, conservation, and public enhancement of Group and third-party historical-artistic and archival assets; management of events, sponsorships, and cultural patronage.
  - Compliance with Italian Cultural Heritage Code and relevant national laws; responsibility lies with the Art, Culture and Heritage structure within the CSO area.
- Stakeholder engagement:
  - Ongoing, structured dialogue with civil society and community representatives to identify needs and high-impact action areas.
  - Engagement through meetings, events, partnerships, listening campaigns; co-planning with NPOs to design inclusive, sustainable solutions; the Group contributes resources, skills, and networks to build “solidarity ecosystems.”

nodes.title: Commitment to culture
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.1.2 Commitment to culture
nodes.start_phrase: In order to regulate the protection, conservation and enhancement of the historical -artistic assets and archival assets owned by the Group, as well as those belonging to third parties,
nodes.summary:
- Governance of philanthropic resources (Charity Allowance): clear oversight and decision-making thresholds (Chair, Managing Director consultation, Board approval >300k euro; Chair monitors all initiatives); annual resources plan approved by Board and Shareholders; transparency via public regulations and prior-year disbursement details (by beneficiary and amount) on the Group website.
- Allocation model: a portion of funds is assigned to Banca dei Territori for locally driven initiatives up to 5k euro; post-approval, funds are managed by the Head of Banca dei Territori and delegated to Regional Governance Centres.
- Geographic and strategic focus of giving: primary concentration in Italy, prioritizing areas of greatest need (suburbs, internal areas, marginalized contexts); international support for medium–large projects in countries where the Group operates, coordinated with the International Banks Division; efforts to standardize principles, rules, and reporting across geographies via the Chair’s Technical Secretariat.
- Cultural commitment: internal rules for protection, conservation, and enhancement of historical-artistic and archival assets (owned by the Group or managed via loans/use); governance of events, sponsorships, and cultural patronage; adherence to Italian Cultural Heritage Code (Legislative Decree 42/2004) and local laws for foreign subsidiaries; implementation led by the Art, Culture and Heritage unit within the Chief Sustainability Officer area.
- Engagement and reporting with communities: structured, continuous dialogue with civil society and stakeholder representatives; commitments to maintain communication channels, listen to expectations, analyze needs, and co-develop high social, cultural, and civic impact actions; initiatives co-planned with non-profits to meet local needs and create inclusive, sustainable solutions and “solidarity ecosystems,” with a focus on reducing inequalities and supporting youth and employability.

nodes.title: Engagement processes and reporting channels
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.1.3 Engagement processes and reporting channels
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group shapes its relationship with the community through opportunities for listening and dialogue with the various spheres of civil society.
nodes.summary:
- Governance of community investments (Charity Allowance): Board of Directors oversees resource use and alignment with objectives; Chair selects projects (with Managing Director consultation) for initiatives >€5k and ≤€300k; Board approves >€300k; Chair monitors all supported initiatives. Annual Plan of usable resources approved by Board and ratified by Shareholders’ Meeting.
- Decentralized local support: A share of Plan resources is assigned to Banca dei Territori for community-led initiatives up to €5k each, managed by the Head of Banca dei Territori and delegated to Regional Governance Centres.
- Transparency and rules: Regulations/Guidelines available on the Group website, including prior-year disbursements by recipient and amount.
- Geographic focus: Predominantly Italy, prioritizing high-need areas (suburbs, internal areas, marginalized contexts); international support for medium–large projects in countries where the Group operates, coordinated with the International Banks Division and its foundations to standardize principles, rules, and reporting.
- Engagement and document refinement: Three roundtables with specialized non-profits informed the drafting; ongoing structured dialogue with civil society to identify needs and co-design initiatives with non-profits, leveraging Group resources, skills, and networks.
- Cultural commitment and asset governance: Internal rules for managing historical–artistic and archival assets (owned and third-party loans), events and sponsorships, and cultural patronage; compliance with Italian Cultural Heritage Code (and relevant national laws for subsidiaries). Implementation led by the Art, Culture and Heritage unit under the Chief Sustainability Officer.
- Community engagement processes: Continuous stakeholder communication to listen, assess expectations, and develop high social, cultural, and civic impact actions; methods include meetings, events, partnerships, listening campaigns, and co-planning.
- Social Impact Observatory: Tracks social trends, promotes stakeholder-produced content, and guides Group action; supported by an external Advisory Committee; engagement responsibility rests with the initiating Group structures.
- Reporting channels and human rights: Multiple internal procedures for collecting and addressing possible non-compliance regarding community rights, including a Code of Ethics inbox; no serious human rights incidents identified via these channels.
- Flagship objective and metrics: “Cibo e Riparo per le persone in difficoltà” (Food and Shelter for the needy) program—largest private social plan in Italy—target of 50 million interventions in 2022–2025 Business Plan. By 31.12.2024, 54.1 million interventions achieved (43.5m meals, 3.9m beds, 6.1m drug prescriptions, ~560k clothing), including support for the Ukraine humanitarian emergency; 17.3m interventions in 2024 alone. Delivery via national non-profit partners, with predefined objectives and periodic impact reporting.
- Action areas outlined: Combating poverty; social cohesion and inclusion; youth education and employability; health and healthcare; crowdfunding platforms; Charity Allowance; financial education and literacy; cultural commitments; institutional initiatives supporting communities.

nodes.title: Objectives and metrics related to the communities affected by own operations
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.3 Objectives and metrics related to the communities affected by own operations
nodes.start_phrase: The Group's support to local territories and communities occurs through multiple methods, in terms of tools and initiatives.
nodes.summary:
- Establishment of an Observatory by Intesa Sanpaolo for Social Impact to identify key social trends, amplify stakeholder (academic, scientific, foundations) content, and steer Group social actions, supported by an external Advisory Committee; responsibility for community engagement sits with individual Group structures running initiatives.

- Delivery model based on partnerships with nationally recognized non-profits selected via social needs assessments; co-designed projects with predefined objectives, ongoing monitoring through agreed reporting, and partner-led impact reporting.
