nodes.title: Education and research
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.4.9.4 Education and research
nodes.start_phrase: Intesa Sanpaolo places great attention on young people and their right to education, training and access to the job market, investing in education and research.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Intesa Sanpaolo’s community and inclusion initiatives, highlighting long-standing support to non-profits and projects that foster youth inclusion, active citizenship, and cultural engagement (e.g., “Ponti” project, Fondazione Rava for Haiti’s Saint Damien hospital, Fondazione Severino and Fondazione Tender to Nave).
- Gender equality and women’s empowerment actions, including “About Women” dialogue series, “Women Value Company” award with Fondazione Marisa Bellisario, and focus on pay gap and workplace discrimination.
- Social reintegration through sport (e.g., “META INSIEME” for juvenile detainees) and support for inclusive cultural programs (Holocaust Remembrance Day Concert, “Metamorfosi” instruments crafted from migrant boats, “Progetto Genesi” traveling art collection, Special Olympics, “Campioni di Vita” school tour).
- Environmental partnerships and initiatives: collaboration with FAI’s “I Luoghi del Cuore,” restoration with Venice Gardens Foundation, support to San Patrignano’s Sustainable Economy Forum, One Ocean Foundation (ocean protection), and Daje de Alberi (Rome reforestation and urban regeneration).
- Health promotion and prevention: support for “Tennis & Friends” (free check-ups), “Tour della Salute” nationwide awareness roadshow, European Epilepsy Conference, and partnership with “CORRI LA VITA” for breast cancer prevention and care.
- Education and research investments focused on employability and reducing school dropout: support for 42Firenze (free, inclusive coding school) and “Young Factor” financial education initiative.
- Circular economy and asset reutilization for social value: “Donare per non sprecare” donates decommissioned but functional IT and furniture to nonprofits (in 2024: 1,092 IT assets to 133 entities; 3,170 furniture items to 70 entities); “Immobili che si muovono per il bene” provides properties to nonprofits on favorable terms to enable self-sustaining activities, job creation, and inclusion of vulnerable people; both governed by internal process guides.
- International Banks Division (IBD) community programs targeting educational poverty, inclusion, and healthcare: Nadacia VUB in Slovakia (over €450k; “Every child has a chance” for children with disabilities; flood relief with “People in Need”); Intesa Foundation in Serbia (est. March 2024; over €800k; healthcare and inclusion with partners like UNICEF, SOS Children’s Villages); structured monitoring and reputational benefits.
- Governance of impacts on communities linked to financed projects via the Equator Principles (EPs): Group adherence and implementation overseen by the Risk Chief Officer Governance Area; integration with internal ESG risk and reputational processes; application to specific project-related financial products across all geographies.
- EP-driven social risk assessment and requirements: evaluation of human rights and indigenous peoples’ rights; client obligations for culturally appropriate stakeholder engagement, impact assessment, and mitigation/compensation aligned with community laws and customs; bank monitoring of client compliance and remediation.
- Ongoing attention to external reports from NGOs and community representatives; no quantitative targets yet for actions toward affected communities, with effectiveness monitored through EP application.

nodes.title: IBD Division initiatives
nodes.heading: 4.3.2.4.10 IBD Division initiatives
nodes.start_phrase: In order to address emerging needs in the local contexts where the Group operates, which affect the most vulnerable people in particular, the International Banks Division (IBD) is actively committed to supporting local communities,
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the International Banks Division (IBD) on community support in local contexts, targeting educational poverty among youth, social inclusion, and healthcare.
- Key implementing entities: Nadacia VUB and VUB Banka Foundations in Slovakia; Intesa Foundation (established March 2024) and Banca Intesa Beograd Foundation in Serbia.
- Slovakia initiatives: over 450,000 euro financed via Nadacia VUB, including “Every child has a chance” supporting five organizations assisting children with disabilities and their families, plus aid through NGO People in Need for communities affected by floods.
- Serbia initiatives: over 800,000 euro via Intesa Foundation for healthcare improvements, learning support for children with disabilities or in vulnerable situations, and social inclusion programs, in partnership with NGOs such as UNICEF and SOS Children’s Villages.
- Project monitoring through ongoing dialogue with involved entities to verify implementation and impact objectives; initiatives also strengthen Group reputation locally.
- Governance of affected communities in project finance: adherence to the Equator Principles (since 2007), aligned with IFC Performance Standards and World Bank EHS Guidelines, emphasizing community consultation, indigenous peoples’ rights, and cultural heritage protection.
- Scope: EPs apply Group-wide to specified financial products supporting new project development (e.g., project finance, project-related corporate loans, bridge loans, and related refinancing/acquisitions), with oversight by the Risk Chief Officer Governance Area.
- Complementary internal frameworks: Guidelines for ESG risk management and the ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process (cross-referenced with standard E1 – Climate Change).
- Process: Social/human rights risk assessment and risk rating; based on risk, clients must conduct structured, culturally appropriate stakeholder engagement, disclose potential negative impacts per UN Guiding Principles, and, where indigenous peoples are affected, ensure respect for rights, culture, livelihoods, and tailored mitigation/compensation.
- Roles: Clients maintain direct community engagement; the Bank reviews documentation, monitors compliance with EP obligations, and interfaces with clients to ensure remedial measures when serious issues are reported by impacted communities.
- Additional oversight: Monitoring and addressing reports from NGOs or representatives of affected communities.
- Metrics and targets: No quantitative data or specific objectives yet for actions toward communities impacted by portfolio undertakings; effectiveness monitoring tied to EP application.

nodes.title: Affected communities by the undertakings included in the Group’s portfolios
nodes.heading: 4.3.3 Affected communities by the undertakings included in the Group’s portfolios
nodes.start_phrase: The Equator Principles (EPs) are international guidelines that the Intesa Sanpaolo Group voluntarily adhered to since 2007, applicable to the financing of infrastructure and industrial projects that could have negative impacts on the environment and people,
nodes.summary:
- The International Banks Division (IBD) supports local communities with a focus on combating educational poverty, promoting social inclusion, and strengthening healthcare, primarily through Nadacia VUB and VUB Banka Foundations in Slovakia and Intesa Foundation/Banca Intesa Beograd Foundation in Serbia.
- Slovakia: Nadacia VUB financed over €450k, including “Every child has a chance” supporting 5 organizations aiding disabled children and families, and initiatives with “People in Need” for flood-affected areas.
- Serbia: Intesa Foundation (established March 2024) allocated over €800k to healthcare, learning support for children with disabilities/vulnerable situations, and social inclusion programs, partnering with UNICEF and SOS Children’s Villages.
- Projects are monitored through ongoing dialogue to verify implementation and impact objectives; initiatives meet community needs in health, education, inclusion, and strengthen Group reputation.

- The Group has applied the Equator Principles (EPs) since 2007 to project-related financing globally, aligned with IFC Performance Standards and EHS Guidelines; oversight sits within the Risk Chief Officer Governance Area and is supported by internal ESG risk guidelines and an ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing process.
- EP application includes assessment of social and human rights risks affecting local and indigenous communities; projects receive a risk rating, and clients must conduct culturally appropriate stakeholder engagement and report human rights risks in line with the UN Guiding Principles.
- For projects affecting indigenous peoples, clients must ensure respect for rights, culture, and livelihoods; mitigation and compensation must reflect community laws, institutions, and customs.
- Clients engage directly with communities; the Bank reviews documentation, monitors compliance with EP obligations, and works with clients to ensure remedial actions when serious impacts are reported; it also considers reports from NGOs and community representatives.
- Quantitative metrics on actions toward impacted communities are not yet available; no specific objectives are set, with effectiveness monitoring tied to EP application.

- Under ESRS S4 (Consumers and end-users), the Group conducted a double materiality assessment across own operations and the downstream value chain (no material upstream impacts/risks identified), analyzing controls, policies, and data protection measures.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts on privacy protection, freedom of expression, consumer health and safety, and personal security.
  - Downstream value chain: material positive impacts on access to quality information, non-discrimination, access to products and services, and responsible business practices.
- Financial materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material operational risk related to privacy, leading to material reputational risk; compliance risk also considered.
  - Downstream value chain: strategic risk, with potential reputational implications; no material upstream risk identified.
- Opportunities identified include strengthening stakeholder trust via customer safeguards and communications, and expanding inclusive product offerings to ensure access for all social groups, including the most vulnerable.

nodes.title: ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 4.4 ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users within a consolidated sustainability statement, detailing a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) tailored to the Group’s context.
- Scope and stakeholders: Considers own operations, upstream, and downstream value chains; covers all customer/end-user categories (institutional, corporate, retail, private individuals).
- Methodology: Interviews with internal teams and external experts; qualitative-quantitative analysis using regulatory criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood); review of internal controls, policies, and data protection measures.
- Impact materiality findings:
  - Own operations: Material positive impacts on privacy protection, freedom of expression, health and physical safety, and personal security.
  - Downstream value chain: Material positive impacts on access to quality information, non-discrimination, access to products/services, and responsible business practices (including fair treatment, ethical and transparent conduct, website accessibility). Investment/lending criteria considered in counterparties assessment.
  - Upstream value chain: No material impacts identified due to the nature of the issue.
- Financial materiality (risks):
  - Own operations: Operational and compliance risks identified, leading to potential reputational risk.
  - Downstream value chain: Strategic risk identified, also potentially leading to reputational risk.
  - Upstream value chain: No risks identified.
  - Material financial risk: Operational risk related to privacy deemed material; associated reputational risk also material.
- Financial materiality (opportunities):
  - Own operations: Existing/planned customer safeguards and initiatives that can increase stakeholder trust.
  - Downstream value chain: Potential to expand product range to ensure access for all social groups, including vulnerable customers.
- Overall: Positive consumer/end-user impacts and strong data protection/customer safeguards can translate into financial opportunities, while privacy-related operational risks pose material financial and reputational concerns.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.4.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS2 – General disclosures: Double materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users section of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement for Intesa Sanpaolo Group.
- Method: Double materiality assessment (impact and financial) covering own operations and downstream value chain; upstream value chain deemed non-material for this topic.
- Impact materiality:
  - Approach: Interviews with internal/external stakeholders and qualitative‑quantitative analysis based on scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood.
  - Own operations: Material positive impacts on privacy protection, freedom of expression, health and safety, and personal security.
  - Downstream value chain: Material positive impacts on access to quality information, non-discrimination, access to products/services, and responsible business practices.
- Financial materiality:
  - Risks: 
    - Own operations: Operational and compliance risks (with consequent reputational risk); privacy-related operational risk is material.
    - Downstream value chain: Strategic risk (with consequent reputational risk).
    - Upstream value chain: No risks identified.
  - Opportunities:
    - Own operations: Policies and safeguards that build stakeholder trust; protection of customers and their freedom of expression.
    - Downstream value chain: Expanding product range and access for all social groups, including vulnerable customers.
- Customer feedback: Systematic use of customer input and complaints to refine offerings; ongoing listening and service quality monitoring.
- Human rights commitments:
  - Customer relations grounded in corporate values and respect for human rights; focus on security, fairness, transparency, and financial inclusion of vulnerable groups.
  - Commitments include structured stakeholder dialogue, timely handling of queries/complaints, robust protection of people/assets/data (including digital identity), privacy transparency, non-discrimination, and careful suitability/needs assessment in advice, lending, and insurance.
  - Reporting channels (e.g., Code of Ethics inbox) active; no serious human rights incidents or non-compliance with UNGPs, ILO, OECD guidelines detected.

nodes.title: The Group’s commitment to human rights
nodes.heading: 4.4.2 The Group’s commitment to human rights
nodes.start_phrase: The Group believes that proper customer relations must be based on shared corporate values and respect for human rights in all products and services provided to customers.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s approach to customer-focused sustainability, emphasizing financial materiality findings that highlight opportunities from internal policies/strategies and from offering and enabling access to products and services in the downstream value chain.
- Customer feedback, including complaints, is positioned as a key driver to refine offerings, tailor products to real needs, and monitor service quality.
- The Group’s Code of Ethics underpins a commitment to human rights in all customer relationships, promoting continuous dialogue, fairness, transparency, and protection of customers’ security, assets, information, and digital identity.
- Strong emphasis on financial inclusion, with particular attention to vulnerable social groups, and on non-discrimination across a wide range of protected characteristics.
- Concrete commitments include: systematic stakeholder dialogue tools; timely responses to queries/complaints; high standards of reliability, continuity, and confidentiality; clear privacy information; and careful assessment of customer needs and risk profiles to guide advice, lending, savings, and insurance.
- Governance and accountability mechanisms include multiple internal channels and procedures to collect and address potential non-compliance regarding consumer and human rights; the Code of Ethics inbox is highlighted as a reporting channel.
- The Group reports no detected serious human rights incidents or non-compliance with UNGPs, ILO principles, or OECD Guidelines within the referenced period.
- Policies for service quality, customer satisfaction, and responsible sales ensure clear, comprehensible, and consistent information throughout the customer relationship, with key documents publicly available under “Banking Transparency.”
- Compliance and organizational controls support customer protection regulations, ensuring transparency and fairness at product placement and throughout the contractual lifecycle.
- In investments, customers receive personalized advisory services aligned to their financial profiles; staff must follow specific rules and safeguards for advisory and investment services, issued by the Board of Directors on the compliance area’s proposal and applied across relevant Group entities.

nodes.title: Service Quality – Customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.heading: 4.4.3 Service Quality – Customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.start_phrase: In a context of correct and transparent relationships between intermediaries and customers, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group makes the information it provides to its customers clear and comprehensible in all stages of their relationship through the simplicity of its language, transparent policy statements, and consistent terms and conditions among the various documents relating to the same products/services.
nodes.summary:
- Financial materiality analysis identified opportunities to strengthen internal policies and strategies that protect customers and their freedom of expression, and to expand downstream access to and offering of customer-focused products and services.
- Strong emphasis on capturing and acting on customer feedback and complaints; continuous listening and service quality monitoring to tailor offerings to actual needs.
- Human rights commitment embedded in the Code of Ethics: ongoing dialogue with customers; protection of customer security, assets, and information; fairness and transparency; focus on financial inclusion of vulnerable groups.
- Specific undertakings include:
  - Systematic dialogue tools with customers and their associations.
  - Timely responses to queries and complaints.
  - Protection of people, valuables, assets, and digital identity; organizational measures ensuring reliability, continuity, and confidentiality.
  - Transparent communication on privacy rights and personal data processing.
  - Non-discrimination across a wide range of personal characteristics, including freedom of expression.
  - Careful assessment of customer needs and risk profiles to guide advice, savings management, responsible lending, and insurance.
- Governance and remediation: multiple internal channels (including Code of Ethics inbox) to report potential non-compliance with consumer and human rights; no serious incidents or non-compliance with UNGPs, ILO principles, or OECD Guidelines detected.
- Customer satisfaction and responsible sales policies: clear, comprehensible, and consistent information across documents; transparency via materials available in branches and online (“Banking Transparency”); organizational controls to ensure customer protection and fair conduct throughout the relationship.
- Investment services: highest protection through personalized advisory aligned to each client’s financial profile; staff adhere to defined conduct and safeguard rules; rules issued by the Board on Compliance’s proposal and applied across relevant Italian Group companies.

nodes.title: Policies on customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.heading: 4.4.3.1 Policies on customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.start_phrase: In a context of correct and transparent relationships between intermediaries and customers, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group makes the information it provides to its customers clear and comprehensible in all stages of their relationship through the simplicity of its language, transparent policy statements, and consistent terms and conditions among the various documents relating to the same products/services.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer-centric materiality: identifies opportunities from internal policies that protect customers and freedom of expression, and from enhancing access to products/services across the downstream value chain.
- Emphasis on using customer feedback and complaints to refine offerings; ongoing listening and service quality monitoring are pivotal.
- Strong human rights commitment in customer relations, guided by the Group’s Code of Ethics: continuous dialogue, protection of customer security/assets/information (including digital identity), fairness, transparency, and financial inclusion for vulnerable groups.
- Explicit undertakings include: structured stakeholder dialogue, timely responses to queries/complaints, privacy transparency, non-discrimination, and careful assessment of customer needs and risk profiles for advice, savings, lending, and insurance.
- Governance and reporting on human rights: multiple internal channels (e.g., Code of Ethics inbox) to report potential non-compliance; no serious incidents found against UNGPs, ILO principles, or OECD guidelines.
- Customer satisfaction and responsible sales policies: clear, comprehensible information at all relationship stages; standardized transparent documents available in branches and online; organizational safeguards and compliance checks ensure fairness and regulatory adherence.
- Investment advisory aligned with EU/Italian regulations: personalized recommendations based on client profiles; internal rules approved by the Board and accessible on the intranet; post‑MiFID II framework strengthens investor protection, product governance, staff competence, and cost transparency.
- Integration of sustainability in investments: explicit survey of clients’ sustainability preferences; ESG alignment in portfolio construction; client reports include sustainability preferences and portfolio composition.
- “Valore Insieme” offers an advanced, personalized advisory platform with dedicated relationship management for comprehensive portfolio construction, protection, and transfer.
- Robust Product Governance process from concept to post‑marketing monitoring: cross‑functional compliance assessments, clear target market definition, ESG considerations, and continuous verification of product/service suitability.
- Complaints management framework: Group guidelines for complaints, supervisory protests, and ADR appeals ensure transparent, fair, and timely resolutions; guidelines issued by the Parent Board, implemented across Group entities; website provides procedures and response times; determinations follow external/internal rules and the Code of Ethics.
- Regulatory reporting: annual reporting to corporate bodies and authorities (Bank of Italy, Consob, IVASS) on complaints, requests, and adequacy of procedures.
- Customer engagement model: business-area service structure with multi-channel coverage in Italy and abroad; dedicated functions monitor customer satisfaction and experience across divisions.

nodes.title: Customer engagement processes
nodes.heading: 4.4.3.2 Customer engagement processes
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has adopted a service model structured by business area, with an organisational structure that ensures coverage in Italy and in the other countries in which it operates, with the task of developing the best service quality through various channels, in order to make the commercial offer more effective across the different types of customers.
nodes.summary:
- Strong regulatory alignment and transparency: Group rules are consistent with EU Directives and Italian laws, accessible on the #Legislation intranet portal. Post‑MiFID II, the Group enhanced investor protection through stricter governance of financial instruments, staff knowledge requirements, and comprehensive ex ante/ex post cost and incentive disclosures.
- Integration of sustainability in investments: Suitability processes now capture customers’ sustainability preferences per ESMA guidelines, including minimum ESG allocations; staff and customers receive specific sustainability information, and periodic client reports include ESG preferences and portfolio composition.
- Advisory offering: “Valore Insieme” provides an advanced, personalized, end‑to‑end wealth advisory service via branch managers and a dedicated platform.
- Robust Product Governance framework: End‑to‑end lifecycle oversight (concept, feasibility, clearing, approval, monitoring) for Group and third‑party products, with clear target market definition, ESG assessment, and continuous post‑marketing checks; ongoing compliance verification ensures fairness, customer protection, and information quality; framework aligned with Bank of Italy, IVASS, and Consob provisions.
- Structured complaints management: Group guidelines define transparent, fair handling of complaints, protests, and ADR appeals; multiple channels (app/website, email/PEC, mail, fax); dedicated IT system maintains a Complaint Register, tracks timelines, and ensures clear, timely responses with reasons or remedies; website outlines how to file and response timeframes.
- Regulatory reporting: Compliance function provides at least annual reporting to corporate bodies and authorities on complaints, requests received, and adequacy of procedures.
- Customer engagement and service quality: Service model by business area with continuous monitoring by Customer Satisfaction/Experience teams; tools include NPS, NSI, and the SEIok program; Banca dei Territori operates a comprehensive feedback system to identify and act on improvement areas.
- Continuous improvement actions: “Close the loop” mechanisms convert feedback into concrete actions, including customer re‑contact to address unmet expectations and reduce dissatisfaction; monthly complaint analyses sent to business owners to drive remediation; ongoing staff training and intranet resources.
- Quality monitoring tools and roll‑outs: “Customer Experience in Branch” portal expanded in 2024 to Enterprise, Agribusiness, and Impact areas; Digital Branch testing started Nov 2024 with release planned early 2025.
- Approach to targets: Focus on maintaining high service standards through constant monitoring and guidance rather than fixed quantitative targets, using NPS and related metrics to steer actions.

nodes.title: Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.heading: 4.4.3.3 Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.start_phrase: Complaints are handled by means of a dedicated IT procedure, which records the complaints and generates a “Complaint Register”.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer satisfaction management within Intesa Sanpaolo’s Banca dei Territori Division, outlining a structured feedback system using NPS (Net Promoter Score), NSI (Net Satisfaction Index), and the SEIok Programme to identify improvements and support service quality.
- Clear customer complaint channels via the Group’s app and website, information sheets, and written agreements (email, certified email, mail, fax), with handling governed by internal regulations.
- Detailed remediation and complaint-handling process: a dedicated IT procedure creates a Complaint Register, tracks all steps, and ensures compliance with response-time laws; alignment with Bank of Italy guidance (18 March 2016); timely, clear communications including acknowledgments, delay notices if needed, and outcome letters explaining reasons for rejection or measures/reimbursements when upheld.
- Approach to targets emphasizes continuous improvement and active monitoring over fixed quantitative goals, leveraging NPS within customer engagement processes.
- Ongoing actions to improve experience and responsible sales: monthly reporting of complaints to business owners to drive mitigation; “close the loop” initiatives; proactive customer re-contact based on survey feedback to strengthen relationships and reduce dissatisfaction.
- Strengthened quality oversight in Banca dei Territori: integration of quality management and control; expansion of the “Customer Experience in Branch” portal—launched in 2023 (Retail and Exclusive), extended in 2024 (Enterprise, Agribusiness, Impact), with Digital Branch testing in Nov 2024 and release planned early 2025.
- Staff enablement through regular alignment and training for complaint-handling teams; regulations accessible on the intranet.
- Group-level reporting includes an annual assessment of the complaints framework and its adequacy, plus trend analysis covering complaints and reiterations (“customer appeals”), ADR appeals, and clarification requests.

nodes.title: Targets related to customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.heading: 4.4.3.4 Targets related to customer satisfaction and responsible sales
nodes.start_phrase: One of the fundamental drivers of a service quality culture is the continuous process of improving the customer experience.
nodes.summary:
- Customer feedback system: Banca dei Territori Division uses NPS, NSI, and the SEIok Programme to gather feedback, spot issues early, and drive continuous service improvements.
- Complaint channels: Customers can submit complaints via the app, website “Complaints and Dispute Resolution” sections, and multiple written channels (email/PEC, mail, fax); processes are governed by internal regulations.
- Complaint management process: A dedicated IT system logs all complaints in a “Complaint Register,” tracks workflow steps, and monitors compliance with legal response times.
- Regulatory alignment: Procedures follow internal rules and Bank of Italy guidance (18 March 2016 communication on complaints offices).
- Customer communication standards: Clear, simple, timely responses are required; customers are notified upon receipt, and informed if investigation delays exceed statutory limits.
- Outcome handling: Responses explain reasons when unfounded; when (partly) founded, they specify corrective measures, reimbursement/compensation details, and timelines.
- Service quality governance: The Group emphasizes continuous monitoring rather than fixed quantitative targets, leveraging NPS within customer engagement to assess effectiveness.
- Actions to improve satisfaction: Monthly reporting of complaints to business owners to trigger corrective actions; a “close the loop” system translates insights into concrete improvements.
- Re-contact initiatives: Follow-up calls to survey respondents strengthen relationships, use NPS insights, and reduce dissatisfaction/complaints through active listening.
- Division-wide quality oversight: Banca dei Territori enhances monitoring and fosters a quality culture; the “Customer Experience in Branch” portal provides customer-perceived quality insights and operational support.
- Portal rollout: Launched in 2023 for Retail and Exclusive; expanded in 2024 to Enterprise, Agribusiness, and Impact; Digital Branch testing started Nov 2024 with release planned early 2025.
- Staff enablement: Regular alignment and training for complaint-handling teams; applicable regulations available on the intranet.
- Oversight and reporting: An annual Group report reviews the complaint-handling setup, its adequacy, and trends across complaints, reiterations (“customer appeals”), ADR appeals, and requests for clarifications.

nodes.title: Policies on customer data protection
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.1 Policies on customer data protection
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has always maintained a high and constant commitment to protecting its customers’ personal data, ensuring that such data is collected and processed in compliance with current legislative provisions.
nodes.summary:
- Complaints governance and monitoring
  - Group submits a Complaints Report to supervisory authorities and publishes a “Complaints Management Report” on its website.
  - Quarterly tracking of complaint trends against Group-level early warning thresholds.
  - Continuous monitoring of complaint handling times, reported in dedicated metrics.

- Customer satisfaction and responsible sales metrics
  - Branch network: Italy 2,971; Other Europe 770 + 1 Representative Office; America 2 + 1 Rep Office; Asia 7 + 6 Rep Offices; Africa 174 + 1 Rep Office; Australia/Oceania 1.
  - Net Promoter Score (approx. 657,000 interviews across phone, email, app, internet banking):
    - Retail 38; Exclusive 34; Enterprises 24; Non-Profit 33; Agribusiness 24.

- Complaint response performance (average processing times vs. regulatory limits)
  - Banking Services (ORD): 16 days vs 60 days.
  - Investment Services (SIM): 35 days vs 60 days.
  - Insurance Services/Products (ASS): 18 days vs 45 days.
  - Payment Systems (PAG): 14 days vs 15 business days.

- Customer data protection policies and governance
  - GDPR-based framework embedded in the Group’s Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct; principles include accountability, privacy by design/default, PIAs, Records of Processing, third-party roles, and data breach management.
  - Privacy policy clarified and made more transparent (with charts); explicit, free, unambiguous consent required for marketing; no processing for unstated secondary purposes; disciplinary actions for non-compliance.
  - Compliance across EU and non-EU jurisdictions through Group Guidelines and Corporate Rules; annual reviews and coordinated approval process; detailed operating instructions for processors.

- Data Protection Officer (DPO) and privacy function
  - DPO appointed by the Board; privacy function within the Chief Compliance Officer area.
  - Tasks: GDPR compliance monitoring; prior checks on new initiatives; PIAs; supplier/third-party role assessment and appointments; handling data subject rights; managing regulator and complainant responses; Group guidance/coordination; maintaining the Record of Processing Activities; breach assessment; third-party list maintenance; training oversight.

- Cybersecurity and security organization
  - Cybersecurity process guide defining monitoring/issue management processes, aligned with Legislative Decree 231/01; available on intranet.
  - 2024 establishment of the Chief Security Officer Governance Area overseeing cybersecurity, business continuity/resilience, corporate and physical security strategy, policies, and models.

- Customer engagement and remediation
  - Public privacy policy detailing data types, purposes/legal bases, retention, recipients, data subject rights and how to exercise them, and DPO contacts; consent requirements for marketing reiterated; 2023 revision incorporated customer feedback.
  - Critical event management model to mitigate reputational and compliance risks; DPO handles non-compliance events and breach notifications to the Authority and, where high risk, to data subjects.
  - Updated (2023) Guidelines and Corporate Rules reinforce roles, principles, obligations, and sanctions.
  - Complaint channels: data subjects can contact the DPO via email/PEC or hard copy; privacy function tracks and ensures responses within GDPR timeframes (normally within one month).
  - Internal controls: control functions and Chief Audit Officer perform periodic, risk-based audits; outcomes reported to the Board; DPO submits at least an annual report to the Board on significant data protection issues.

nodes.title: Customer engagement processes
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.2 Customer engagement processes
nodes.start_phrase: The Group makes the privacy policy available to all the persons with whom it interacts.
nodes.summary:
- Establishment of the Chief Security Officer (CSeO) Governance Area in 2024, responsible for Groupwide cybersecurity, business continuity/resilience, and physical/corporate security strategy, policies, and models.
- Customer privacy approach: public, accessible privacy policy detailing data types, purposes and legal bases, retention, recipients, data subject rights and how to exercise them, and DPO contacts; processing limited to stated purposes only.
- Marketing data processing requires free, explicit, unambiguous consent; absence or denial of consent prevents use for marketing.
- 2023 update of the customer privacy policy to improve clarity and transparency (including charts), informed by customer focus groups.
- Channels for complaints and rights requests: data subjects can contact the DPO via website-listed contacts (email/PEC or hard copy); requests are handled confidentially and monitored by the privacy function for timely processing per GDPR (generally within one month, extendable to two).
- Critical event management model for incident handling to mitigate reputational risks in data processing; DPO manages non-compliance, assesses data breach risks, notifies the Authority and, when required, affected data subjects.
- 2023 updates to personal data protection guidelines and corporate rules: define compliance risk management model, roles and responsibilities, obligations for processing and protection, and sanctions for non-compliance.
- Integrated internal control system: Control Functions conduct compliance checks and report outcomes to the Board of Directors; Chief Audit Officer performs periodic and risk-based audits, evaluates the effectiveness of the data protection compliance risk management model, and reports irregularities.

nodes.title: Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.3 Remediation processes and channels to submit complaints
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group has adopted a critical event management model that sets out the steps for the efficient management of incidents.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and security: Establishment of the Chief Security Officer (CSeO) Governance Area in 2024 to define groupwide strategy, policies and models for cybersecurity, business continuity/resilience, and corporate/physical security.
- Customer privacy policy and transparency: Publicly available policy detailing data types, purposes and legal bases, retention, recipients, data subject rights, and DPO contacts; processing limited to stated purposes; explicit consent required for marketing. Policy was revised in 2023 for greater clarity and transparency, incorporating customer feedback and visual aids.
- Complaints and remediation: A critical event management model guides incident handling. The DPO manages non-compliance, assesses breach risks, and notifies authorities/data subjects when required. Updated 2023 guidelines and corporate rules define roles, obligations, and sanctions. Multiple channels to contact the DPO are provided; requests are processed confidentially within GDPR timelines. Control Functions and Internal Audit conduct periodic, risk-based checks and report to the Board; the DPO provides at least annual reporting on significant issues.
- Targets and monitoring: While no quantitative targets are set, customer data protection is governed by policies and ongoing monitoring, with metrics used in incident and threat analysis to assess performance and effectiveness.
- Customer privacy actions: Risk-based compliance applying privacy by design/default. Ongoing mandatory e-learning with monitored completion. Third-party oversight in 2024 via 106 supplier self-assessments and 10 on-site visits, with generally medium/high control levels; 2025 focus on gaps. Data protection setup for the new Isybank and continued development of an integrated platform for Records of Processing and privacy processes through 2025. Continued coordination with EU companies and tighter controls for higher-risk non-EU branches.
- Fraud prevention: Rising 2024 threats include phishing/social engineering, malware, payment swindles, and money muling. Countermeasures include behavioral customer monitoring, the Customer Security Enforcement program (device certification and phasing out SMS in favor of a non-transferable dynamic logo), rule optimization, and data analytics/machine learning—ongoing through 2025. Expanded anti–money muling awareness and prevention, and participation since 2024 in industry/system initiatives (e.g., FPAD) to strengthen international anti-fraud defenses.

nodes.title: Targets related to customer data protection
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.4 Targets related to customer data protection

- Third-party privacy oversight in 2024: self-assessment questionnaires (106 suppliers) and 10 on-site visits, generally showing medium/high control levels; 2025 focus on non-responders and suppliers with weaker controls.
- Compliance setup for the new Isybank, defining processes and controls continuing into 2025.
- Development of an integrated platform to strengthen Records of Processing Activities and core privacy processes; development, testing, and fine-tuning through 2025.
- International oversight: coordination and information flows for EU companies; tighter controls for non-EU branches with higher volumes of personal data to reduce compliance risk.
- Overview of 2024 fraud trends: phishing and social engineering (mainly retail), malware (mainly corporate), authorized push payment swindles, and money muling.

nodes.title: Customer privacy actions
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.5 Customer privacy actions
nodes.start_phrase: Using a risk -based approach, the Data Protection Officer controls compliance risk by applying the principles of privacy by design, and privacy by default, to control of the risk of non -compliance with data protection legislation both at the stage when personal data processing is designed or significantly modified and during the data processing by adopting, as a default setting, the appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure an appropriate level of security.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer data protection through policies, continuous monitoring, and a critical event management model using performance metrics; no fixed quantitative targets but emphasis on high service standards.
- Privacy governance based on a risk-based approach, applying privacy by design and by default, with the Data Protection Officer overseeing compliance at design/change and processing stages.
- Employee awareness and mandatory e-learning with testing; participation and pass rates monitored.
- Third-party privacy oversight in 2024 via 106 supplier self-assessments and 10 on-site visits; most showed medium/high controls. 2025 priorities target non-completers and low-control suppliers.
- Establishment of data protection requirements, processes, and controls for the new Isybank, continuing into 2025.
- Ongoing development of an integrated platform to strengthen Record of Processing Activities (ROPA) and core privacy processes, with rollout/testing through 2025.
- International oversight: coordination and information flows for EU companies; tighter controls for non-EU branches with higher processing volumes to reduce compliance risk.
- Rising fraud sophistication in 2024: phishing/social engineering (mainly retail), malware (mainly corporate), swindles, and money muling.
- Anti-fraud measures include:
  - Behavioral Customer Monitoring (BCM) to risk-score transactions, continuing in 2025.
  - Customer Security Enforcement (CSE): device certification and phasing out SMS in favor of a dynamic, non-transferable logo.
  - Rule optimization from ongoing fraud analysis.
  - Data analytics and machine learning initiatives started in 2022 and continuing to 2025.
- Expanded, structured initiatives against money muling since 2023: customer awareness, detection, and prevention, ongoing to 2025.
- Since 2024, participation in industry/system-level anti-fraud collaborations, including the Fraud Pattern and Anomaly Detection (FPAD) project.

nodes.title: Actions to protect customers against fraudulent transactions
nodes.heading: 4.4.4.6 Actions to protect customers against fraudulent transactions

- Fraud risk landscape and countermeasures: 2024 saw advanced phishing/social engineering (primarily retail), malware (primarily corporate), swindles/APP scams, and money muling. Countermeasures include continuous threat analysis; Behavioral Customer Monitoring (ongoing to 2025); Customer Security Enforcement (device certification and phasing out SMS in favor of a non-transferable dynamic logo); rule optimization; data analytics and machine learning (launched 2022, continuing to 2025); expanded money muling awareness/detection/prevention (since 2023, continuing to 2025); and industry collaboration (e.g., FPAD).
- Privacy metrics (2024): In Italy, 186 customer data breach cases assessed (78 at Intesa Sanpaolo); 171 posed no risk and required no notification; 15 were notified to the Authority, with 4 also reported to data subjects. EU foreign companies reported 85 incidents; 4 notified to local authorities (2 also to data subjects); 81 posed no risk.
- Anti-fraud metrics (2024): Blocked fraudulent transactions totaling about €76.4m for private customers and €20.2m for corporate customers. Starting 2024, figures distinguish frauds vs. swindles: blocked frauds of ~€8.4m (private) and ~€4.2m (corporate); swindles of ~€68m (private) and ~€16m (corporate).

nodes.title: Customer privacy metrics

nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, 186 cases (78 of which related to Intesa Sanpaolo) of loss or theft of Group customers’ data (Data Breaches) were assessed in Italy, 171 of which (65 related to Intesa Sanpaolo) were not found to pose a risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects and therefore did not need to be notified to the Italian Data Protection Authority.
nodes.summary:
- Customer privacy metrics (2024): In Italy, 186 data breach cases assessed (78 at Intesa Sanpaolo); 171 posed no risk and required no notification; 15 were notified to the Italian Data Protection Authority; 4 were also communicated to data subjects (all at Intesa Sanpaolo, 3 involving employees). EU-based foreign subsidiaries reported 85 alleged breaches; 4 notified to local authorities, 2 also to data subjects; 81 assessed as no risk, so no notification required.

nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group maintains a constant dialogue with its customers to ensure top -tier service.
nodes.summary:
- Framework for classifying sustainable finance: 277 categories across environmental, social, and other sustainability; credit products flagged by internal working groups; lending classified as sustainable if tied to eligible activities, zero‑emission sectors, or KPI‑linked sustainability targets. Classification occurs at application and is monitored for stability over the loan’s life.

- Customer engagement and transparency: use of surveys, listening tools, and industry initiatives (e.g., ACEPI) to align products with evolving needs and improve advisory clarity; direct dialogues and feedback loops (e.g., Social Impact Roadshow 2024) to capture non‑economic impacts and drive continuous improvement.

- Inclusive credit solutions: Banca dei Territori Division develops socially oriented products to bridge gaps (e.g., low university attainment), using market research (Istat, Eurostat) and focus groups; Gamma Impact products for students and unemployed offer favorable terms and extended repayment to expand access to credit; ongoing customer experience and satisfaction monitoring across channels; staff feedback informs process and service enhancements.

- Complaints and remediation: multiple submission channels (online, app, mail, email, branch); emphasis on timely, effective resolution; compliance function provides regular (at least annual) reporting on complaint handling; Code of Ethics enables reporting of non‑compliance via a dedicated email for substantive dispute resolution.

- ESG targets and support for businesses: ESG prioritized in the 2022–2025 Business Plan; support for companies and supply chains to assess sustainability levels and develop transition plans aligned with the NRRP; expansion of ESG Workshops (exceeding one per Regional Centre) offering guidance with institutional and technical partners; broad promotion via press, website, social media, and partner channels; aim to embed ESG in decision‑making and position ecological transition as an innovation and growth opportunity.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.4 Targets and metrics related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has set itself the objective of promoting ESG practices, included as a priority in the 2022 -2025 Business Plan, by raising awareness among companies and their supply chains and helping them to understand their own level of sustainability, as well as in establishing a transition plan geared towards more responsible and innovative models, in line with the ecological transition of the NRRP.
nodes.summary:
- Defines a sustainability classification framework for credit products and lending, spanning 277 categories (environmental, social, other). Loans qualify if they fund activities within classified categories, target zero-emission sectors, or are tied to sustainability KPIs aligned with company strategies. Classification occurs at application and is monitored for stability throughout the loan’s life.

- Describes customer engagement and product design practices focused on transparency and needs-based innovation:
  - Collaboration with industry bodies (e.g., ACEPI) to classify complex instruments and improve advisory.
  - Use of listening tools, market research, focus groups, and continuous satisfaction/experience surveys to refine offerings.
  - Direct consultations with beneficiaries; Social Impact Roadshow 2024 to discuss non-economic impacts.
  - Banca dei Territori Division (BdT) develops inclusive credit (e.g., Gamma Impact) for students and unemployed, with favorable terms and extended maturities; staff feedback feeds process improvements.

- Outlines remediation and complaint channels: submissions via website/app, mail, email, and branches; timely handling with annual compliance reporting; Code of Ethics provides a dedicated inbox for reporting non-compliance, aiming for effective dispute resolution.

- Presents ESG capability-building via Workshops:
  - Goal to help companies assess sustainability, set transition plans, and align with NRRP ecological transition.
  - Workshops co-developed with institutions and partners; promoted through Group and partner channels.
  - Expansion across Italy since 2021 (e.g., Brescia, Milan, Turin, Genoa, Padua, Bari, Palermo).
  - KPI: 16 ESG Workshops active as of 31.12.2024 (target 12 by 2025; no baseline value).

- Details actions and financial solutions for social inclusion and support to production:
  - S-Loan lines for SMEs/corporates:
    - S-Loan Diversity to advance women’s empowerment and gender equality.
    - S-Loan ESG to improve overall sustainable performance, including for non-profit enterprises and cooperatives.
  - Business Microcredit using the SME Guarantee Fund for start-ups, freelancers, and associations with limited credit access.
  - Business Gemma for female-led businesses and self-employed women.
  - Anti-usury loans enabled via foundations/associations under Law 108/96, using guarantees to prevent financial exclusion; results monitored monthly (exposures/benefit by region); available as personal and mortgage loans.
  - Cre.S.Co. (Credit for Community Development): partner-backed guarantee funds and subsidised loans for NPOs (including ATS), supporting socially beneficial projects and small organisations’ growth.
  - Gamma Impact via the Fund for Impact: subsidised rates and up to 30-year terms for high-potential individuals lacking access to traditional credit; approx. €110m disbursed in 2024, including:
    - Per Merito (unsecured student loans; ~€107m in 2024)
    - mamma@work (for new working mothers; ~€2m)
    - Newer products: Obiettivo Pensione, Per Crescere, Per avere Cura, Per Esempio.
  - Emphasis on measurable social impact and ongoing monitoring.

nodes.title: Actions related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.5 Actions related to social inclusion and supporting production
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group provides its customers with a wide range of medium - to long -term products with the aim of helping to find ESG solutions and supports the most vulnerable groups by promoting access to credit through specific projects and local partnerships.
nodes.summary:
- Expansion of ESG workshops in Italy: launched in 2021 (Brescia) and scaled to 16 workshops across multiple cities by 31 Dec 2024; 2025 target set at 12.
- Broad social inclusion and access-to-credit offering:
  - S-Loan lines for SMEs and corporates (Diversity and ESG) to improve sustainability and gender equality.
  - Business Microcredit Financing via the SME Guarantee Fund.
  - Business Gemma loans for female-led businesses and self-employed women.
  - Anti-usury loans guaranteed by foundations/associations under Italian Law 108/96, monitored monthly to estimate regional benefits.
  - Cre.S.Co. (Credit for Community Development): subsidised loans to NPOs via partner-backed guarantee/cost-coverage funds.
  - Gamma Impact via the Fund for Impact: subsidised, long-tenor credit for people excluded from traditional credit; ~€110m disbursed in 2024, including Per Merito (~€107m) and mamma@work (~€2m). New products include Obiettivo Pensione, Per Crescere, Per avere Cura, and Per Esempio. Impact measured with the mandatory RIM questionnaire.
- Retail customer support in housing:
  - Mutuo Giovani: up to 100% LTV, subsidised rates, fee waivers, flexibility; accessible to non-standard workers; strong market positioning.
  - Participation in Italy’s Guarantee Fund for Main Home Purchases (Sostegni-bis and extensions) to provide high LTV and competitive rates to priority borrowers (e.g., under 36, single-parent households).
- Consumer protection and governance: strict adherence to Consumer Credit Rules, automated usury and debt-to-income monitoring, robust complaints management, and controlled product development with transparent data and impact measurement.
- Financial education: “Finanza Insieme” (launched Sept 2023), a free, interactive platform with 350+ topics across Savings, Investment, Risk, Insurance, Pensions, Credit, Inheritance; modules span context, bias awareness, training exercises, and topical deep-dives.
- SME and ecosystem programs: Women Value Company (with Marisa Bellisario Foundation), Resto al Sud, Crescibusiness (ESG growth path), Imprese Vincenti, and Supply Chain Development including Sustainable Supply Chains.
- Corporate ESG enablement: group ESG training and in-person/remote ESG workshops and advisory.
- Social-impact lending governance and measurement:
  - Negative EVA impact ceiling (since 2023) to support high-social-impact loans with limited immediate economic return.
  - RIM-based impact assessment for “impact products” and NPO loans (≥€50k, ≥6 months), including outcome/impact analysis and SROI; ex-ante questionnaires active, ex-post planned/underway; feedback shared with clients and presented in meetings/roadshows.
- Support for women victims of violence: adherence to ABI agreement enabling 18-month suspension of mortgage/personal loan instalments (ISP also suspends the entire instalment); valid until 25 Nov 2025.
- Youth-focused banking: XME Conto UP! (zero-fee account for minors with free services) and Flash Up Studio prepaid card/app for students (payments, scholarships, campus services where applicable).
- Remittances: international money transfers via Western Union for migrant customers.
- IMI Corporate & Investment Banking: full suite of ESG financing (sustainability-linked loans/bonds/guarantees/securitisations/hedging) and use-of-proceeds instruments (green/social/sustainable bonds, green convertibles, renewable energy project finance); ESG Advisory Team (since 2023) supports clients’ transition plans.
- International Banks Division:
  - Bank of Alexandria (Egypt): microfinance-led inclusion strategy; ~€34m loans in 2024; client training with WFP; partnerships with NGOs, ministries, private sector; strong focus on small farmers, livestock, crafts.
  - First-home youth mortgages in six entities (CIB Bank, Eximbank, ISP Slovenia, ISP Albania, BiH, VÚB Banka): ~€263m disbursed in 2024.
  - Women/Youth in Business support (e.g., EBRD program in Serbia): ~€22m disbursed in 2024.
  - Pensioner-focused products in five geographies: ~€113m disbursed in 2024.
  - Training: webinars/workshops on circular economy, green/S-Loan financing, EU Taxonomy alignment, and sector impacts (e-mobility, food & beverage).
- Sustainable finance metrics and reporting:
  - Internal classification rules (end-2022) and reporting (from 2023) across three categories: environmental, social, and other sustainability (e.g., sustainability-linked covenants/KPIs).
  - 2024 disbursements: environmental €7.6bn; social €4.5bn (excludes disaster/urban regeneration loans); other sustainability €7.0bn.
  - 2024 stock: environmental €20.3bn; social €20.1bn; other sustainability €15.8bn; methodology notes on accounting vs operational balances.
- Investment and insurance with sustainability focus:
  - Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR: integrates sustainability risks, considers principal adverse impacts, and embeds sustainability in remuneration.
  - Coverage of products under SFDR Articles 6 (risk integration), 8 (ESG characteristics), and 9 (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.title: Sustainable finance metrics
nodes.heading: 4.4.6.6 Sustainable finance metrics
nodes.start_phrase: For the purpose of greater internal and external transparency with respect to products and transactions deemed sustainable, the Group has decided to draw up specific rules for the classification of sustainable credit products and lending transactions, approved at the end of 2022.
nodes.summary:
- The Group established internal rules (approved end-2022) for classifying sustainable credit products, applied from 2023, covering environmental, social, and “other” sustainability categories.
- Category scope:
  - Environmental: targeted loans to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
  - Social: anti-usury loans, products for vulnerable groups, Non-Profit loans, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted loans with sustainability covenants/KPIs for Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
- 2024 loans disbursed: €7.6bn environmental; €4.5bn social (excludes disaster relief and urban regeneration); €7.0bn other.
- 2024 loan stock: €20.3bn environmental; €20.1bn social; €15.8bn other.
- Measurement approach: environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (incl. IMI C&IB) and operational balances for the IBD; social and other figures are entirely from operational balances.
- The Group emphasizes ongoing client dialogue to deliver sustainability-conscious investment, responsible lending, and insurance solutions, outlining policies, objectives, actions, and metrics across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Asset Management Division’s fiduciary duty includes integrating ESG, based on the view that high-ESG issuers support long-term performance.
- SFDR-aligned Sustainability Policy: integrates sustainability risks into investment processes and remuneration (Art. 5), considers principal adverse impacts (Arts. 4 and 7), and defines selection/monitoring methodologies.
- Product coverage spans SFDR categories: Article 6 (risk integration), Article 8 (ESG characteristics with good governance), and Article 9 (sustainable investment objectives), across all asset classes for mutual funds and portfolio management with appropriate pre-contractual disclosures.

nodes.title: Sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7 Sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance
nodes.start_phrase: The Group considers it essential to maintain an ongoing dialogue with customers, as a fundamental starting point for offering advice, services and products, in the knowledge that it plays a key role in investment assistance, prudent management of savings, and responsible lending, in addition to offering insurance protection.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective from 2023 reporting) for classifying sustainable credit products and lending into three categories: environmental sustainability, social sustainability, and other sustainability.
- Defines categories:
  - Environmental sustainability: targeted lending/products to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit Sector, and Corporate & Project Finance classified as “environmental.”
  - Social sustainability: targeted lending/products such as anti-usury loans, offerings for vulnerable groups, loans to the Non-Profit Sector, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted transactions featuring sustainability-linked covenants/KPIs for Businesses and the Non-Profit Sector, and Corporate & Project Finance.
- Reports 2024 disbursements: €7.6bn (environmental), €4.5bn (social; excludes disaster relief and urban regeneration), €7.0bn (other sustainability).
- Reports 2024 stock: €20.3bn (environmental), €20.1bn (social), €15.8bn (other sustainability).
- Explains methodology: environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (including IMI C&IB Division) plus operational balances for the IBD component; social and other sustainability figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance, highlighting the Group’s client-centric advisory role across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Details Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR (Reg. 2019/2088):
  - Integrates sustainability risk into investment processes and advice; considers principal adverse impacts (Articles 4 and 7); embeds sustainability risks in remuneration (Article 5).
  - Applies Sustainability Policy across all asset classes and product types:
    - Article 6 products (integration of sustainability risks),
    - Article 8 products (promote environmental/social characteristics with good governance),
    - Article 9 products (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.title: Sustainability-conscious investment products
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1 Sustainability-conscious investment products
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its fiduciary commitment to the Group’s customers and investors, the Asset Management Division (hereinafter, also “AM Division”), being a financial market participant, also has a fiduciary commitment to its clients and investors and, more generally, to stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective for 2023 reporting onward) for classifying sustainable credit products into three categories: environmental sustainability, social sustainability, and other forms of sustainability, with definitions and eligible loan types (Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, Corporate & Project Finance; anti-usury and vulnerable-group products for social; non-targeted transactions with sustainability covenants/KPIs for “other”).
- Presents 2024 sustainable lending volumes disbursed: €7.6bn environmental, €4.5bn social (excludes loans for natural disasters and urban regeneration), €7.0bn other sustainability.
- Provides 2024 stock of sustainable loans: €20.3bn environmental, €20.1bn social, €15.8bn other.
- Explains calculation methodology: environmental figures combine Parent Company accounting balances (incl. IMI C&IB Division) and IBD operational balances; social and “other” figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces the Group’s approach to sustainability-conscious investment products and sustainable insurance, emphasizing ongoing client dialogue and responsible advice across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Details Asset Management Division policies aligned with EU SFDR (Reg. 2019/2088): integration of sustainability risk into investment processes and advice, consideration of principal adverse impacts (Arts. 4 and 7), and incorporation of sustainability risks into remuneration (Art. 5).
- Clarifies product categorization under SFDR in pre-contractual disclosures across all asset classes: Article 6 (integration of sustainability risks), Article 8 (promotion of environmental/social characteristics with good governance), and Article 9 (sustainable investment objectives).

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.1 Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its fiduciary commitment to the Group’s customers and investors, the Asset Management Division (hereinafter, also “AM Division”), being a financial market participant, also has a fiduciary commitment to its clients and investors and, more generally, to stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Group-wide rules (approved end-2022, effective from 2023) for classifying sustainable credit products into three categories:
  - Environmental sustainability: targeted loans to Individuals, Businesses, Non-Profit, and Corporate & Project Finance.
  - Social sustainability: anti-usury, products for vulnerable groups, Non-Profit, and other social loans.
  - Other sustainability: non-targeted loans tied to sustainability covenants/KPIs for Businesses/Non-Profit and Corporate & Project Finance.
- 2024 sustainable lending metrics:
  - Disbursements: €7.6bn environmental; €4.5bn social (excludes disaster/urban regeneration loans); €7.0bn other.
  - Stock: €20.3bn environmental; €20.1bn social; €15.8bn other.
- Measurement approach:
  - Environmental figures use accounting balances for the Parent Company (incl. IMI C&IB) and operational balances for IBD.
  - Social and “other sustainability” figures are based entirely on operational balances.
- Introduces sustainability-conscious investment and insurance approach, emphasizing ongoing client dialogue and responsible advisory across asset management, private banking, and insurance.
- Asset Management Division (AM Division) policies aligned with EU SFDR:
  - Integrates sustainability risks into investment processes and remuneration (Articles 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9).
  - Considers Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIs).
  - Applies to mutual funds and portfolio management that disclose under SFDR; excludes mandates with limited discretion.
- Shareholder engagement framework:
  - Commitment Policy for issuer dialogue.
  - Strategy for exercising intervention and voting rights at investee meetings.
- Governance for sustainability within AM Division:
  - Board of Directors defines and oversees the Sustainability Policy.
  - CEO/GM supported by ESG Committee; multiple committees (Risk, Sustainability) and functions (Compliance & AML, Risk Management) oversee implementation, risk monitoring, and policy adherence.
- External engagement and initiatives:
  - Signatory/member of CDP, Italian Stewardship Principles (Assogestioni), UN PRI, ICGN, IIGCC, Net Zero Engagement Initiative, NZAMI (with note on 13 Jan 2025 review and suspended reporting).
  - Ongoing participation in ESG best-practice forums and training.
- Annual review of sustainability policies by ESG & Strategic Activism with Compliance & AML to maintain alignment with evolving best practices.
- Private Banking (Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking) policies:
  - Integrates sustainability risks and PAIs into product selection, advisory, and insurance distribution; policies published internally and on the website.
  - Assesses product companies (asset managers and insurers) for sustainability risk management, PAI consideration, regulatory compliance, and adherence to ESG principles/codes (e.g., Net Zero, Stewardship Principles, Climate Action 100+, Nature Action 100), also via subsidiaries FAM and FAMI.

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.2 Policies on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking , in line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s commitment to sustainable economic development, in accordance with the principles outlined in the Group’s Code of Ethics and aware of the importance of allocating resources according to social and environmental sustainability criteria for long -term value creation, has adopted policies on the integration of sustainability risks and information on the main adverse impacts on sustainability factors when selecting issuers, creating the financial product catalogue and providing investment advice and insurance distribution services (hereafter, these services are jointly referred to as “Advice”).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Portfolio management mandates with prescriptive investment policies are excluded from certain sustainability processes due to limited manager discretion.
- Shareholder engagement: Activities are guided by a Commitment Policy (issuer dialogue, methods, topics) and a Strategy for exercising intervention and voting rights at investee shareholder meetings.
- Sustainability governance at Eurizon Capital SGR S.p.A.:
  - Board of Directors sets and oversees the Sustainability Policy.
  - CEO/General Manager, supported by the ESG Committee, propose integration of sustainability risks in investment, remuneration policies, and identification of principal adverse impacts; ESG Committee monitors implementation, screening strategies, portfolio processes, and external governance activities.
  - Financial, Credit and Operational Risk Committee oversees product risk exposure, including sustainability risks.
  - Sustainability Committee ensures fund management aligns with ethical principles in fund regulations.
  - Compliance & AML monitors adherence to the Sustainability Policy and regulatory controls.
  - Risk Management monitors sustainability risk of managed products.
- External engagement and initiatives: Active participation in ESG best-practice platforms, training and conferences; signatory/member of CDP, Italian Stewardship Principles, UN PRI, ICGN, IIGCC, NZEI, and NZAMI; note that NZAMI commenced a review on 13 Jan 2025, suspending implementation tracking and reporting.
- Policy review: Annual review by the ESG & Strategic Activism unit with Compliance & AML to align methodologies with evolving national/international best practices.
- Private Banking (Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking) policies:
  - Integrates sustainability risks and principal adverse impacts (PAIs) into issuer selection, product catalogue construction, investment advice, and insurance distribution; policies are available to employees and clients.
  - Counterparty due diligence covers: adherence to ESG principles/codes (e.g., Net Zero, Stewardship Principles, Climate Action 100+, Nature Action 100), governance and organization for sustainability, integration of sustainability risks into investment and remuneration, SFDR/Taxonomy-compliant product ranges and EET usage, compliance with ESMA 14 May 2024 guidelines on fund names using ESG/sustainability terms, and PAI consideration per SFDR RTS. Applied at onboarding and updated regularly within Product Governance.
- Advisory process and product alignment:
  - Collects client sustainability preferences during profiling.
  - Applies internal rules and a product classification model (primary/secondary markets) to match products with client preferences.
  - When mismatches occur, provides reasons so clients can reconsider preferences for the specific transaction.
- Private Banking sustainability governance and controls:
  - Sustainability Manager provides integrated oversight and alignment with Group initiatives.
  - Steering Committee holds a quarterly ESG session to set strategic initiatives and assess financial impacts.
  - ESG & Strategic Activism team ensures proper ESG management in asset management companies.
  - The Intesa Sanpaolo Chief Compliance Officer is responsible for implementing sustainability-risk and PAI policies in advisory and insurance distribution under a centralized internal control model.
  - Ongoing monitoring embedded in Product Oversight and Governance with metrics on product scope and consistency with client sustainability preferences.
- Targets and metrics (Eurizon, Business Plan 2022–2025):
  - AuM of UCIs under SFDR Articles 8 and 9: baseline 110 bn euro (31/12/2021); 156.6 bn euro achieved (31/12/2024); 2025 target 156 bn euro.
  - Share of AuM in Articles 8 and 9 UCIs: baseline 46% (31/12/2021); 76% achieved (31/12/2024); 2025 target 60%.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.3 Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the definition of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s 2022 -2025 Business Plan, Eurizon contributed to the Group’s expressed commitment to achieving global climate objectives, by committing to foster the transition to a low -carbon economy, starting with the evolution of its product range.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines Fideuram – Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking’s and the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s ESG governance, regulatory alignment, product oversight, and advisory practices within a consolidated sustainability framework.
- Governance and compliance: establishment of internal ESG-focused structures, policies integrating sustainability risks into investment and remuneration, and centralized oversight under the Group Chief Compliance Officer; policy monitoring embedded in Product Oversight and Governance with specific metrics.
- Regulatory alignment: adherence to SFDR and the EU Taxonomy, incorporation of Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIs), compliant product documentation (including use of the European ESG Template – EET), and an internal framework to meet ESMA’s 14 May 2024 Guidelines on funds’ names using ESG/sustainability terms.
- Counterparty oversight: comprehensive sustainability due diligence of all product companies during onboarding and through regular updates, formalized within Product Governance processes.
- Client advisory integration: collection of clients’ sustainability preferences during MiFID profiling; internal product-selection rules to match those preferences; a cross-instrument product classification model and pre-trade consistency checks, with explanations and the option for clients to adjust preferences if a proposed transaction is not aligned.
- Sustainability governance: a Sustainability Manager with integrated oversight; a quarterly “Sustainability (ESG)” session within the Steering Committee to set priorities and assess financial feasibility; and an ESG & Strategic Activism team managing ESG topics across asset management companies.
- Targets and metrics (Asset Management – Eurizon): commitment to expand Article 8/9 SFDR products within total UCIs AUM—baseline 110 billion euro (46%) at 31.12.2021; final 156.6 billion euro (76%) at 31.12.2024; 2025 targets 156 billion euro (60%).
- Targets and metrics (Private Banking): monitoring the share of Article 8/9 SFDR products in total client AUM—baseline 19% at 31.12.2021; final 78% at 31.12.2024; 2025 target 70%.
- Asset Management methodologies (per Sustainability Policy, updated Nov 2024): 
  - Negative screening (SRI Binding by sector; PAI Binding by adverse impacts; ESG Binding by issuer rating; for sovereigns, carbon intensity vs GDP and FATF blacklist).
  - Positive screening (ESG integration and/or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives).
  - Stewardship/active ownership via engagement and voting.
  - Compliance monitored by Risk Management with Compliance & AML support.
- Product range and strategies: c. 156.56 billion euro in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024; most 2024 UCIs integrate ESG; key strategies include capital-protection solutions, flexible step-in equity exposure, and buy & watch bond portfolios.
- Mandates: all institutional mandates apply negative screening; extensive ESG and engagement reporting (e.g., 50 mandates worth 12.5 billion euro with ESG reports); 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~9.5 billion euro) with specific restrictions/engagement support; 82 insurance/captive pension mandates (~48 billion euro) with Article 8 ESG integration.
- Private Banking actions: continued enhancement of the Group ESG Programme (launched June 2021), integration of sustainability across operations, development of ESG advisory in line with the 2022–2025 Business Plan, and adoption of a more detailed sustainability preferences questionnaire at end-2024.

nodes.title: Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.4 Targets and metrics on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: In order to measure the percentage penetration of sustainability -focused assets under management, it was decided to monitor the percentage incidence of (AUM) products classified as Article 8 and 9 SFDR in the total AUM held by customers, as shown below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Measurement and enhancement of sustainability-conscious investment products across Asset Management and Private Banking within a consolidated sustainability framework.
- Key metric: Share of customer AUM invested in SFDR Article 8 and 9 products. Baseline 19% (31.12.2021); 78% achieved by 31.12.2024; 2025 target set at 70%.
- Asset Management ESG integration:
  - Policy framework updated November 2024; methodologies to integrate sustainability risks into the investment process.
  - Approaches:
    - Negative screening: sectoral exclusions (SRI), adverse impacts (PAI), ESG risk ratings; sovereign exclusions based on carbon intensity and FATF blacklist.
    - Positive screening: ESG integration and sustainable investment objectives.
    - Stewardship/engagement: active ownership via voting and dialogue.
  - Oversight: Risk Management with Compliance & AML monitor adherence.
  - Scale and products: About €156.56bn in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024. Most 2024 UCIs (Eurizon Capital SGR, Eurizon Capital SA, Epsilon SGR) integrate ESG; strategies include capital protection, flexible “step-in” equity exposure, and buy & watch bond funds.
- Mandates and reporting:
