  - Institutional mandates: all apply negative screening; ESG reports produced for 50 mandates (€12.5bn); engagement reports available on request.
  - Non-captive clients: 37 mandates for 22 clients totaling ~€9.5bn, with specific investment restrictions and engagement/corporate governance support (including Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR and Epsilon SGR mandates).
  - Insurance and captive pension mandates: 82 mandates totaling ~€48bn with Article 8 ESG integrations.
- Private Banking actions:
  - Intensified Group ESG Programme (launched June 2021) to embed sustainability across operations amid evolving regulation and stakeholder expectations.
  - ESG advisory development aligned with the 2022–2025 Business Plan: Fideuram enhanced its advisory model to capture and manage client sustainability preferences.
  - Client profiling: MiFID-based sustainability preferences collected since 2021; a more detailed questionnaire introduced at end-2024.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.5 Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its Sustainability Policy131, the Asset Management Division has defined special methodologies for selecting and monitoring financial instruments aimed at integrating sustainability risks into the AUM Investment Process.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Sustainability-conscious investment products across Asset Management and Private Banking, with targets, methodologies, product ranges, mandates, reporting, and advisory enhancements.
- Key metric (Private Banking): Percentage of customers’ AUM in SFDR Article 8/9 products monitored.
  - Baseline (31.12.2021): 19%
  - Achieved (31.12.2024): 78%
  - Target (2025): 70%
- Asset Management ESG methodologies (per Sustainability Policy, updated Nov 2024):
  - Negative screening: sector-based SRI binding; PAI binding for adverse impacts; ESG binding via sustainability ratings for corporates; for sovereigns, carbon intensity vs GDP and FATF blacklist.
  - Positive screening: ESG integration into analysis/selection or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives, with good governance.
  - Stewardship/Active Ownership: engagement through voting and dialogue with issuers.
  - Oversight: Risk Management monitors compliance, supported by Compliance & AML.
- AUM and product offering (end-2024):
  - ~€156.56bn in Article 8 and 9 funds promoting environmental/social characteristics or with sustainable objectives.
  - Most 2024 UCI launches by Eurizon Capital SGR, Eurizon Capital SA, and Epsilon SGR integrate ESG; strategies include capital-protected products, flexible “step-in” equity exposure, and “buy & watch” bond portfolios.
- Mandates and reporting:
  - All institutional mandates apply negative screening; ESG reports produced for 50 mandates totaling €12.5bn, with optional engagement reporting.
  - 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~€9.5bn): specific investment restrictions and engagement/corporate governance support (7 via Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR; 1 via Epsilon SGR).
  - Insurance mandates and captive open pension funds: 82 mandates (~€48bn) with Article 8 ESG integration.
- Private Banking actions:
  - Intensified ESG program (launched June 2021) aligning with regulatory developments and societal expectations; integration of sustainability across business operations.
  - ESG advisory development per 2022–2025 Business Plan: since 2021, collection of client sustainability preferences via MiFID profiling; enhanced, more detailed sustainability preferences questionnaire adopted end-2024.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.1.6 Actions on sustainability-conscious investment products - Private Banking
nodes.start_phrase: Regulatory developments envisaged by regulators and the civil society’s continued attention to the transition to a more sustainable economy have led the Group to further intensify its commitment, initiatives and improved approach to sustainability, confirming the focus and strategic importance of the ESG Programme launched in June 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the excerpt: how the Group integrates ESG across Asset Management, Private Banking, and Insurance, with concrete targets, methodologies, product development, governance, and training.

- KPI and progress (Private Banking AUM mix): tracking the share of client AUM invested in SFDR Articles 8 and 9 products; baseline 19% (31.12.2021), 78% achieved (31.12.2024), versus a 2025 target of 70%.

- Asset Management ESG methodologies:
  - Negative screening: exclusions based on sector (SRI binding), adverse impacts (PAI binding), and ESG ratings for corporates; for sovereigns, exclusions tied to carbon intensity (per GDP) and FATF blacklist.
  - Positive screening: ESG integration and/or pursuit of sustainable investment objectives.
  - Stewardship: active ownership through voting and engagement.
  - Oversight: Risk Management monitors compliance with support from Compliance & AML.

- Asset Management portfolio and products:
  - ~€156.56bn in Article 8/9 funds at end-2024.
  - 2024 launches by Eurizon Capital SGR/SA and Epsilon SGR integrated ESG across:
    - Capital-protection products with varying horizons.
    - Flexible “step-in” strategies with staged equity exposure.
    - “Buy & watch” bond funds with decreasing duration.

- Institutional and insurance mandates:
  - All institutional mandates apply negative screening; ESG reports provided for many (50 mandates, €12.5bn), including portfolio-vs-benchmark positioning and optional engagement reporting.
  - 37 mandates for 22 non-captive clients (~€9.5bn; 7 via Eurizon Capital Real Assets SGR, 1 via Epsilon SGR) include specific investment restrictions and governance/engagement support.
  - Insurance mandates and captive open pension funds: 82 mandates, ~€48bn, with Article 8 ESG integrations.

- Private Banking ESG initiatives and offer:
  - ESG Programme (launched June 2021) intensified; sustainability preferences gathered via MiFID profiling since 2021; enhanced, more detailed questionnaire adopted end-2024.
  - 2022–2025 commercial goals to grow Article 8/9 share among total and new placements; in 2024, >85% of new products were Article 8/9.
  - Product alignment: 44 portfolio management lines brought to Article 8 (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections).
  - “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) expanded: clients can build bespoke portfolios from Article 8/9 strategies or choose risk-based “guided pathways” following a High Conviction, thematic ESG approach.
  - Fideuram AM Ireland: launched Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions (Article 9) in June; introduced ETF D‑X platform (6 equity/bond solutions, 7 ISINs) classified Article 8.
  - Guided Open Architecture includes third‑party ESG solutions from leading managers.

- ESG culture and training:
  - Creation of “ESG Ambassador” role to promote sustainability, support sales/marketing, and capture client/partner needs; pilot finalized in 2024, full rollout in 2025.
  - Mid‑2024 event captured Ambassador proposals for role evolution; “Fideuram for the Environment” initiative initiated; end‑year proposal presented to top management.

- Insurance ESG governance and policies:
  - An Insurance Group Sustainability Policy defines governance, management, control, disclosure, and concrete E/S/G commitments; reviewed as regulations/context evolve and approved by the boards of all Insurance Group companies.
  - Investment Policy for ESG integration guides responsible investing, monitors risks/opportunities (e.g., climate adaptation, GHG, non‑renewable energy use), applies engagement (focus on long-term transition plans) and exclusions for non‑responsible/critical sectors; principles set by the Board and apply across the Insurance Group.
  - Non‑life: an Underwriting Policy (for Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione) establishes principles and macro-processes for underwriting in line with ESG considerations (details truncated in the excerpt).

nodes.title: Sustainable insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2 Sustainable insurance
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategic objectives and the materiality that the integration of ESG factors has assumed for the financial and insurance sector, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group (hereinafter also referred to as the “Insurance Group”) has continued its development of environmental and social matters over the years, implementing concrete actions and initiatives aimed at increasingly consolidating internal governance and at the same time generating a concrete and material impact on its customers.
nodes.summary:
- The Division set escalating 2022–2025 targets to expand ESG offerings, aiming to increase the share of SFDR Article 8 and 9 products across total and new placements; in 2024, over 85% of new products qualified as Articles 8/9.
- Fideuram Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking Asset Management SGR aligned 44 portfolio management lines to Article 8 SFDR (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections) and expanded “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) to let clients build custom ESG portfolios or select model portfolios using a High Conviction, ESG-thematic approach.
- Fideuram Asset Management Ireland dac broadened Article 9 and Article 8 ranges by launching Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions (Article 9) and an ETF D-X platform with multiple equity and bond solutions (Article 8).
- Through a Guided Open Architecture, the Group complements in-house solutions with third-party ESG products from leading international managers.
- To support ESG advisory quality, the Group ran education and training initiatives and created the “ESG Ambassador” role: piloted in 2024 with full rollout planned for 2025. Ambassadors contributed proposals on role evolution, sales/marketing support, and training; the “Fideuram for the Environment” initiative was launched; end-of-year proposals were presented to top management.
- In Sustainable Insurance, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group strengthened ESG governance and risk management with defined roles, policies, processes, and monitoring tools aligned with evolving regulations.
- A Group-wide Sustainability Policy sets governance, management, control, disclosure frameworks, and concrete E, S, and G commitments, subject to ongoing review and Board approvals for all Insurance Group companies.
- An Investment Policy integrates ESG factors into the insurance investment process, monitoring negative impacts (e.g., climate adaptation gaps, GHG emissions, non-renewable energy use), growing ESG options, conducting issuer engagement on transition plans, and applying exclusions to critical sectors; it is Board-approved and applies across the Insurance Group.
- In non-life insurance, an Underwriting Policy for Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione establishes principles and macro-processes for risk selection (details partially provided).

nodes.title: Policies on sustainability-conscious insurance products - Insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2.1 Policies on sustainability-conscious insurance products - Insurance
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s strategic objectives and the materiality that the integration of ESG factors has assumed for the financial and insurance sector, the Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group (hereinafter also referred to as the “Insurance Group”) has continued its development of environmental and social matters over the years, implementing concrete actions and initiatives aimed at increasingly consolidating internal governance and at the same time generating a concrete and material impact on its customers.
nodes.summary:
- ESG investment expansion in Private Banking:
  - 2022–2025 targets to increase the share and launch of SFDR Article 8 and 9 asset management products; in 2024, over 85% of new products were Article 8/9.
  - Alignment of 44 portfolio management lines to Article 8 SFDR (2 Fogli Fideuram, 17 Fideuram Omnia, 25 Wealth Collections).
  - Enrichment of “Il Mio Foglio ESG” (Article 8) with a curated ESG investment universe and guided model portfolios built on a High Conviction, thematic ESG approach.
  - Fideuram Asset Management Ireland launched the Fonditalia Clean Energy Solutions fund (Article 9) and the ETF D‑X platform (6 equity/bond solutions; 7 ISINs, all Article 8).
  - Guided Open Architecture broadened to include leading third‑party ESG products.
  - ESG culture and training: creation of ESG Ambassadors to promote sustainability and gather client/consultant feedback; 2024 pilot completed, full rollout in 2025; mid‑2024 workshops shaped role evolution, sales/marketing/training support; launch of “Fideuram for the Environment”; proposals presented to top management.

- Sustainable insurance governance and policies:
  - Group‑wide Sustainability Policy integrating ESG into governance, management, control, and disclosure, with Board approvals and periodic updates.
  - Investment Policy integrating ESG, with ongoing monitoring, issuer engagement on climate transition, and exclusion strategies for “not socially responsible”/critical sectors.
  - Non‑life Underwriting Policy (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione) embedding ESG risk criteria; top management oversight.
  - Commitments to SDGs, PSI, UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Equator Principles; membership in NZAOA (since 2021) and FIT (since April 2024).

- Insurance climate actions and product measures:
  - Decarbonization targets: 50% reduction in EVIC‑weighted carbon intensity by 2030 vs. 2021; net‑zero by 2050.
  - Exclusion thresholds include: unconventional weapons; ≥18% revenue from thermal coal mining/power or new coal projects; ≥10% revenue from unconventional oil & gas; issuers with low ESG ratings.
  - Active ownership: bilateral engagements with the 20 highest‑emitting portfolio issuers; focused dialogue with oil & gas to set science‑based targets, publish transition plans, align capex/strategy, cut methane, avoid unconventional/high‑carbon sources and sensitive‑area drilling.
  - Use of measurement and monitoring indicators; continuous application of exclusions and offering of SFDR Article 8/9 investment options.
  - Non‑life: emissions monitoring where data are available; participation in initiatives to advance ESG awareness and best practices.

- Insurance product offering with ESG focus:
  - Life and non‑life products primarily for Intesa Sanpaolo Group clients.
  - Life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni—renamed from Intesa Sanpaolo Vita—and Fideuram Vita): Article 8‑oriented products integrating ESG; tailored solutions for families of disabled persons, minors/incapacitated (with Guardianship Judge), and non‑profit entities.
  - Non‑life (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione): protection for people, homes, vehicles, SMEs/Corporate; features supporting sustainable mobility (e.g., EV breakdown services, distance‑based policies); coverage for catastrophic risks/natural events and renewable energy plants; support for clients’ digitalization and ecological transition.

nodes.title: Actions on sustainability-conscious products - Insurance
nodes.heading: 4.4.7.2.2 Actions on sustainability-conscious products - Insurance
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group is committed to supporting the transition to a net -zero-emission future, strictly complying with the IPCC’s scientific indications and the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the NZAOA Protocol.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni Group’s ESG governance for underwriting risks, with Top Management responsible for implementing and monitoring governance per Board directives.
- Public commitments to international ESG frameworks: UN SDGs, PSI (2019), UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, Equator Principles; joined NZAOA (2021) and Forum for Insurance Transition to Net Zero (FIT) in April 2024.
- Climate strategy and targets: alignment with IPCC, Paris Agreement, NZAOA Protocol; 50% reduction in EVIC-weighted carbon intensity by 2030 vs. 2021; net-zero by 2050; focus on a just and inclusive transition.
- Investment decarbonisation levers under the ESG integration policy:
  - Exclusions: unconventional weapons; ≥18% revenue from thermal coal mining/power; new coal projects; ≥10% revenue from unconventional oil & gas; issuers with low ESG ratings.
  - Active ownership and engagement: dialogue with top 20 portfolio emitters; engagement with oil & gas and third parties on science-based targets, credible transition plans, methane reduction, avoidance of unconventional, carbon-intensive projects, and no new drilling in sensitive areas (e.g., Arctic).
  - Ongoing measurement and monitoring using specific indicators; application of SFDR Article 8 and 9 investment options and exclusions.
- Non-life portfolio: monitoring of investee emissions where data allow; participation in national/international initiatives to raise ESG awareness and spread best practices; development of new solutions and process strengthening.
- Product offering aligned with sustainability:
  - Life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Vita/Intesa Sanpaolo Assicurazioni and Fideuram Vita): insurance, pension, and financial products primarily for Group customers; strong focus on SFDR Article 8 and tailored solutions for vulnerable groups (families of disabled persons, minors/incapacitated with guardianship) and non-profits.
  - Non-life business (Intesa Sanpaolo Protezione): protection for people, homes, vehicles, SMEs/Corporate; features for sustainable mobility (EV breakdown services, usage-based policies); cover for catastrophic and climate-related events; products safeguarding renewable energy plants; support for companies’ digital and green transition.
- ESRS G1 – Business Conduct: double materiality assessment methodology covering own operations, upstream suppliers, and downstream portfolios; engagement with internal/external stakeholders; analysis using scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood metrics.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: positive impacts from policies on integrity, whistleblowing, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in high-impact sectors on business ethics.
- Financial materiality and risk assessment:
  - Own operations: operational, compliance, and reputational risks, including cybersecurity and sanctions.
  - Upstream: reputational risk from suppliers lacking structured ethics controls (Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policy).
  - Downstream: credit, market, strategic, and reputational risks tied to counterparties.
- Integrated risk approach: considers geography, sector, and business type; monitors penalties for internal violations; selects suppliers on ethical/compliance grounds; performs legal compliance checks on counterparties; assesses risks across countries and activity areas for the Group, suppliers, and financed/invested entities.

structure.title: Governance information
structure.heading: 5 Governance information
structure.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
structure.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS G1 – Business Conduct within the Group’s Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Approach: Double materiality assessment covering impact materiality (inside-out impacts) and financial materiality (outside-in risks/opportunities) across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/investments).
- Methodology for impact materiality:
  - Interviews with internal teams and external experts.
  - Use of ESRS materiality metrics: scale, scope, irremediable character, likelihood.
  - Own operations: evaluation of internal controls and corporate culture (ethics, anti-corruption, whistleblowing, political engagement/lobbying).
  - Upstream: ESG questionnaires to suppliers and analysis of responses.
  - Downstream: portfolio exposure analysis to high-impact industries on business ethics; consideration of investment/lending criteria.
- Impact materiality outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts from robust policies and culture (integrity, anti-corruption/bribery, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying principles).
  - Upstream: material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in sectors with high business-ethics risks.
- Methodology for financial materiality:
  - Dual quantitative and qualitative assessment across scopes.
- Risk assessment highlights:
  - Own operations: operational, non-compliance, and reputational risks, notably cybersecurity and potential sanctions.
  - Upstream: reputational risk from suppliers lacking structured ethical governance (e.g., Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policies).
  - Downstream: credit, market, strategic, and resultant reputational risks.
- Integrated risk management approach:
  - Considers location, business type, sector, and operational structure.
  - Monitors penalties for regulatory/procedural violations in own operations.
  - Selects and monitors suppliers for corporate soundness and ethical compliance.
  - Verifies counterparties’ legal compliance before providing products/services.
  - Incorporates country and activity-area risk for the Group, suppliers, and financed/invested counterparties.

nodes.title: ESRS G1 - Business Conduct
nodes.heading: 5.1 ESRS G1 - Business Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Section covers ESRS G1 – Business Conduct within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, focusing on a double materiality assessment.
- Defines impact materiality (inside-out impacts across own operations and value chain) and financial materiality (outside-in risks and opportunities affecting financial performance, financing, and cost of capital over different time horizons).
- Scope includes own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/portfolios), assessed against the Group’s business framework, controls, and risk profile.
- Impact materiality methodology: interviews with internal teams and external experts; qualitative and quantitative analysis using ESRS criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
  - Own operations: assessed via internal controls and corporate culture (ethics, responsible practices).
  - Upstream: ESG supplier questionnaire and feedback analysis.
  - Downstream: analysis of portfolio exposures to high-impact sectors for business ethics (human rights, compliance, anti-tax evasion, AML, anti-competitive behavior), considering investment/lending criteria.
- Impact outcomes:
  - Own operations: material positive impacts from policies and strategies on integrity, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: material indirect negative impacts from exposure to sectors with higher business-ethics risks.
- Financial materiality approach combines quantitative and qualitative assessments across scopes.
  - Own operations risks: operational, non-compliance, reputational—highlighting cybersecurity and potential sanctions.
  - Upstream risks: primarily reputational where suppliers lack robust ethics frameworks (e.g., Code of Ethics, anti-corruption policy).
  - Downstream risks: credit, market, strategic risks with associated reputational risk.
- Integrated risk management approach considers location, business type, sector, and operational structure.
  - Own operations: monitoring of penalties for regulatory/procedural violations.
  - Upstream: supplier monitoring/selection based on corporate soundness and ethical compliance.
  - Downstream: legal compliance checks before offering products/services.
- Country and sectoral contexts for the Group, suppliers, and financed/invested counterparties are factored into analyses.

nodes.title: Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.1.1 Materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As explained in the chapter “ESRS 2 – General disclosures: Materiality assessment”, the Group carried out a double materiality assessment of the main material sustainability matters, from the dual perspective of:
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Part of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement under ESRS G1 – Business Conduct, focused on double materiality assessment and corporate culture policies.
- Double materiality approach:
  - Impact materiality: Inside-out assessment across own operations, upstream (suppliers), and downstream (clients/portfolios), using stakeholder interviews and qualitative/quantitative criteria (scale, scope, irremediability, likelihood).
  - Financial materiality: Outside-in assessment of risks and opportunities via qualitative and quantitative analysis across the same scopes.
- Methods and data sources:
  - Own operations: Evaluation of internal controls, ethical culture, cybersecurity, and sanctions exposure.
  - Upstream: ESG supplier questionnaire, analysis of supplier responses and ethical policies (e.g., anti-corruption).
  - Downstream: Portfolio exposure analysis to high-impact sectors on business ethics, incorporating lending/investment criteria.
- Impact materiality findings:
  - Own operations: Material positive impacts from policies promoting integrity, whistleblower protection, political engagement/lobbying transparency, anti-corruption/anti-bribery.
  - Upstream: Material positive impacts from ethical supplier management and responsible payment practices.
  - Downstream: Material indirect negative impacts linked to exposures in sectors with higher risks in corporate culture and supplier relationship management.
- Financial materiality findings (risks):
  - Own operations: Operational risk and associated reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream: Reputational risk concerning whistleblowing protection and corruption/bribery issues among suppliers.
  - Downstream: Credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management; market and strategic risks considered.
  - Integrated risk approach considers geography, sector, business type, and operational structure; monitoring of penalties, supplier selection, and counterparty compliance checks.
- Financial materiality (opportunities): No opportunities assessed as financially material within business conduct.
- Corporate culture policies and governance:
  - Corporate culture positioned as foundational, aligned with integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Key instruments: Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct.
  - Code of Ethics:
    - Applies to all Group companies; part of sustainability management; covers stakeholder relations and key areas (human rights, labor, environment, anti-corruption).
    - Governance: Approved by the Board of Directors with Risks and Sustainability Committee support; monitoring by Chief Sustainability Officer Area and Chief Audit Officer; potential third-party assessment per UNI EN ISO 26000:2020; reporting to BoD, RSC, MCC, and Surveillance Body.
    - Alignment with leading standards (OECD Guidance and Guidelines, UN Global Compact, Istanbul Convention, EU Charter).
    - Implementation: Public availability; mandatory distribution and acknowledgment for directors, employees, collaborators; dedicated reporting channel with confidentiality and non-retaliation; constructive remediation via training for non-fraud cases.
    - Training: Mandatory, role-based programs; 2024 content update with tiered depth on compliance; ongoing awareness activities led by CSO.
  - Internal Code of Conduct: Adopted and overseen by governance/control functions; operationalizes conduct aligned with the Code of Ethics (section truncated).

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions related to corporate culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2 Policies, targets and actions related to corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate culture is the foundation of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s identity and strategies.
nodes.summary:
- Part of the Consolidated Sustainability Statement focusing on corporate culture, governance, and financial materiality assessment.
- Financially material risks identified:
  - Own operations: operational risk and related reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream value chain: reputational risk regarding whistleblower protection and corruption/bribery.
  - Downstream value chain: credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management.
- Opportunities mapped in business conduct considered non-material from a financial standpoint.
- Corporate culture policies:
  - Corporate culture presented as core to strategy, integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct as key tools ensuring ethical, compliant, and inclusive conduct.
  - Governance and oversight: Board of Directors (with support from Risks and Sustainability Committee), Management Control Committee, Surveillance Body; monitoring by Chief Sustainability Officer and Chief Audit Officer through risk-based audits; potential independent third-party review aligned with UNI EN ISO 26000:2020.
  - Alignment with major international standards (OECD Due Diligence and Guidelines, UN Global Compact Ten Principles, Istanbul Convention, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights).
  - Non-compliance managed with proportionate measures and a constructive, training-oriented approach; protected reporting channels with confidentiality and non-retaliation.
  - Wide dissemination: publication on intranet/website; mandatory acknowledgment by directors, employees, and collaborators.
  - Training and awareness: compulsory, role-based programs; 2024 update introduces a general module plus three deep-dive levels on compliance with corporate rules.
  - Internal Code of Conduct adopted and monitored by governance/control functions, detailing expected and prohibited behaviors.

nodes.title: Policies related to corporate culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2.1 Policies related to corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate culture is the foundation of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s identity and strategies.
nodes.summary:
- Financial materiality assessment:
  - Own operations: operational risk and related reputational risk tied to corporate culture.
  - Upstream value chain: reputational risk linked to whistleblower protection and corruption/bribery.
  - Downstream value chain: credit and reputational risks from counterparties with potential issues in corporate culture and supplier management.
  - No financially material opportunities identified in business conduct.

- Corporate culture framework:
  - Core instruments: Code of Ethics and Internal Code of Conduct underpin integrity, sustainability, and social responsibility.
  - Governance and oversight: Code approved by the Board of Directors with support from the Risks and Sustainability Committee; monitored by the Chief Sustainability Officer area and Chief Audit Officer; reporting to BoD, RSC, Management Control Committee, and Surveillance Body; potential third-party review aligned with UNI EN ISO 26000:2020.
  - Alignment with international standards: OECD Due Diligence Guidance, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, UN Global Compact Ten Principles, Council of Europe Istanbul Convention, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
  - Scope and adoption: Applies to all employees, directors, external collaborators, non-employee advisors, agents, and interns; subsidiaries adopt with possible stricter/localized provisions subject to Parent approval; branches may adapt to local law without altering principles.
  - Accessibility and accountability: Codes published on intranet and website; mandatory receipt and compliance declaration; dedicated email channel for reporting with confidentiality and non-retaliation.

- Training and implementation:
  - Ongoing mandatory digital and classroom training for all personnel, tailored by role and available in multiple languages across the Group (including IBD).
  - 2024 update to training content with a general part and three levels of in-depth requirements; reinforcement of courses on Code of Ethics, Internal Code, Corruption Risk, and Whistleblowing.
  - Incentive-linked mechanisms for non-completion of compulsory training.
  - Cybersecurity/customer data protection addressed separately under ESRS S4; related people development details under ESRS S1; governance under ESRS 2.

- Targets:
  - No specific quantitative targets for corporate culture; effectiveness pursued through comprehensive training and safeguards to prevent breaches.

- Anti-corruption policies and controls:
  - Zero-tolerance approach formalized in Group Anti-Corruption Guidelines, integrated with the Code of Ethics, Internal Code, and the 231/2001 Organizational Model.
  - Defined high-risk areas: gifts and entertainment, charitable donations and sponsorships, third-party relationships (including suppliers), investments/assets, hiring, and real estate transactions.
  - Objectives include robust knowledge of counterparties and preservation of stakeholder trust.

- Anti-corruption monitoring cycle:
  - Legal and regulatory watch, risk assessment, first- and second-line controls, verification of guideline implementation, and quality assurance.

nodes.title: Targets related to corporate culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2.2 Targets related to corporate culture
nodes.start_phrase: As illustrated in the section “Policies on Corporate Culture”, the Group closely monitors corporate culture issues through a series of policies and actions.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and scope of conduct standards: The Group’s Internal Code of Conduct and Code of Ethics define expected behavior based on professionalism, diligence, honesty, fairness, and responsibility. They apply to all employees, management and supervisory bodies, non-employee financial advisors, agents, external collaborators, and interns.
- Oversight and approval: The Chief People & Culture Officer Area updates the Internal Code of Conduct, with approval by the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Board of Directors.
- Adoption across the Group: Subsidiaries must formally adopt the Internal Code and may add stricter or tailored provisions subject to Parent Company approval. Foreign branches can adapt the Code to local regulations while preserving core principles.
- Cybersecurity reference: Customer data protection and cybersecurity are addressed under ESRS S4 and considered in the financial materiality analysis for own operations.
- Corporate culture approach: While no quantitative culture targets are set, the Group ensures implementation of the Codes through comprehensive, mandatory training and safeguards against breaches.
- Training and reinforcement: Ongoing digital and classroom training on the Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Corruption Risk, and Whistleblowing is available in multiple languages across the Group. Completion is monitored and linked to incentive mechanisms for compliance.
- Anti-corruption framework: The Group’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines establish a zero-tolerance stance, define roles and processes, and align with international standards to prevent corruption and strengthen stakeholder trust.
- High-risk areas identified: Gifts and entertainment; charitable donations and sponsorships; relations with third parties (suppliers and service providers); purchase, management, and disposal of equity investments and other assets; staff hiring; and real estate transactions.
- Monitoring and controls: Continuous activities include legal framework analysis, risk assessment, first- and second-level controls, implementation verification, and quality assurance.
- Cross-references to ESRS: Links to ESRS 2 (Sustainability Governance), ESRS S1 (Training and Development), and ESRS S4 (Consumers and End-Users, Customer Data Protection).

nodes.title: Actions related to enterprise culture
nodes.heading: 5.1.2.3 Actions related to enterprise culture
nodes.start_phrase: The “Code of Ethics” has been drawn up on the basis of a context analysis and external benchmarking and involving the Parent Company’s Sustainability Managers, all the Governance Functions and Business Divisions.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance of conduct standards: The Group Internal Code of Conduct and Code of Ethics set essential conduct rules for all personnel (including management, non-employee advisors, agents, external collaborators, and interns). The Chief People & Culture Officer Area updates the Internal Code, subject to approval by the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Board (ESRS 2 reference). Subsidiaries must adopt the Internal Code, may add stricter or context-specific provisions with prior Parent approval; foreign branches can adapt to local laws while preserving principles. The Code is publicly available on the Group website.
- Cybersecurity linkage: Customer data protection and related cybersecurity aspects are addressed under ESRS S4 and considered in the financial materiality analysis for own operations.
- Corporate culture targets and actions: While no quantitative targets are set yet, the Group ensures effective implementation of the Codes through comprehensive training and safeguards against breaches. The Code of Ethics was developed via context analysis, benchmarking, and broad internal involvement. Compulsory digital and classroom training is ongoing, multilingual, and available Group-wide (including IBD). Incentive-linked mechanisms address non-completion of mandatory training within deadlines (see ESRS S1). Training on the Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Corruption Risk, and Whistleblowing is regularly updated.
- Anti-corruption policy framework: Activities are conducted with integrity, aligned with the Code of Ethics, Internal Code, and the Organizational Model under Legislative Decree 231/2001. Group Anti-Corruption Guidelines set principles, roles, responsibilities, and macro-processes, adopting a zero-tolerance stance and aligning with international standards. High-risk areas include gifts and entertainment, donations and sponsorships, third-party relationships (suppliers/other providers), equity investments and asset transactions, staff hiring, and real estate transactions. The Guidelines enhance counterparty knowledge and stakeholder trust and define management and organizational safeguards for risk mitigation.
- Monitoring and control: Implementation of the Anti-Corruption Guidelines is supported by continuous monitoring through legal framework analysis, risk assessment, first- and second-level controls, verification of implementation, and quality assurance.

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.heading: 5.1.3 Policies, targets and actions related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.start_phrase: The Group carries out its activities with the aim of providing banking and financial services to its customers in compliance with the value of integrity, which in turn is embodied in the principles of professionalism, diligence, honesty, fairness and responsibility, and in accordance with the values and restrictions contained in the “Code of Ethics”, the “Group Internal Code of Conduct” and the “Organisational, Management and Control Model” adopted pursuant to Legislative Decree 231/2001.
nodes.summary:
- Governance of conduct and ethics: The Group’s Internal Code of Conduct applies to all personnel, management/supervisory bodies, non-employee advisors, agents, external collaborators, and interns. The Chief People & Culture Officer updates the Code, with approvals by the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Board.
- Group-wide adoption: Subsidiaries must adopt the Internal Code via their corporate bodies; stricter/localized amendments require prior Parent Company approval. Foreign branches may adapt the Code to local regulations while preserving core principles.
- Reference to cybersecurity: Customer data protection and cybersecurity are addressed under ESRS S4 – Consumers and End-Users.
- Corporate culture governance: While no quantitative targets are set yet, the Group enforces the Code of Ethics and Internal Code through ongoing compulsory training, accessible in multiple languages and delivery modes (digital and classroom), across all Group entities including the International Banks Division.
- Training enforcement: Mechanisms tied to the incentive system address non-compliance with mandatory training deadlines. Courses on Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Corruption Risk, and Whistleblowing are regularly updated.
- Development of ethics framework: The Code of Ethics was created using context analysis, external benchmarking, and broad internal involvement (Sustainability Managers, Governance Functions, Business Divisions).
- Anti-corruption policy framework: Guided by integrity principles and aligned with the Code of Ethics, Internal Code, and Model 231, the Group’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines define zero tolerance, roles, responsibilities, macro-processes, and compliance with applicable regulations.
- High-risk areas for corruption: Gifts/entertainment, charitable donations/sponsorships, third-party relationships (including suppliers), acquisition/management/disposal of equity investments and other assets, staff hiring, and real estate transactions.
- Monitoring and controls: Ongoing activities include legal framework analysis, risk assessment, first- and second-level controls, verification of guideline implementation, and quality assurance to maintain stakeholder trust and transparency.

nodes.title: Policies related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.heading: 5.1.3.1 Policies related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.start_phrase: The Group carries out its activities with the aim of providing banking and financial services to its customers in compliance with the value of integrity, which in turn is embodied in the principles of professionalism, diligence, honesty, fairness and responsibility, and in accordance with the values and restrictions contained in the “Code of Ethics”, the “Group Internal Code of Conduct” and the “Organisational, Management and Control Model” adopted pursuant to Legislative Decree 231/2001.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and conduct: The Group’s Internal Code of Conduct and Code of Ethics set essential rules for all personnel, management, non-employee advisors, agents, external collaborators, and interns. The Chief People & Culture Officer Area updates the Internal Code, with approval by the Risks and Sustainability Committee and the Board. Subsidiaries must adopt the Code (with possible stricter or specific additions subject to Parent approval); foreign branches may adapt it to local regulations. The Code is publicly available.
- Cybersecurity: Customer data protection is managed under ESRS S4 – Consumers and End-Users.
- Corporate culture: While no quantitative targets are set, the Group ensures implementation of the Codes through ongoing mandatory training (digital and classroom, multilingual) for all personnel, including IBD banks. Training covers Code of Ethics, Internal Code of Conduct, Corruption Risk, and Whistleblowing, is regularly updated, and linked to incentive mechanisms for timely completion.
- Anti-corruption policy: The Group Anti-Corruption Guidelines define principles, roles, responsibilities, and macro-processes, adopting a zero-tolerance approach across all Group companies and countries, and extending to third parties (suppliers, agents, consultants, partners, etc.). High-risk areas include gifts/entertainment, donations/sponsorships, third-party relationships, investments/assets, hiring, and real estate. Guidelines are approved by Corporate Bodies and overseen by the Chief Compliance Officer Governance Area.
- Monitoring and controls: Ongoing legal monitoring, risk assessment, first- and second-level controls, implementation verification, and quality assurance. Transactions executed on client instruction are monitored via AML/CFT systems (Legislative Decree 231/2007).
- Reporting and whistleblowing: Personnel must report violations to supervisors, who forward to the Anti-Corruption Officer and internal audit; internal whistleblowing channels are also available. Group rules and Model 231/2001 ensure confidentiality and protection from retaliation.
- International standards and certification: Alignment with OECD, UN (including Global Compact), and Council of Europe anti-corruption conventions. The Group holds ISO 37001:2016 anti-corruption certification (valid to 2025), with renewal planned in 2025.
- Targets: No specific quantitative targets for corporate culture or anti-corruption yet; robust controls are in place to ensure ethical, compliant operations.
- Actions and methodology: Annual review of the Anti-Corruption Guidelines (latest update in 2024); updated rules on gifts and entertainment; action plans to meet ISO certification recommendations. A qualitative-quantitative risk model assesses inherent risk (seven factors plus geography) and organizational vulnerability (thirteen categories) using questionnaires and indicators (e.g., training completion). Semiannual audits by Compliance include level-one and level-two checks.

nodes.title: Targets related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.heading: 5.1.3.2 Targets related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.start_phrase: As reported in the paragraphs in this section, the Intesa Sanpaolo Group has implemented a number of policies and actions to monitor corruption topics, including an anti -corruption policy and dedicated assessments in the ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing processes, carried out on the portfolio, for social and governance topics, although it has not yet established specific quantitative targets in this governance area.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s anti-corruption and AML/CFT framework within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement.
- Anti-Corruption Guidelines apply to corporate officers, all personnel, and Group companies in all countries (excluding entities offering only ancillary or research services), and extend to third parties (suppliers, agents, consultants, partners, etc.); they are publicly available and shared when formalizing relationships, including with sponsorship/charity beneficiaries.
- Governance: Guidelines approved by Corporate Bodies; oversight by the Chief Compliance Officer Governance Area.
- Reporting: staff must promptly report suspected breaches to supervisors, who escalate to the Company’s Anti-Corruption Officer and internal audit; internal whistleblowing channels are available.
- Protection: internal reporting systems and the Organisational, Management and Control Model under Legislative Decree 231/2001 ensure confidentiality and protection from retaliation.
- International alignment: approach based on OECD, UN, and Council of Europe anti-corruption conventions and the UN Global Compact; Group holds UNI ISO 37001:2016 certification (valid until 2025) with renewal planned in 2025.
- Targets: while no quantitative anti-corruption targets are set, the Group implements policies, controls, and ESG & Reputational Risk Clearing assessments to prevent corruption and ensure ethical, compliant conduct.
- Ongoing actions: annual review of the Anti-Corruption Guidelines (last Board-approved in 2024), updates to gifts and entertainment rules, and implementation of ISO 37001 certification body recommendations.
- Risk assessment model: qualitative-quantitative evaluation of residual risk combining inherent risk (seven risk factors plus geography, using quantitative indicators like third-party order values) and organizational/control vulnerability (13 categories via qualitative questionnaires and quantitative mitigation indicators such as training completion).
- Audits: semiannual audits on higher-risk areas by the Chief Compliance Officer Area, including level 1 checks (enhanced due diligence) and level 2 checks.
- AML/CFT: monitoring of transactions executed on customer instructions through systems designed to manage money laundering and terrorist financing risks in line with Legislative Decree 231/2007.

nodes.title: Actions related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.heading: 5.1.3.3 Actions related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.start_phrase: The main actions implemented in the area of corruption prevention consist of the constant revision of the “Group Anti -Corruption Guidelines” (last update approved by the Board of Directors in 2024), the updating of the rules on the management of gifts and entertainment expenses, and the planning of compliance with the recommendations of the certification body for ISO 37001:2016.
nodes.summary:

  - Apply to all corporate officers, employees, Group companies, countries of operation, and relevant third parties (suppliers, agents, consultants, partners), excluding entities offering only ancillary or research services.

  - Approved by Corporate Bodies; supervised by the Chief Compliance Officer Governance Area; violations reported to supervisors, the Corporate Anti-Corruption Officer, and Internal Audit, with whistleblowing channels also available.

- Standards and certifications:

- Actions and risk assessment:

  - Risk assessment model combines inherent risk (seven risk factors plus geography with quantitative indicators) and organizational/control vulnerability (thirteen categories via qualitative questionnaire and quantitative indicators, e.g., training completion).

  - Governed by Group rules under the Chief Audit Officer Area; accessible to employees, former workers, collaborators, suppliers’ workers, freelancers, consultants, volunteers, trainees, shareholder individuals, and persons with administrative/control/supervisory roles.
  - 24/7 multilingual channels (email/voice) on website and intranet; confidentiality and anti-retaliation protections ensured; whistleblower identity restricted to authorized personnel.

nodes.title: Metrics related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.heading: 5.1.3.4 Metrics related to the prevention of corruption
nodes.start_phrase: There have been no convictions and/or penalties for violations of anti -corruption and anti -extortion laws; consequently no fines or sanctions have been imposed on the Intesa Sanpaolo Group.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and reporting: The Chief Audit Officer, independent from audited structures, must promptly inform the Corporate Anti-Corruption Officer of suspected unlawful conduct and take appropriate actions. Anti-corruption reporting is integrated into the Chief Compliance Officer Area’s information flows, with annual risk identification/assessment and management planning, and semi-annual updates on activities, issues, and remedies.

- Anti-corruption training: Mandatory, traceable training for officers and staff strengthens understanding of the legal framework and corporate Guidelines. Updates are provided when Guidelines change, primarily via digital delivery; non-attendance impacts the Broad-based Short-Term Plan (PVR). Content covers group-wide rules and business unit-specific processes; 100% of structures in higher-risk sensitive areas are trained.

- “Tone from the Top”: Annual online training for top management, including induction for the parent company’s Board of Directors and a program for corporate bodies and top management of Italian/international subsidiaries and the foreign perimeter, promoting honesty, integrity, and lawfulness.

- Metrics: No convictions, penalties, fines, or sanctions for anti-corruption or anti-extortion violations within the Group.

- Whistleblowing framework: An internal system covers violations of national/EU regulations affecting the public interest or Group integrity, as well as breaches of internal policies/procedures (e.g., Legislative Decree 231/01, banking rules, conflicts of interest). Rules, overseen by the Chief Audit Officer Area, are available on the intranet, with a summary on the public website.

- Eligibility and channels: Reports can be made by current/former employees, collaborators, third-party workers, freelancers/consultants, volunteers, trainees, individual shareholders, and persons with administrative/control/supervisory/representative roles. 24/7 channels (email and voice messaging) are accessible via the website and intranet in Italian, English, or the local language.

- Protections: Confidentiality of the report and whistleblower identity is safeguarded and shared only with authorization or the whistleblower’s consent. Whistleblowers are protected against retaliation, including attempts or threats.

- Oversight of whistleblowing: The Chief Audit Officer heads whistleblowing systems for the Parent Company and Service Companies, is appointed by the Board of Directors, and is supported by a Delegated Manager and a dedicated team.

nodes.title: Whistleblowing policies, targets and actions
nodes.heading: 5.1.4 Whistleblowing policies, targets and actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has an internal whistleblowing system relating to both national and European regulations which harm the public interest or the integrity of Intesa Sanpaolo and the Group Companies (for example: administrative, accounting, civil or criminal offences; unlawful conduct pursuant to Legislative Decree no. 231/01; rules governing banking activities; conduct giving rise to conflicts of interest) or relating to internal company policies and/or procedures, which the whistleblower has discovered in the work context.
nodes.summary:
- Anti-corruption governance and reporting: The Chief Audit Officer, independent from audited structures, must promptly inform the Corporate Anti-Corruption Officer of suspected unlawful conduct and take appropriate action. Anti-corruption reporting is integrated into periodic reports by the Chief Compliance Officer Area under the Regulation on Integrated Internal Control Systems, with annual risk identification/assessment/action planning and semi-annual activity/issues/remedies updates.
- Mandatory anti-corruption training: Compulsory, traceable, and primarily digital, aligned with the Anti-Corruption Guidelines and business unit operations; updated upon significant guideline revisions. Non-attendance affects the Broad-based Short-Term Plan (PVR). Coverage includes 100% of structures in higher-risk sensitive areas.
- Leadership “Tone from the Top”: Annual online sessions including induction for the parent company’s Board and a programme for board members and top management across Italian and international subsidiaries, promoting honesty, integrity, and lawfulness.
- Metrics: No convictions, penalties, fines, or sanctions for anti-corruption or anti-extortion violations within the Group.
- Whistleblowing framework: Group-wide internal system for reporting violations of national/EU regulations or internal policies that affect the public interest or Group integrity (e.g., administrative, accounting, civil/criminal offenses, Legislative Decree 231/01, banking rules, conflicts of interest). Rules managed by the Chief Audit Officer Area; full policy on the intranet with a public summary on the website.
- Eligible reporters and channels: Accessible to current/former employees, contract workers, suppliers’ workers, freelancers/consultants, volunteers, trainees, natural-person shareholders, and individuals with administrative/control/supervisory/representative roles. 24/7 email and voice channels available on the website and intranet, in Italian, English, or local languages.
- Safeguards and oversight: Confidentiality of information and whistleblower identity (disclosed only with consent), and protection from retaliation or discrimination, including attempts or threats. The Chief Audit Officer (appointed by the Board) leads the whistleblowing system, supported by a Delegated Manager and a dedicated team.

nodes.title: Whistleblowing policies
nodes.heading: 5.1.4.1 Whistleblowing policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has an internal whistleblowing system relating to both national and European regulations which harm the public interest or the integrity of Intesa Sanpaolo and the Group Companies (for example: administrative, accounting, civil or criminal offences; unlawful conduct pursuant to Legislative Decree no. 231/01; rules governing banking activities; conduct giving rise to conflicts of interest) or relating to internal company policies and/or procedures, which the whistleblower has discovered in the work context.

- Whistleblowing targets and actions: formal rules and mandatory training; commitment to timely handling and protection without quantitative KPIs; 2024 delivery of tailored mandatory courses (Italy, Insurance, selected international branches) and specialized training per Legislative Decree 24/2023 for report-handling staff; about 73,000 employees trained.

nodes.title: Targets related to Whistleblowing

nodes.title: Supply chain management metrics

nodes.title: Policies, targets and actions related to political engagement and lobbying activities

nodes.summary:
- Supplier ESG oversight: Target to complete ESG propensity assessments of all active suppliers by 2025, supported by webinars on “workers in the value chain” for suppliers using the Group Supplier Portal.
- Procurement Code of Conduct: To be adopted in 2025, distributed via the Supplier Portal, and required to be shared by suppliers with all their workers; goal of full acceptance by suppliers impacting “green” and “social” categories by 2028. The Code will be a mandatory-read document at supplier registration.
- Supply chain payment performance: In 2024 the Group averaged 10 business days from the start of the contractual/legal term to actual payment. Standard terms are negotiated; for Intesa Sanpaolo and Isybank the default is 60 days unless otherwise specified. No legal proceedings for late payments. Metrics refer to suppliers on the Parent Company’s procurement platform, primarily Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. and Isybank S.p.A., covering most invoice volume.
- Political engagement and lobbying policy: No donations or sponsorships to political parties/movements per Anticorruption Guidelines. The only allowable new loan type is an advance on the annual “2x1000 contribution,” subject to Board approval; none were granted in 2024.
- Governance of institutional relations: A structured internal regulatory system ensures compliant, coordinated, transparent engagement with legislative, regulatory, and supervisory bodies to protect corporate interests and strategic positioning.
- Interaction model with authorities: Defined roles include “pivot structures” at the Parent Company to centralize and coordinate communications (e.g., Institutional Affairs for antitrust matters) and “functional owners” engaged by topic to manage content and identify risk mitigation/opportunities. Rules apply Group-wide with limited exceptions.
- Alignment with external standards: Internal regulations adhere to ECB, European Commission, and Financial Stability Board standards, and are shaped by the needs of consumers, regulators, market partners, and other stakeholders.

nodes.title: Policies on political engagement and lobbying activities
nodes.heading: 5.1.6.1 Policies on political engagement and lobbying activities
nodes.start_phrase: The Intesa Sanpaolo Group’s internal policies provide that political parties and movements may not be recipients of donations and sponsorships, as set out in the Group’s “Anticorruption Guidelines” in the section “Policies related to the prevention of corruption”.
nodes.summary:
- Supplier ESG management: By 2025, the Group aims to complete an overall ESG propensity assessment of active suppliers and will deliver webinars on “workers in the value chain” via the Supplier Portal. A Procurement Code of Conduct will be adopted in 2025, required to be disseminated by suppliers to all workers, published on the Supplier Portal, and accepted by all suppliers impacting “green” and “social” categories by 2028.
- Supply chain metrics: In 2024, average payment time was 10 business days from the start of contractual/legal terms to actual payment. Payment practices are contract-based; for Intesa Sanpaolo and Isybank the standard term is typically 60 days. No legal proceedings for late payments occurred. Metrics are based on suppliers managed through the Parent Company’s procurement platform (Intesa Sanpaolo S.p.A. and Isybank S.p.A.), covering most Group invoice volumes.
- Political engagement and lobbying policies: No donations or sponsorships to political parties or movements; the only permissible new lending to political entities is Board-approved advances against Italy’s “2x1000” contributions—none granted in 2024. The Group maintains structured internal rules for interactions with supervisory, resolution, and regulatory authorities, using “pivot structures” to coordinate with authorities and “functional owners” for subject-matter input. Internal regulations align with ECB, European Commission, and Financial Stability Board standards and consider key stakeholder needs.
- Targets: No specific quantitative targets have been set for political engagement and lobbying.
- Actions: Proactive monitoring and advocacy on regulatory proposals affecting banking, finance, insurance, and the EU ESG framework, including collaboration with trade associations (e.g., ABI) and engagement with EU policymakers through the European Regulatory and Public Affairs unit to share best practices and technical insights.
- Metrics and transparency: As of 31 Dec 2024, no Director held a comparable public administration role in the prior two years. The Group is registered in the EU Transparency Register (code 24037141789-48).
- 2024 lobbying highlights (ESG-related): 
  - Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU) 2024/1275: supported building decarbonization, proposed adjustments to enable bank financing for upgrades.
  - Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU) 2024/1760: welcomed for reinforcing human rights and environmental due diligence; contributed via trade associations to address critical issues.
  - ESG Ratings Regulation (EU) 2024/3005: supported greater integrity and transparency of ESG ratings; responded to consultations and provided written inputs.
  - SFDR (EU) 2019/2088 referenced for sustainability-related disclosures.

  - Active regulatory monitoring and advocacy on banking, financial, insurance, and European ESG frameworks; collaboration with national/EU/international trade associations (e.g., ABI) and direct engagement with EU policymakers via the European Regulatory and Public Affairs unit.
  - Metrics: as of 31 Dec 2024 no Directors previously held comparable public administration roles in the prior two years; Group is registered in the EU Transparency Register (code 24037141789-48).
  - 2024 lobbying activity highlights:
    - ESG legislation: Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EU) 2024/1275; Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU) 2024/1760; ESG Ratings Regulation (EU) 2024/3005; SFDR review inputs; Environmental Delegated Act (EU) 2023/2486 with feedback on Green Asset Ratio methodology.
    - Non-ESG: CRR III (EU) 2024/1623 with advocacy on FRTB timing; Benchmark Regulation reform proposal; Retail Investment Strategy package (MiFID/IDD/UCITS/AIFMD/PRIIPs) with stance on inducements; CMDI framework proposals (SRMR/BRRD/DGSD) focusing on irrevocable payment commitments; securitisation framework review; Digital Euro proposal; Financial Data Access (open finance) proposal.

- ESRS-based disclosure index (Table of Contents)

  - People and workplace: retraining numbers; diversity metrics and targets (women in senior roles, new management positions); talent development participation; health and safety; adequate wages; equal pay and pay gap.
  - Customers: number of branches; complaint response times; NPS; fraud prevention outcomes; privacy incidents.
  - Communities: interventions under “Food and shelter for the needy.”

- Cross-references to other EU legislation
  - List of ESRS datapoints deriving from SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, and EU Climate Law, with page links.
  - Notes on non-material topics and items planned for reporting from 2025 onward.

- EU Taxonomy and banking KPIs (Annex I – Taxonomy Template)
  - Detailed Green Asset Ratio (GAR) templates for 2024 and 2023, covering:
    - On-balance sheet assets in numerator/denominator by counterparty type (financials, non-financials, households) and by environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, water, circular economy, pollution, biodiversity), including taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned splits and enabling/transitional activities.
    - Specific breakdowns for mortgages and building renovation loans.
    - Off-balance sheet exposures (financial guarantees; assets under management) with taxonomy-eligibility/alignment.
  - Separate GAR template focused on CapEx basis for 2024.

structure.title: Template 1: Assets for the calculation of GAR (CapEx)
structure.heading: 3.6.3 Template 1: Assets for the calculation of GAR (CapEx)
structure.summary:
The excerpt presents the bank’s EU Taxonomy disclosures within the Consolidated Sustainability Statement, focusing on the calculation of the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) for 2024 with 2023 comparatives. All figures are shown in millions of euro.

- Template 1 (Assets for the calculation of GAR): Comprehensive breakdown of “covered assets” included in both numerator and denominator by asset class and counterparty type, mapped to the six environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and Marine Resources, Circular Economy, Pollution Prevention and Control, Biodiversity and Ecosystems). For each objective it distinguishes:
  - Taxonomy-eligible vs Taxonomy-aligned exposures
  - Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities (where applicable)

- 2024 covered assets detail:
  - Loans and advances, debt securities and equity not held for trading: granular splits across financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations—investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings) and non-financial undertakings, with eligible/aligned amounts per environmental objective.
  - Households: 178,565 total; of which loans collateralised by residential immovable property 132,742 (taxonomy-eligible), with 13,615 taxonomy-aligned; building renovation loans 2,329.
  - Local government financing and collateral obtained (real estate) listed separately.
  - Assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator: 296,109; further breakdowns of exposures to SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD and non-EU counterparties.
  - Totals: Total GAR assets 565,941; assets not covered for GAR calculation 200,883 (including central governments and supranational issuers 115,121; central banks 44,297; trading book 41,465); total assets 766,824.

- 2023 comparative table mirrors the 2024 structure:
  - Total GAR assets 564,034; assets not covered for GAR calculation 235,295; total assets 799,329.
  - Households: 177,896 total; mortgages taxonomy-eligible 132,942 and aligned 9,923; building renovation loans 168.
  - Similar counterparty and asset-class splits, and numerator/denominator treatment.

- Off-balance sheet exposures (undertakings subject to NFRD):
  - Financial guarantees and assets under management (AuM), reported with taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts by objective, and “of which” splits for debt and equity instruments.
  - 2024 examples: financial guarantees 5,936; AuM 223,769 (with detailed eligible/aligned breakdowns and instrument splits).
  - 2023 comparatives provided on the same basis.

- Template 2 (GAR – Sector information, Turnover): NACE 4‑digit sectoral view for non-financial corporates (subject to NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD), showing gross carrying amounts and the share that is environmentally sustainable per objective, and in total. The excerpt lists several manufacturing activities (e.g., industrial gases, plastic packaging, bricks/tiles, cement, steel products, fabricated metal products, electronic components, computers, measuring instruments, electromedical equipment, electric motors and distribution apparatus) with the corresponding environmentally sustainable portions (e.g., industrial gases 25 total, 5 sustainable; plastic packing goods 1 total, 1 sustainable; bricks/tiles 25 total, 25 sustainable; cement 34 total, 5 sustainable; steel tubes/pipes 120 total, 112 sustainable; computers 14 total, 10 sustainable; instruments 19 total, 13 sustainable).

Overall, the section documents how the bank’s balance sheet and selected off-balance sheet items map to EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment across environmental objectives, the treatment of exposures in the GAR numerator and denominator, exclusions, and the sectoral distribution of sustainable activities.

structure.title: Template 2: GAR – Sector information (Turnover)
structure.heading: 3.6.4 Template 2: GAR – Sector information (Turnover)
structure.start_phrase: Breakdown by sector - NACE 4 digits level
structure.summary:
The excerpt is a section of a Consolidated Sustainability Statement presenting Template 2: GAR – Sector information for both Turnover and CapEx. It discloses the bank’s exposures by NACE Rev. 2 4‑digit sectors, showing gross carrying amounts and the portion that is environmentally sustainable under the EU Taxonomy across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO). Data are split between Non‑Financial Corporates subject to the NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD, with all figures in EUR millions and totals per sector.

Key features and observations:
- High granularity sectoral breakdown covering manufacturing, energy and utilities, construction, transport, ICT, real estate, engineering, and research.
- Turnover table highlights notable environmentally sustainable portions in several sectors, particularly:
  - Energy and utilities: electricity transmission (232/334), distribution (13/14), and production (30/48); gas distribution (65/99); water collection/treatment (5/6).
  - Manufacturing tied to low‑carbon technologies or efficiency: batteries (61/65), steel tubes (112/120), special‑purpose machinery (51/460), motor vehicles (56/245), baked clay products (25/25), cement (5/34), doors/windows (3/5), computers (10/14), measuring instruments (13/19), electrical equipment (various).
  - Construction and installations: development of building projects (186/318), plumbing/heat and air‑conditioning installation (200/240), electrical installation (29/33), rail construction (15/54), roads (17/93), bridges (11/13), residential/non‑residential buildings (76/92).
  - Transport: passenger rail (39/127), freight rail (21/21), pipelines (47/368), other passenger land transport (5/139).
  - Services and real estate: IT and research activities (e.g., programming 4/8; other IT 9/41; research 31/195), real estate buying/selling (39/173) and leasing (12/18).
- CapEx table mirrors the turnover structure and shows sustainable CapEx concentrated in basic materials and selected manufacturing: basic iron and steel (83/91), baked clay (26/27), plastic packaging (3/3), cement (10/37), concrete products (10/48), computers (7/16), measuring instruments (14/18), with many other sectors showing low or zero sustainable CapEx.
- Across both templates, the majority of environmentally sustainable amounts are associated with Non‑Financial Corporates subject to NFRD; SMEs/other NFC columns are often blank or minimal.

structure.title: Template 2: GAR – Sector information (CapEx)
structure.heading: 3.6.5 Template 2: GAR – Sector information (CapEx)
structure.start_phrase: Breakdown by sector - NACE 4 digits level
structure.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement presenting EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures. It includes Template 2 (GAR – Sector information on CapEx) and Template 3 (KPI GAR – Turnover stock) for 2024.

- Template 2 (Sector information – CapEx):
  - Provides a detailed NACE Rev.2 4‑digit breakdown of gross carrying amounts (EUR million) of exposures to non‑financial corporates, split between entities subject to NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - For each sector, shows “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts mapped to the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), plus the total across objectives.
  - Coverage spans manufacturing (e.g., industrial gases, tyres, plastics, bricks/tiles, cement, concrete, steel, electronics, batteries, machinery, motor vehicles, ships, rail stock, motorcycles), energy and utilities (electricity generation, transmission, distribution; gas manufacture/distribution; steam and air‑conditioning; water collection/treatment), waste management and recycling, construction and civil works (roads, railways, bridges, utilities; electrical/plumbing installations), transport services (passenger/freight rail, urban transport, pipelines, postal), telecom/IT services, real estate, engineering/R&D, and leasing.
  - Key highlights indicate concentrations of taxonomy‑aligned amounts in CCM, notably:
    - Electricity: Production (1,272; of which 1,223 sustainable), transmission (53; 34), distribution (557; 455).
    - Transport and infrastructure: Roads and motorways (335 total; with notable CCM and some CCA/CE), passenger rail (327; 232), freight rail (145; 33).
    - Manufacturing critical to the transition: Batteries (67; 66), basic iron and steel (91; 83), motor vehicles (464; 168).
    - Water supply (135; 101).
  - Minimal or no amounts reported under WTR, CE, PPC, and BIO for many sectors, underscoring a primary focus on CCM at this stage.

- Template 3 (KPI GAR – Turnover stock):
  - Reports the proportion of total assets covered by GAR and, within covered assets, the shares that fund taxonomy‑relevant sectors (taxonomy‑eligible) and those that are taxonomy‑aligned, by each environmental objective.
  - Identifies activity tags within aligned exposures (“Use of Proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling”).
  - Breaks down by product type (loans and advances; debt securities, including use‑of‑proceeds bonds; equity instruments) and counterparty type (financial undertakings, credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies).
  - Example indications: covered assets for credit institutions around 0.81% (0.59% loans; 0.22% debt securities), other financial corporations around 1.16%, and small aligned portions in debt securities via use‑of‑proceeds. The table aggregates total taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned proportions across objectives for 2024.

- The excerpt presents Template 3 KPI disclosures for the EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR), covering both Turnover stock and CapEx stock.

- Metrics shown include:
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR perimeter.
  - Taxonomy-eligible and Taxonomy-aligned shares across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Breakdowns by counterparty and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral obtained (immovable properties). Instruments include loans and advances, debt securities (including Use of Proceeds bonds), and equity.

- 2024 GAR (Turnover stock) highlights:
  - Overall GAR-covered assets and taxonomy-eligible shares increased versus 2023.

structure.summary:
- The excerpt is from a Consolidated Sustainability Statement reporting EU Taxonomy KPIs, focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- It presents Template 3 (GAR based on CapEx stock) for 2024 with a 2023 comparator, and Template 4 (GAR based on turnover/new origination flow) for 2024.
- Coverage spans the six EU environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), and Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
- Metrics disclosed include: proportion of total assets/new assets covered; proportions that are Taxonomy-eligible and Taxonomy-aligned per objective; and “of which” breakdowns for Use of Proceeds (UoP), transitional, and enabling activities.
- Breakdown by counterparty and instrument includes: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (notably mortgages and building renovation loans), local governments, and collateral obtained; and by product type (loans and advances, debt securities including UoP/green bonds, equity instruments).
- 2024 stock highlights: Total GAR assets covered are 28.45% of the denominator; Taxonomy-eligible shares by objective include approx. CCM 4.35%, CCA 2.43%, WTR 0.14%, CE 1.01%, PPC 0.08%, BIO 0.01%. Households dominate coverage (c. 23.99%), mainly mortgages (c. 23.45%); building renovation loans are a small but identified subset (c. 0.41%).
- Non-financial undertakings and financial undertakings contribute smaller eligible shares, largely within CCM and CE; UoP/green bond exposures are identified but limited; transitional and enabling activity shares are reported as minimal.
- Year-on-year (2023 to 2024) the stock shows broader coverage and higher eligibility: total covered GAR assets increase (c. 23.66% to 28.45%), with rises in eligibility across objectives (e.g., CCM from ~3.31% to ~4.35%; CCA from ~1.77% to ~2.43%; CE from ~0.84% to ~1.01%; WTR from ~0.05% to ~0.14%; PPC from ~0 to ~0.08%). Building renovation loans grow from ~0.03% to ~0.41%.
- 2024 turnover flow (new assets) indicates covered new business of ~32.67%, with Taxonomy-eligible portions concentrated in CCM (~8.11%) and CCA (~4.32%), and smaller shares in CE (~1.96%), WTR (~0.35%), PPC (~0.12%), and negligible BIO; eligibility is broken down across financial undertakings (including credit institutions and other financial corporations) with modest UoP components.
- Taxonomy-aligned figures are included in the templates but appear limited or not populated across many categories in the excerpt.

- KPI coverage: 60.14% of total AuM (excluding sovereigns), equal to 211,680.
- Taxonomy alignment: Weighted average taxonomy-aligned investments equal to 2.08% (turnover-based) and 3.37% (CapEx-based), corresponding to 4,402 and 7,127 respectively.
- Eligibility and alignment mix within covered assets:
  - Not taxonomy-eligible: 91.49% (turnover-based) / 90.26% (CapEx-based), amounts 193,676 / 191,069.
  - Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned: 6.43% / 6.37%, amounts 13,602 / 13,484.
- Counterparty and geography/regulatory breakdown of covered assets:
  - Derivatives: 0.84% (1,785).
  - EU undertakings not subject to Articles 19a/29a: non-financial 7.28% (15,400); financial 1.87% (3,963).
  - Non-EU undertakings not subject to Articles 19a/29a: non-financial 49.07% (103,861); financial 2.53% (5,362).
  - Undertakings subject to Articles 19a/29a: non-financial 13.52% (28,624); financial 11.52% (24,384).
  - Other counterparties/assets: 13.37% (28,301).
- Breakdown of taxonomy-aligned numerator:
  - Aligned exposures to undertakings subject to Articles 19a/29a:
    - Non-financial: 1.82% turnover-based (3,855); 3.07% CapEx-based (6,504).
    - Financial: 0.26% turnover-based (547); 0.30% CapEx-based (623).
  - Aligned exposures to other counterparties/assets: 0.00%.
- Environmental objectives allocation of aligned activities:
  - Climate change mitigation: 2.02% (turnover) / 3.22% (CapEx), including transitional 0.15%/0.21% and enabling 1.03%/1.47%.
  - Climate change adaptation: 0.06% (turnover) / 0.15% (CapEx), enabling 0.02%/0.06%.
  - Other objectives (water, circular economy, pollution, biodiversity): no reported aligned share.
